title: Graphene-enabled dynamic H-J switching of dipole-dipole coupling
summary: Environmental modification of dipole interactions has long been explored in energy transport. Here we consider the effects of a tunable graphene monolayer upon nearly H-type or J-type molecular aggregates, concentrating on the inversion of one type of coupling to the other. Modelling the graphene as being deposited on a metallic substrate, we find that as the surface conductivity of the graphene is varied, there is a corresponding change in the parameter region over which coupling inversion is predicted. This provides a route towards observing the predicted coupling inversion in a real system by dynamically changing the surface conductivity during a single run of an experiment.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates how a tunable graphene monolayer deposited on a metallic substrate can modulate dipole interactions in H-type or J-type molecular aggregates, specifically exploring the conversion (inversion) of one coupling type to the other. Varying the graphene's surface conductivity shifts the parameter region where coupling inversion occurs, offering a path to experimentally observe this inversion dynamically in real-time.
AI.motivation: Coupling inversion between H-type and J-type molecular aggregates is a theoretically predicted phenomenon that has been difficult to observe experimentally. The authors aim to provide a practical, dynamic route to realize and observe this coupling inversion in a realistic system using graphene's tunable surface conductivity.
AI.method: The authors model graphene deposited on a metallic substrate interacting with nearly H-type or J-type molecular aggregates. They analyze how varying the graphene's surface conductivity changes the dipole interaction environment and thereby modifies the parameter region over which coupling inversion is predicted to occur.
AI.result: As the surface conductivity of the graphene is varied, the parameter region over which coupling inversion (H to J or J to H) is predicted changes correspondingly.
AI.conclusion: Dynamically varying the graphene surface conductivity during a single experimental run provides a feasible route to observe the predicted coupling inversion in a real physical system.

title: A Unified Description of Dirac-Cone Anisotropies in Two Dimensions
summary: Anisotropies in two-dimensional materials are responsible for a variety of effects that significantly modify their physical properties. In this paper, we present a covariant modification of the Dirac equation that incorporates anisotropies into the effective low-energy description around the Dirac point. The model is constructed by analogy with a Lorentz-violating extension of the Standard Model of elementary particles and yields a (2+1)-dimensional framework describing physical effects such as shifted, tilted, and distorted Dirac cones through its free parameters. The proposed model thus provides a general and unified framework in which distinct anisotropy-induced modifications of the Dirac spectrum and their combinations can be systematically characterized. We further apply the model to strained graphene and show that its effective parameters can be quantitatively extracted from first-principles electronic band structures while retaining a direct geometrical interpretation. These results establish a connection between the microscopic electronic structure and a material-independent effective description of anisotropic two-dimensional Dirac systems.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a covariant modification of the Dirac equation, constructed by analogy with Lorentz-violating extensions of the Standard Model, to incorporate anisotropies into the effective low-energy description of 2D materials around the Dirac point. The model provides a unified framework describing shifted, tilted, and distorted Dirac cones through free parameters with geometrical interpretation, and is validated by extracting effective parameters from first-principles band structures of strained graphene.
AI.motivation: Anisotropies in two-dimensional materials significantly modify their physical properties, yet existing descriptions of these effects lack a unified, general framework. The authors seek a systematic way to characterize distinct anisotropy-induced modifications of the Dirac spectrum, including shifts, tilts, and distortions, within a single covariant formalism.
AI.method: The Dirac equation is covariantly modified by analogy with a Lorentz-violating extension of the Standard Model of elementary particles, yielding a (2+1)-dimensional framework. The model's free parameters encode shifted, tilted, and distorted Dirac cones. The approach is applied to strained graphene, where effective parameters are quantitatively extracted from first-principles electronic band structures while maintaining a direct geometrical interpretation.
AI.result: The model successfully provides a general and unified framework capable of systematically characterizing distinct and combined anisotropy-induced modifications of the Dirac spectrum. Application to strained graphene demonstrates that the effective parameters can be quantitatively extracted from first-principles band structures, establishing a connection between microscopic electronic structure and a material-independent effective description.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework bridges microscopic electronic structure calculations and a material-independent effective description of anisotropic two-dimensional Dirac systems, offering a powerful and general tool for studying anisotropy effects in 2D materials.

title: Tuning Andreev reflection and conductance in proximitized nanowires through the spin-orbit field direction
summary: We investigate the Andreev reflection (AR) and the nonlinear conductance in a normal-superconductor junction realized with a proximitized semiconductor nanowire exposed to a magnetic field along its axis. We show that, while at zero energy the AR coefficient is determined by the topological phase of the superconducting side of the junction, at finite energy the AR is strongly affected by the directions of the Rashba spin-orbit field characterizing the normal and the proximitized sides. The tunability of the AR and the nonlinear conductance as a function of the spin-orbit misalignment angle is particularly pronounced when the proximitized side is in the topologically trivial phase. The spin-orbit field direction is revealed to be an efficient knob to control the electron transport through the hybrid junction, realizing an electrically widely tunable device. The implementation in realistic setups is discussed.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes Andreev reflection and nonlinear conductance in a normal-superconductor junction based on a proximitized semiconductor nanowire under an axial magnetic field, showing that finite-energy AR depends strongly on the Rashba spin-orbit field directions of both sides, with the misalignment angle serving as an efficient electrical control knob—especially pronounced in the topologically trivial phase.
AI.motivation: To understand how Rashba spin-orbit field alignment affects Andreev reflection and transport in hybrid normal-superconductor nanowire junctions, and to explore the spin-orbit direction as a tunable parameter for device control.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis of Andreev reflection coefficients and nonlinear conductance in a normal-superconductor junction formed by a proximitized semiconductor nanowire in an axial magnetic field, examining the dependence on the relative direction of Rashba spin-orbit fields between the normal and superconducting sides.
AI.result: At zero energy the AR coefficient is governed by the topological phase of the superconductor, while at finite energy AR is strongly affected by the mutual orientation of the Rashba spin-orbit fields. The spin-orbit misalignment effect on AR and nonlinear conductance is most pronounced when the superconducting side is topologically trivial, making the spin-orbit direction a powerful transport control knob.
AI.conclusion: The relative Rashba spin-orbit field direction provides an efficient and electrically tunable mechanism to control electron transport through such hybrid junctions, with practical implementation in realistic devices being feasible.

title: Flux noise without flux tunability in superconducting qubits
summary: Flux noise is unanimously recognised as a leading dephasing mechanism for flux-tunable superconducting qubits. However, our microscopic understanding remains incomplete, and basic effects like Faraday's law of induction have only very recently come into focus. Based on a quantum geometric description of the Faraday effect, we provide an in-depth derivation of the coupling of generic magnetic sources to thin film superconducting structures, under appropriate consideration of the device geometry. We apply the resulting framework to time-varying magnetic dipoles, describing surface or substrate spins, as well as current-carrying flux lines. We show that flux noise not only affects dephasing, but also provides a fundamental limit for the qubit quality factor - notably, even when the qubit contains no loops and is thus nominally not flux-tunable. Assuming surface spins as the origin for universal flux noise, we expect that this quality factor limit might be reached in the near term. For flux lines, we formulate a minimal safety distance to conserve the qubit performance, potentially constraining the scale-up of quantum hardware. This distance is boosted in the presence of large capacitor wings typical for transmons, due to a lensing of the electromotive field which is largely independent of Meissner screening.

AI.tldr: This paper derives a quantum geometric description of the Faraday effect to model how generic magnetic sources couple to thin film superconducting structures, and shows that flux noise not only causes dephasing but also fundamentally limits qubit quality factor, even for qubits without flux-tunable loops. It formulates safety distances for flux lines and reveals that transmon capacitor wings create an electromotive field lensing effect that boosts this distance.
AI.motivation: Flux noise is a leading dephasing mechanism for flux-tunable superconducting qubits, yet its microscopic understanding is incomplete. Basic effects such as Faraday's law of induction have only recently come into focus, motivating a deeper theoretical framework to understand and mitigate these noise sources.
AI.method: The authors use a quantum geometric description of the Faraday effect to derive the coupling of generic magnetic sources to thin film superconducting structures, carefully accounting for device geometry. The framework is applied to time-varying magnetic dipoles (surface/substrate spins) and current-carrying flux lines.
AI.result: Flux noise imposes a fundamental limit on qubit quality factor even for nominally non-flux-tunable qubits without loops. Assuming surface spins as the origin of universal flux noise, this quality factor limit may be reached in the near term. For flux lines, a minimal safety distance is formulated to preserve qubit performance; this distance is enhanced by large transmon capacitor wings due to an electromotive field lensing effect largely independent of Meissner screening, potentially constraining the scale-up of quantum hardware.
AI.conclusion: The developed framework provides a comprehensive microscopic understanding of flux noise coupling to thin film superconducting qubits, revealing additional fundamental limits on qubit quality and practical constraints on hardware scaling, with implications for future device design and control-line layout.

title: The Greedy Bump Bias: Local Profiling Geometry and the Look-Elsewhere Effect
summary: When fitting a localized signal whose position or shape is not known in advance, one typically allows these parameters to vary together with the signal amplitude and chooses the values that maximize the likelihood. This freedom has two related statistical consequences. If a genuine signal is present, its fitted amplitude will be affected by a positive bias; otherwise, the same freedom increases the chance of finding an unusually signal-like background fluctuation, giving rise to the look-elsewhere effect. We show that these two effects can be understood as consequences of the same local geometry of the family of signal templates. We study this connection in a Gaussian matched-filter model, where a smooth D-dimensional family of normalized templates describes the unknown signal location or shape. In the normalized matched-filter problem, the curvature of a genuine signal peak and the fluctuations that determine the curvature of a high background peak are governed by the same template metric. This allows us to derive an explicit asymptotic relation. We then follow the problem away from the strong-signal and high-threshold limits. Separating the signal-associated maximum from the best competing maximum gives an exact decomposition of the global bias into a local profiling contribution and a contribution from remote-peak competition. In a one-dimensional Gaussian example, the second factorial cumulant accounts for most of this correction, while the third brings the prediction into close agreement with simulation. A two-point Kac--Rice calculation reproduces the second cumulant and reveals a quartic short-distance suppression of nearby maxima. The resulting picture separates the roles of local dimension, model-dependent curvature, and global extremal competition within a common framework.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that the positive amplitude bias of genuine signals and the look-elsewhere effect from background fluctuations are two manifestations of the same local geometric property—the template metric—in Gaussian matched-filter models. The authors derive an asymptotic relation between signal peak curvature and background peak curvature fluctuations, and develop an exact decomposition of the global bias into local profiling and remote-peak competition contributions using factorial cumulants and Kac–Rice calculations.
AI.motivation: When fitting a localized signal with unknown position or shape parameters that are profiled (maximized over), two related statistical issues arise: genuine signals exhibit a positive amplitude bias, and background fluctuations more readily produce signal-like artifacts (the look-elsewhere effect). The authors aim to show both effects share a common geometric origin and can be understood within a unified framework.
AI.method: The analysis is conducted in a Gaussian matched-filter model with a smooth D-dimensional family of normalized templates. The authors study the template metric governing curvature, derive an explicit asymptotic relation between signal peak curvature and background peak curvature fluctuations, then go beyond strong-signal/high-threshold limits by separating the signal-associated maximum from the best competing maximum. This yields an exact decomposition of global bias into local profiling and remote-peak competition terms. A one-dimensional Gaussian example is analyzed using factorial cumulants, and a two-point Kac–Rice calculation reproduces the second cumulant and reveals quartic short-distance suppression of nearby maxima.
AI.result: The authors establish that both the positive bias in fitted amplitude of genuine signals and the look-elsewhere effect are governed by the same template metric. The exact decomposition into local profiling and remote-peak competition is derived. In the 1D Gaussian example, the second factorial cumulant accounts for most of the correction while the third brings predictions into close agreement with simulation. The two-point Kac–Rice calculation reproduces the second cumulant and reveals quartic short-distance suppression of nearby maxima.
AI.conclusion: The framework separates the roles of local dimension, model-dependent curvature, and global extremal competition, providing a common understanding of amplitude bias and the look-elsewhere effect in matched-filter problems. This geometric perspective unifies previously disparate statistical corrections.

title: Scaling Neural Network Quantum States for Ab Initio Quantum Chemistry
summary: Neural-network quantum states (NNQSs) can represent many-electron wave functions without explicitly enumerating the determinant space, but their accuracy depends jointly on model size and variational-optimization effort. Here we characterize this dependence for a physics-conditioned autoregressive NNQS trained separately on two six-molecule source benchmarks. Across eight model sizes and five optimization milestones, we find that model size and optimization steps jointly shape the energy error. The capacity advantage of larger models becomes more apparent with sufficient optimization, while the returns from additional optimization vary with model size. We capture this coupling using an interaction scaling law and quantify the cumulative compute of each evaluated configuration. The resulting error-compute Pareto frontiers provide a practical decision rule for jointly selecting model size and optimization steps under a given compute budget within the evaluated range. Furthermore, we find that this beneficial scaling trend persists during fine-tuning on held-out N$_2$. Pretrained models show decreasing error with increasing model size, with a steeper reduction following pretraining on the Hard benchmark. Together, these results place autoregressive neural quantum states within the broader landscape of empirical neural scaling and open a quantitative route toward the systematic scaling of neural quantum solvers for ab initio quantum chemistry.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how model size and variational-optimization effort jointly affect the accuracy of physics-conditioned autoregressive neural-network quantum states (NNQS) for molecular wave functions, revealing an interaction scaling law and error-compute Pareto frontiers that guide joint selection of model size and optimization steps under compute budgets. Fine-tuning on held-out N₂ shows beneficial scaling persists, with steeper error reduction after pretraining on a harder benchmark.
AI.motivation: NNQS accuracy depends jointly on model size and optimization effort, but this coupled dependence is not well characterized. Understanding this interaction is necessary for systematically scaling neural quantum solvers for ab initio quantum chemistry under practical compute constraints.
AI.method: Train a physics-conditioned autoregressive NNQS on two six-molecule source benchmarks across eight model sizes and five optimization milestones. Fit an interaction scaling law capturing the coupled effects of model capacity and optimization steps, and quantify cumulative compute per configuration to construct error-compute Pareto frontiers. Additionally, fine-tune on held-out N₂ to test generalization of the scaling trend.
AI.result: Model size and optimization steps jointly shape energy error, with larger models gaining clearer advantage as optimization progresses and optimization returns depending on model size. The interaction scaling law captures this coupling, and error-compute Pareto frontiers offer a decision rule for resource allocation. Fine-tuning on N₂ preserves the scaling trend, with steeper error reduction after pretraining on the Hard benchmark.
AI.conclusion: The findings place autoregressive NNQS within the broader empirical neural-scaling landscape and open a quantitative path toward systematic scaling of neural quantum solvers for ab initio quantum chemistry.

title: Classical dipolar Heisenberg models on the Archimedean and Laves lattices
summary: We study classical Heisenberg spins interacting through the dipole--dipole interaction on the eleven Archimedean and eight Laves planar lattices at canonical geometry, which reduce to fifteen distinct vertex sets. For each lattice we compute the Fourier-space interaction matrix $\Am(\bk)$, extract the Luttinger--Tisza ordering wave vector $\bk_{0}$, determine the classical ground state by unconstrained minimization on the commensurate magnetic cell, and evaluate the linearized spin-wave dispersion $\varepsilon_{i}(\bk)$ along the high-symmetry path of the (magnetic) Brillouin zone together with the Holstein--Primakoff moment reduction. The ground states fall into three classes: five are collinear, two are non-collinear at angles commensurate with the lattice symmetry, and eight cant at transcendental angles, which we determine to thirty digits. Across the family, failure of the Luttinger--Tisza strong condition coincides exactly with the appearance of incommensurate canting, with no exceptions in either direction. Truncating the interaction range shows that whether a lattice cants is fixed by the local coordination geometry, whereas the value of the canting angle is set by the long-range tail. The quantum corrections are governed by the magnon spectrum through the size of the magnetic basis and are uncorrelated with frustration, so that the frustration and fluctuation classifications are independent; the corner-sharing lattices host the narrowest low-energy branches. The results constitute a spectral atlas of dipolar Heisenberg systems on the full family of $1$-uniform planar tilings and their duals, and provide predictions for inelastic neutron scattering in materials whose magnetic ions occupy Archimedean or Laves lattices, and for artificial arrays of dipolar-coupled nanomagnets.

AI.tldr: This paper studies classical Heisenberg spins with dipole-dipole interactions on all eleven Archimedean and eight Laves planar lattices (fifteen distinct vertex sets). The authors compute Fourier interaction matrices, Luttinger-Tisza ordering wave vectors, ground states via unconstrained minimization, and spin-wave spectra. Ground states fall into three classes: five collinear, two non-collinear at commensurate angles, and eight canted at transcendental angles. Failure of the Luttinger-Tisza strong condition exactly coincides with incommensurate canting. Whether a lattice cants is fixed by local coordination, while the canting angle is set by the long-range tail. Quantum corrections correlate with magnetic basis size, not frustration.
AI.motivation: To provide a comprehensive spectral atlas of dipolar Heisenberg systems across the complete family of 1-uniform planar tilings (Archimedean lattices) and their duals (Laves lattices), establishing systematic classifications of ground-state order, canting behavior, and frustration effects.
AI.method: For each of the fifteen distinct vertex-set lattices, the authors compute the Fourier-space interaction matrix A(k), extract the Luttinger-Tisza ordering wave vector k0, determine ground states by unconstrained minimization on the commensurate magnetic cell, and compute linearized spin-wave dispersions along high-symmetry Brillouin-zone paths with Holstein-Primakoff moment reduction. They also test truncation of interaction range to separate local coordination from long-range effects.
AI.result: Ground states partition into five collinear, two commensurate non-collinear, and eight transcendentally canted configurations (angles determined to 30 digits). Luttinger-Tisza strong condition failure exactly matches incommensurate canting. Local coordination governs whether canting occurs; long-range tail sets the canting angle. Corner-sharing lattices host the narrowest low-energy magnon branches. Quantum fluctuations correlate with magnetic basis size, not frustration.
AI.conclusion: The study delivers a complete spectral atlas of dipolar Heisenberg magnets on Archimedean and Laves lattices, establishing the independence of frustration and fluctuation classifications, and providing direct predictions for inelastic neutron scattering experiments and artificial dipolar nanomagnet arrays.

title: Spectral properties of deterministic matrices multiplied by rotationally invariant random non-Hermitian ensembles
summary: In this paper, we study spectral properties of multiplicative deformations of non-Hermitian random matrices. We consider matrices of the form $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}$, where $\mathbf{A}$ is a deterministic $N\times N$ matrix (not necessarily Hermitian) and $\mathbf{B}$ is a rotationally invariant random matrix. We show that, as $N\to\infty$, the boundary of the complex eigenvalue distribution of $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}$ is governed by simple equations involving the $\mathcal{R}_1$ and $\mathcal{R}_2$ transforms of $\mathbf{B}$.

AI.tldr: The paper studies the spectral properties of multiplicative deformations of non-Hermitian random matrices of the form AB, where A is a deterministic matrix and B is a rotationally invariant random matrix. As N→∞, the boundary of the complex eigenvalue distribution is governed by simple equations involving the R₁ and R₂ transforms of B.
AI.motivation: To understand how multiplying a deterministic (possibly non-Hermitian) matrix by a rotationally invariant random matrix affects the limiting spectral distribution, particularly the boundary of the complex eigenvalue support, and to characterize this boundary in terms of free probability transforms.
AI.method: The approach involves studying multiplicative deformations of non-Hermitian random matrices, where A is deterministic non-Hermitian and B is rotationally invariant. The analysis connects the boundary of the complex eigenvalue distribution to simple equations involving the R₁ and R₂ transforms of B in the large-N limit.
AI.result: It is shown that, as N→∞, the boundary of the complex eigenvalue distribution of AB is governed by simple closed-form equations expressed through the R₁ and R₂ transforms of the random matrix B.
AI.conclusion: The complex eigenvalue boundary of multiplicative deformations of non-Hermitian matrices admits a tractable description via R-diagonal free probability transforms, providing a clean characterization of the limiting spectrum.

title: Valley polarization dependence of candidate even-denominator fractional quantum Hall states in monolayer graphene
summary: We investigate even-denominator fractional quantum Hall (EDFQH) states in monolayer graphene, focusing on the experimentally observed filling fractions $ν= 1/2$ and $ν= 1/4$. Owing to the approximate SU(4) symmetry arising from spin and valley degrees of freedom, graphene hosts a rich variety of multi-component fractional quantum Hall states with different polarization configurations. Using the Chern-Simons composite fermion framework for SU(4) systems, we construct candidate variational wave functions corresponding to distinct spin, valley, and mixed polarization states. The ground-state energies of these states are evaluated numerically using the Coulomb interaction in spherical geometry. By comparing energies across different polarization sectors, we identify the energetically favored configurations at $ν= 1/2$ and $ν= 1/4$. Our variational energy comparison suggests that the energetically favored candidate states correspond to multi-component correlated quantum Hall liquids. Within the restricted family of trial states considered here, these states differ from a simple composite-fermion Fermi-sea description. These findings provide insight into the role of valley polarization and SU(4) symmetry in stabilizing even-denominator fractional quantum Hall states in graphene.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates even-denominator fractional quantum Hall states (ν=1/2 and ν=1/4) in monolayer graphene using a Chern-Simons composite fermion framework that incorporates the approximate SU(4) symmetry from spin and valley degrees of freedom. It constructs and numerically evaluates candidate variational wave functions for different polarization configurations and identifies the energetically favored multi-component correlated quantum Hall liquid states.
AI.motivation: To understand the role of spin and valley degrees of freedom (SU(4) symmetry) in stabilizing even-denominator fractional quantum Hall states in monolayer graphene, specifically at experimentally observed fillings ν=1/2 and ν=1/4, and to determine which polarization configurations are energetically favored.
AI.method: The authors use the Chern-Simons composite fermion formalism generalized to SU(4) symmetric systems to construct variational trial wave functions for multi-component EDFQH states with different spin, valley, and mixed polarization configurations. Ground-state energies are evaluated numerically using Coulomb interaction in spherical geometry, and energies are compared across polarization sectors.
AI.result: The variational energy comparison identifies energetically favored candidate states at ν=1/2 and ν=1/4, which correspond to multi-component correlated quantum Hall liquids. These favored states differ from a simple composite-fermion Fermi-sea description within the restricted family of trial states considered.
AI.conclusion: The findings reveal that multi-component correlated quantum Hall liquid states, rather than a composite-fermion Fermi sea, are favored energetically at even-denominator fillings in monolayer graphene, highlighting the importance of valley polarization and SU(4) symmetry in stabilizing these states.

title: FrOGS: Discrete Neural Sampler for Independent Alloy Configurations Across Chemical Conditions
comment: Submitted to the AI4Mat workshop at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Predicting the thermodynamic properties of an alloy requires sampling its configurations across many chemical conditions and recovering free energies on a common absolute scale. Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) is the standard tool, but it requires separate simulations at different conditions, and auxiliary free-energy methods such as thermodynamic integration are used to place results on a common absolute scale. Modern discrete neural samplers typically use reverse KL divergence as the objective and can be mode-seeking or biased. We present Free energy Offering Generative Sampler (FrOGS), a hybrid discrete neural sampler that couples an autoregressive model to a continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC) to be trained jointly under a single shared loss. FrOGS draws i.i.d. configurations, returns an unbiased estimate of the partition function, and gives consistent estimates of thermodynamic observables. We train a single model across a wide range of chemical conditions to produce estimates on a common absolute free-energy scale. FrOGS matches exact finite-size results on the 2D Ising model and reference phase diagrams for AgPd and CuAu, without mode collapse. We additionally compare to SEGAL, a published autoregressive baseline, and find that only FrOGS recovers the stability range of the CuAu$_3$ phase.

AI.tldr: FrOGS is a hybrid discrete neural sampler combining an autoregressive model with a continuous-time Markov chain trained under a single shared loss, enabling i.i.d. configuration sampling and unbiased partition function estimates on a common absolute free-energy scale across wide chemical conditions for alloys.
AI.motivation: Predicting alloy thermodynamic properties requires sampling configurations across many chemical conditions and recovering free energies on a common absolute scale. Standard MCMC methods require separate simulations at different conditions and auxiliary techniques like thermodynamic integration. Existing discrete neural samplers using reverse KL divergence can be mode-seeking or biased, limiting their reliability.
AI.method: FrOGS couples an autoregressive model to a continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC) and trains them jointly under a single shared loss. It draws independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) configurations, provides an unbiased estimate of the partition function, and yields consistent thermodynamic observable estimates. A single model is trained across a wide range of chemical conditions to produce estimates on a common absolute free-energy scale.
AI.result: FrOGS matches exact finite-size results on the 2D Ising model and reproduces reference phase diagrams for AgPd and CuAu without mode collapse. Compared to SEGAL (an autoregressive baseline), only FrOGS successfully recovers the stability range of the CuAu3 phase.
AI.conclusion: FrOGS provides a robust alternative to MCMC-based approaches for alloy thermodynamics, offering unbiased free-energy estimation on a common absolute scale across multiple chemical conditions with a single model, and outperforms published autoregressive baselines in accuracy for phase boundary recovery.

title: BU-MBAR: A hybrid solution strategy for the MBAR equations
summary: The multi-state Bennett acceptance ratio (MBAR) equations combine the data collected under different thermodynamic conditions in a statistically optimal way. Due to their practical importance, several solution strategies have been devised to optimize the convergence of the resulting set of coupled equations. However, even with graphics processing unit (GPU) acceleration, the convergence of these methods can still be either unstable or slow. We propose a new approach where the equations are interpreted as the limit of infinitesimal bin width of the respective weighted histogram analysis method (WHAM). In the proposed binned-to-unbinned MBAR (BU-MBAR) method, the bin width is adapted dynamically to ensure a stable and efficient convergence to the asymptotic solution.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a new approach called binned-to-unbinned MBAR (BU-MBAR) for solving the multi-state Bennett acceptance ratio equations, where the equations are interpreted as the limit of infinitesimal bin width of the weighted histogram analysis method (WHAM). The bin width is dynamically adapted to ensure stable and efficient convergence to the asymptotic solution.
AI.motivation: Existing solution strategies for the MBAR equations can be unstable or slow to converge, even with GPU acceleration. A more robust and efficient approach is needed.
AI.method: The MBAR equations are reinterpreted as the limit of WHAM as bin width approaches zero. A binned-to-unbinned MBAR (BU-MBAR) method is proposed where the bin width is adapted dynamically during iteration to guarantee stable and efficient convergence to the asymptotic solution.
AI.result: The proposed BU-MBAR approach achieves stable and efficient convergence to the asymptotic MBAR solution through dynamic bin-width adaptation.
AI.conclusion: Interpreting MBAR as the infinitesimal bin-width limit of WHAM, coupled with dynamic bin-width adaptation, provides a novel and effective strategy for solving MBAR equations with improved stability and convergence speed.

title: Deterministic nanofabrication for engineering nanowire quantum dot devices
comment: Main: 26 pages, 5 figures SI: 16 pages, 13 figures
summary: Semiconductor quantum dots (QDs) are a leading platform for realising bright, wavelength-tunable sources of single and entangled photon pairs for photonic quantum technologies. Site-selected nanowire quantum dots (NWQDs) are a promising platform for fabricating such photonic devices in a scalable manner. However, implementing additional structures around the photonic nanowire while maintaining its vertical growth geometry has remained a challenge. In this work, we develop a deterministic pick-and-place technique to conduct a vertical-to-vertical transfer of NWQDs from the growth substrate to arbitrary templates. Using this transfer technique, we enhance the photon extraction efficiency to 75% by implementing a bottom gold mirror and tune the emission wavelength by 3.6 GHz via implementing electrostatic gates around the QD. Importantly, we measure low-multiphoton probability (g^(2)(0) = 0.002) and high indistinguishability (>80% for +/-100 ps) of the QD emission after the transfer process, yielding high-quality devices. These results demonstrate the repeatability and versatility of the developed transfer technique, which is an enabling step towards scalable single and entangled photon sources.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a deterministic pick-and-place technique for vertical-to-vertical transfer of semiconductor nanowire quantum dots (NWQDs) from growth substrates to arbitrary templates, enabling enhanced photon extraction efficiency (75%) via bottom gold mirrors and wavelength tuning (3.6 GHz) via electrostatic gates while preserving high-quality single-photon emission (g^(2)(0)=0.002, indistinguishability >80%).
AI.motivation: Semiconductor quantum dots are a leading platform for bright, wavelength-tunable single and entangled photon sources for photonic quantum technologies. While site-selected nanowire quantum dots promise scalable fabrication, integrating additional photonic/electrostatic structures around the nanowire while preserving its vertical growth geometry has remained a significant challenge.
AI.method: A deterministic pick-and-place technique is developed to conduct vertical-to-vertical transfer of NWQDs from the growth substrate to arbitrary target templates. This transfer enables integration of a bottom gold mirror for enhanced photon extraction and electrostatic gates for wavelength tuning around the quantum dot.
AI.result: The technique achieves 75% photon extraction efficiency using a bottom gold mirror, tunes the emission wavelength by 3.6 GHz via electrostatic gating, and maintains high device quality after transfer with low multiphoton probability (g^(2)(0)=0.002) and high indistinguishability (>80% within ±100 ps).
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate the repeatability and versatility of the developed vertical-to-vertical transfer technique, establishing it as an enabling step towards scalable single and entangled photon sources based on nanowire quantum dots.

title: Reduced latent leakage does not reliably predict lower likelihood bias in collider inference
summary: Reusable collider representations can be evaluated through downstream discrimination and probes of retained information, but neither quantity directly tests the behaviour of score templates in a profiled likelihood. We test a specific prediction in a controlled two-channel routing protocol: if reduced physics-label readability in a nuisance branch indicates a more inference-robust representation, it should accompany a smaller profiled signal-strength bias under fixed unmodelled shifts. In a public Compact Muon Solenoid $H\rightarrow ZZ\rightarrow4\ell$ workflow, a downstream split of fixed EveNet embeddings preserves signal/background area under the receiver operating characteristic curve ($0.9894\pm0.0004$) while reducing nuisance-branch physics readability from $0.961\pm0.013$ to $0.593\pm0.030$. Probe-sensitivity and effective-rank controls exclude a failed readout and branch collapse. In a separate top quark jet-tagging workflow, the leakage reduction recurs with preserved task performance. Across two development event shards, however, its Spearman association with maximum absolute profiled bias is $0.036$, and three of six material leakage-improving transitions do not reduce that bias. A one-shot preregistered confirmation on an independently accessed shard produces material leakage reductions in all three paired seeds, while the maximum absolute bias increases in two. Thus, within the tested protocol, latent readability is a useful routing diagnostic but not a likelihood-robustness certificate. The result supports a practical validation rule: claims about inference robustness require a prespecified likelihood-facing stress test and held-out confirmation.

AI.tldr: This paper tests whether reduced physics-label readability in a nuisance branch of collider representations predicts improved profiled-likelihood robustness. Using CMS H→ZZ→4ℓ and top quark jet-tagging workflows with fixed EveNet embeddings, leakage reduction preserves discrimination but shows essentially no correlation (Spearman=0.036) with maximum absolute profiled signal-strength bias, and preregistered confirmations increase the bias in two of three seeds. The authors conclude that latent readability is a useful routing diagnostic but not a likelihood-robustness certificate, advocating prespecified likelihood-facing stress tests and held-out confirmation for inference-robustness claims.
AI.motivation: To determine whether downstream discrimination and retained-information probes—commonly used to evaluate reusable collider representations—can substitute for directly testing score-template behavior in a profiled likelihood, thereby validating representations for inference-robustness claims.
AI.method: The authors use a controlled two-channel routing protocol comparing a downstream split of fixed EveNet embeddings against the original, measuring nuisance-branch physics readability and profiling signal-strength bias under fixed unmodelled shifts. They apply this across a CMS H→ZZ→4ℓ workflow and a top quark jet-tagging workflow, with probe-sensitivity and effective-rank controls, plus a one-shot preregistered confirmation on an independent data shard across three paired seeds.
AI.result: The H→ZZ→4ℓ split preserves signal/background AUC (0.9894±0.0004) while reducing nuisance-branch readability from 0.961±0.013 to 0.593±0.030, with controls excluding readout failure and branch collapse. Leakage reduction recurs in jet tagging with preserved task performance, yet the Spearman correlation with maximum absolute profiled bias is only 0.036 across two shards, and three of six material leakage-improving transitions do not reduce bias. In the preregistered confirmation, all three seeds show leakage reduction but maximum absolute bias increases in two seeds.
AI.conclusion: Within the tested protocol, latent readability is a useful routing diagnostic but not a certificate of likelihood robustness. Robust inference claims require a prespecified likelihood-facing stress test and confirmation on held-out data.

title: Molecular Transferability of a Noble-Gas Coordinate for Electronegativity Equalization
comment: 46 pages, 9 figures, 9 tables. Supporting Information and data/code archive included as ancillary files
summary: Charge-equilibration models predict how electrons redistribute over a molecule more cheaply than quantum chemistry, and each begins from a table of atomic electronegativities and hardnesses. A recent table replaces ionization energies and electron affinities with one geometric quantity: each main-group atom's fractional distance to the noble gas closing its row. Holding geometries, electrostatic damping and the molecule list fixed, we compare it with spectroscopic values, with its own kernel refitted, and with a quadratic control, over a primary set of fifty-two molecules and ions at the B3LYP/def2-TZVP level. Two structural consequences follow from the table construction rather than the equalization solver. Atoms at equal fractional distance receive identical electronegativities, so the dipole moments of chlorine monofluoride, iodine monobromide and sulfur dioxide vanish exactly, and the measured $0.72$ debye $\mathrm{HF}/\mathrm{HCl}$ gap is lost. Because the first period is excluded, hydrogen retains its spectroscopic electronegativity above every geometric value, reversing $\mathrm{O{-}H}$, $\mathrm{N{-}H}$ and hydrogen-halide polarity. Fitted alike, geometric and quadratic kernels agree to $0.0022$ electron per atom, so predictions are set by the fitted energy scales, not the kernel shape. Resolving the electronegativity scale period by period restores correct polarity in all five polyatomic heavy-atom-hydrogen tests.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates a geometric charge-equilibration model where atomic electronegativities are derived solely from each main-group atom's fractional distance to the noble gas closing its row, comparing it against spectroscopic values, refitted kernels, and a quadratic control on 52 molecules/ions at the B3LYP/def2-TZVP level.
AI.motivation: Charge-equilibration models offer a cheap alternative to quantum chemistry for predicting electron redistribution, but their accuracy depends on the underlying atomic electronegativity/hardness table. A recent geometric table replacing ionization energies and electron affinities warrants rigorous benchmarking.
AI.method: Geometric electronegativity values (fractional distance to the closing noble gas) are compared with spectroscopic values, its own kernel refitted, and a quadratic control, across 52 molecules/ions at the B3LYP/def2-TZVP level, with geometries, electrostatic damping, and molecule list held fixed. Structural consequences are analyzed per period scaling.
AI.result: Atoms at equal fractional distance get identical electronegativities, causing exact zero dipoles for ClF, IBr, and SO2, and losing the measured 0.72 D HF/HCl gap. Because the first period is excluded, H retains its spectroscopic electronegativity above every geometric value, reversing O-H, N-H, and hydrogen-halide polarity. Fitted alike, geometric and quadratic kernels agree to 0.0022 e/atom, indicating predictions are set by fitted energy scales, not kernel shape. Period-resolved scaling restores correct polarity in all five polyatomic heavy-atom-hydrogen tests.
AI.conclusion: The geometric electronegativity table introduces structural artifacts (degenerate electronegativities across rows and exclusion of period 1) that distort polarity predictions. The kernel shape is not the limiting factor; fitted energy scales dominate. A period-resolved resolution of the electronegativity scale fixes polarity in hydrogen-containing polyatomic systems.

title: Dipolar order across Bravais lattice space: classification, spin waves, and a four-attractor phase diagram
summary: Every crystal is a Bravais lattice decorated by a basis, so the dipolar ordering of the fourteen Bravais lattices is the natural starting point for any systematic theory of dipolar magnetism in three dimensions. We determine it here in a single common framework: the interaction tensor is Ewald-summed, the classical ground state is obtained by minimising the lowest Luttinger--Tisza band over the entire Brillouin zone, and the linear spin-wave spectrum with its zero-point corrections is computed for every lattice whose order is collinear. Three results emerge that are not properties of individual lattices but of the landscape. First, two structural principles --- the exact tracelessness of the dipolar tensor in three dimensions, and its identical vanishing at $\mathbf k=0$ for every cubic-symmetric lattice --- explain the ordering type, the absence of first-order cubic anisotropy, and the systematics of the zero-point moment reduction. Second, exactly one lattice defeats the Luttinger--Tisza construction: for face-centred orthorhombic the optimal eigenvector is not circular, the single-$\mathbf k$ state is a spin-density wave of non-constant length, and the tabulated energy is a strict lower bound; direct supercell minimisation gives the true ground state. Third, optimising each family over its free metric parameters collapses the whole of Bravais space onto only \emph{four} attractors, with body-centred tetragonal the global optimum and a single interior optimum at rhombohedral $α=62.42^\circ$ lying below face-centred cubic. Three independent published benchmarks are reproduced.

AI.tldr: The paper systematically determines the dipolar magnetic ground state and spin-wave properties of all fourteen Bravais lattices in a single Ewald-summation and Luttinger-Tisza framework, revealing structural principles governing ordering, one anomalous lattice (face-centred orthorhombic) that defeats the Luttinger-Tisza construction, and that optimizing lattice parameters collapses all Bravais space onto four attractors.
AI.motivation: Since every crystal is a Bravais lattice decorated by a basis, understanding dipolar ordering of the fourteen Bravais lattices provides a natural systematic foundation for any theory of dipolar magnetism in three dimensions.
AI.method: The dipolar interaction tensor is Ewald-summed; the classical ground state is obtained by minimizing the lowest Luttinger-Tisza band over the full Brillouin zone; linear spin-wave spectra with zero-point corrections are computed for all lattices with collinear order; direct supercell minimization is used where the single-k state fails.
AI.result: Three general results emerge: (1) exact tracelessness of the dipolar tensor and its vanishing at k=0 for cubic lattices explain ordering type, absent first-order cubic anisotropy, and zero-point moment reduction systematics; (2) face-centred orthorhombic uniquely defeats the Luttinger-Tisza construction, requiring direct supercell minimization for the true ground state; (3) family optimization over free metric parameters collapses Bravais space onto four attractors, with body-centred tetragonal as global optimum and a rhombohedral interior optimum at α=62.42° below face-centred cubic. Three independent published benchmarks are reproduced.
AI.conclusion: A complete and unified determination of dipolar order across all Bravais lattices is achieved, revealing landscape-level structural principles and exceptional cases that go beyond individual lattice properties.

title: Design Principles for Reproducible Networks
comment: 27 pages, 5 figures, 89 page supplement, 8 supplementary figures
summary: From protein complexes to electronic circuits, many natural and engineered systems function only if assembled in an exact, reproducible fashion. The structure of each of these systems can be understood as a network, yet network science lacks the mechanisms to consistently reproduce exact topologies, focusing instead on generating network ensembles. We introduce the framework of network design where we encode the local constraints obeyed by a system's building blocks in a design set, and derive the Unigraphical Design Theorem, which determines when these constraints guarantee reproducible assembly into a unique structure, a process we call unigraphical assembly. For systems whose design sets do not specify a unique outcome, we identify guided assembly as a second route to reproducibility, in which temporal ordering decomposes construction into unigraphical steps. Applying these results to 3,618 reproducible systems, including protein complexes, molecules, and robots, we classify those that undergo unigraphical assembly and those that require guided assembly. We further identify a diversity-redundancy boundary that explains how systems trade component variety for structurally interchangeable parts while retaining unique assembly. Finally, we experimentally test the theory using 3D-printed components to re-engineer generative construction sets into systems that assemble unigraphically into prescribed topologies. Network design thus reframes reproducibility as a mathematically testable property of real networks, opening a route to the rational engineering of complex systems.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces "network design," a framework that encodes local constraints of building blocks in a design set and derives the Unigraphical Design Theorem, which determines when these constraints guarantee unique, reproducible assembly. Applying this to 3,618 systems (protein complexes, molecules, robots), the authors classify systems into unigraphical vs. guided assembly, identify a diversity-redundancy boundary, and experimentally validate the theory with 3D-printed components.
AI.motivation: Many natural and engineered systems require exact, reproducible assembly to function, yet network science lacks mechanisms to consistently reproduce exact topologies, focusing instead on generating ensembles of networks. This gap prevents a general, mathematically testable understanding of when reproducible assembly is guaranteed.
AI.method: The authors propose a framework encoding local constraints of building blocks into a "design set," and derive the Unigraphical Design Theorem to determine conditions for unique assembly. They also identify "guided assembly" as a temporal-ordering route when design sets are not unique, analyze 3,618 real systems to classify assembly routes, define a diversity-redundancy boundary, and validate the theory experimentally using 3D-printed components re-engineered into unigraphically assembling systems.
AI.result: The framework successfully classifies reproducible systems into unigraphical and guided assembly categories. A diversity-redundancy boundary is identified that explains trade-offs between component variety and structural interchangeability. Experimental validation with 3D-printed components confirms that construction sets can be re-engineered to assemble unigraphically into prescribed topologies.
AI.conclusion: Network design reframes reproducibility as a mathematically testable property of real networks, providing a rational route to engineering complex systems with guaranteed unique assembly.

title: Orbital current rectifier and linear magnon Edelstein effect in $p$-wave antialtermagnets
summary: We show that $p$-wave magnets efficiently generate magnetization via a linear thermal Edelstein effect arising from the orbital magnetic moments of their magnons. Furthermore, they can generate perfectly nonreciprocal orbital currents through a purely even-order nonlinear response. This makes them promising candidates for orbital-current rectification. Because these transport phenomena originate from the orbital magnetic moment of magnons, they connect magnonics and orbitronics. More generally, we find that odd-parity-wave magnets with coplanar ground states host magnons with zero spin magnetic moment. Instead the magnons carry a collinear, out-of-plane orbital magnetic moment, realizing an orbital version of antialtermagnetism. We establish these general results using symmetry arguments and demonstrate them explicitly for a coplanar ground state with the minimal number of sublattices, inspired by the ground state of CeNiAsO. Our conclusions hold both in absence and presence of spin-orbit coupling.

AI.tldr: p-wave magnets can efficiently generate magnetization through a linear thermal Edelstein effect driven by magnon orbital magnetic moments, and can generate perfectly nonreciprocal orbital currents via even-order nonlinear responses, making them promising for orbital-current rectification and connecting magnonics with orbitronics.
AI.motivation: To explore how p-wave magnets, specifically odd-parity-wave magnets with coplanar ground states, generate magnetization and nonreciprocal orbital currents via magnon orbital magnetic moments, thereby bridging the fields of magnonics and orbitronics.
AI.method: The authors use symmetry arguments to establish general results and demonstrate them explicitly for a coplanar ground state with the minimal number of sublattices, inspired by the ground state of CeNiAsO. The analysis is performed both in the absence and presence of spin-orbit coupling.
AI.result: p-wave magnets efficiently generate magnetization via a linear thermal Edelstein effect from magnon orbital magnetic moments, and can generate perfectly nonreciprocal orbital currents through a purely even-order nonlinear response. Magnons in odd-parity-wave magnets with coplanar ground states carry zero spin but collinear, out-of-plane orbital magnetic moments, realizing an orbital version of antialtermagnetism.
AI.conclusion: Odd-parity-wave magnets with coplanar ground states constitute promising candidates for orbital-current rectification, as their magnons carry orbital (not spin) magnetic moments, establishing a new connection between magnonics and orbitronics.

title: Physics-Informed Neural Network Surrogate for Oxygen Vacancy Dynamics in epitaxial $\mathrm{SrTiO_3}$ on Si memristors via Dynamic Spectral Optimization
summary: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) offer a promising framework for modeling semiconductor devices, yet standard architectures struggle with severe numerical stiffness and multiscale spatial discrepancies inherent to oxide heterostructures. Here, we demonstrate a cascaded PINN architecture coupled with a custom second-order Chebyshev second kind polynomial spectral optimizer (DSO V2 Hybrid) to model ion-electronic drift-diffusion transport in Pt/SrTiO$_3$/Si memristive heterostructures across a 20 nm STO film on a 380 $μ$m Si substrate. By isolating potential, carrier density, and vacancy transport into four sequentially trained sub-neural-networks, our model circumvents condition numbers exceeding $10^{16}$ without operator splitting. The trained surrogate reproduces experimental conductive-AFM current-voltage hysteresis ($R^2 > 0.96$) while ensuring strict Poisson consistency across continuous space. Compared to conventional finite-element solvers (e.g., COMSOL), the PINN surrogate enables differentiable inverse parameter estimation and linear time inference.

AI.tldr: A cascaded PINN architecture with a Chebyshev second-kind spectral optimizer (DSO V2 Hybrid) models ion-electronic drift-diffusion in Pt/SrTiO₃/Si memristive heterostructures, overcoming severe numerical stiffness across a 20 nm STO film on a 380 μm Si substrate by sequentially training four sub-networks.
AI.motivation: Standard PINN architectures struggle with severe numerical stiffness and multiscale spatial discrepancies inherent to oxide heterostructures, limiting their application in semiconductor device modeling.
AI.method: Cascaded PINN with four sequentially trained sub-neural-networks isolating potential, carrier density, and vacancy transport, coupled with a custom second-order Chebyshev second kind polynomial spectral optimizer (DSO V2 Hybrid), avoiding operator splitting despite condition numbers exceeding 10^16.
AI.result: The surrogate reproduces experimental conductive-AFM current-voltage hysteresis with R² > 0.96 while maintaining strict Poisson consistency across continuous space; enables differentiable inverse parameter estimation and linear-time inference compared to COMSOL.
AI.conclusion: The cascaded PINN framework successfully overcomes numerical stiffness in multiscale semiconductor heterostructure modeling, offering advantages over conventional finite-element solvers in inverse parameter estimation and inference speed.

title: Computing high-order mixed derivatives in physics-informed neural networks using multi-index Bell polynomials
summary: Physics-informed neural networks for high-order partial differential equations require mixed input derivatives and their gradients with respect to the network parameters. Standard implementations obtain an order-$K$ derivative by repeated automatic differentiation. We instead organize the forward recursion of the multivariate Faà di Bruno formula and its explicit backpropagation over a prescribed downward-closed set of multi-indices, with the Bell-polynomial convolutions tabulated once. The forward pass carries only the derivatives the differential operator requires. The backward pass propagates gradients from losses formed from any subset of them, including nonlinear products and coupled fields. Both recursions are exact up to roundoff and avoid nested computational graphs. An independent Taylor-jet implementation, symbolic checks of the test problems, and finite differences verify derivatives and loss gradients through order seven. On one CPU core, the method evaluates 330 mixed derivatives with respect to four inputs through order seven and the corresponding loss gradient without the memory failures observed for several nested implementations. Numerical tests include third-, fifth-, and seventh-order dispersive equations, incompressible flow, and a manufactured five-field electrohydrodynamic system. The seventh-order Zakharov-Kuznetsov test in $3+1$ dimensions has a relative solution error of $6\times10^{-4}$.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an alternative approach to computing high-order derivatives in physics-informed neural networks (PINNs). Instead of using nested automatic differentiation, the authors organize the multivariate Faà di Bruno formula into forward and backward recursions over a downward-closed set of multi-indices, with Bell-polynomial convolutions tabulated once. This avoids nested computational graphs, propagates gradients from arbitrary loss subsets, and is verified against Taylor jets, symbolic checks, and finite differences through order seven. Tests include high-order dispersive equations, incompressible flow, and electrohydrodynamic systems.
AI.motivation: PINNs for high-order PDEs need mixed input derivatives and their gradients with respect to network parameters. Standard implementations rely on repeated automatic differentiation (nested AD), which creates computational graph bloat, memory failures, and inefficiency for high-order derivatives.
AI.method: The method organizes the forward recursion of the multivariate Faà di Bruno formula and its explicit backpropagation over a downward-closed set of multi-indices. Bell-polynomial convolutions are precomputed once. The forward pass carries only derivatives needed by the differential operator; the backward pass propagates gradients from losses formed from any subset of these derivatives, including nonlinear products and coupled fields. Both recursions are exact up to roundoff and avoid nested computational graphs.
AI.result: Derivatives and loss gradients are verified through order seven via an independent Taylor-jet implementation, symbolic checks, and finite differences. On one CPU core, the method computes 330 mixed derivatives with respect to four inputs through order seven and the corresponding loss gradient without memory failures observed in nested implementations. The seventh-order Zakharov-Kuznetsov test in 3+1 dimensions achieves a relative solution error of 6×10⁻⁴.
AI.conclusion: The proposed exact, non-nested recursion for high-order derivative computation and backpropagation in PINNs is memory-efficient and accurate, enabling robust training for high-order PDEs without nested computational graph failures.

title: Low stray-field ion pump configuration for cold atom experiments
summary: Ion pumps used in cold-atom experiments generate stray magnetic fields that can perturb magneto-optical trapping, shift Zeeman sensitive energy levels, and introduce systematic errors in precision spectroscopy. We numerically investigate a compact low-stray-field ion pump configuration designed to reduce magnetic flux leakage through the ultrahigh-vacuum port without increasing the overall pump size. Starting from a simplified magnetic model of a standard ion pump, we study two complementary modifications: auxiliary permanent magnets surrounding the original pump magnets with opposite magnetisation, and a soft-magnetic honeycomb field stopper integrated at the pump port. The resulting combined configuration strongly reduces the magnetic flux density outside the pump. In the geometry considered here, the field at 10 mm from the UHV port is reduced by 97.9%, while the calculated reduction in effective pumping speed due to the honeycomb stopper is 17.9%. These results indicate that engineered magnetic compensation and field-guiding structures can support more compact cold-atom vacuum systems while preserving pumping performance. Further work should validate the design with nonlinear magnetostatic modelling, molecular-flow simulations, and measurements on a complete pump geometry.

AI.tldr: The paper numerically investigates a compact low-stray-field ion pump design for cold-atom experiments that reduces external magnetic flux leakage by 97.9% at 10 mm from the UHV port via auxiliary oppositely-magnetized permanent magnets and a soft-magnetic honeycomb field stopper, at the cost of a 17.9% reduction in effective pumping speed.
AI.motivation: Ion pumps used in cold-atom experiments produce stray magnetic fields that perturb magneto-optical trapping, shift Zeeman-sensitive energy levels, and introduce systematic errors in precision spectroscopy. The authors aim to reduce magnetic flux leakage without increasing the overall pump size, to enable more compact cold-atom vacuum systems.
AI.method: The study numerically models a standard ion pump using a simplified magnetic model, then evaluates two complementary modifications: (1) auxiliary permanent magnets surrounding the original pump magnets with opposite magnetization, and (2) a soft-magnetic honeycomb field stopper integrated at the pump port. A combined configuration of both modifications is analyzed for stray-field reduction and pumping speed penalty.
AI.result: In the geometry considered, the magnetic flux density at 10 mm from the UHV port is reduced by 97.9% with the combined configuration. The calculated reduction in effective pumping speed due to the honeycomb stopper is 17.9%.
AI.conclusion: Engineered magnetic compensation and field-guiding structures can substantially suppress stray magnetic fields while preserving acceptable pumping performance, supporting more compact cold-atom vacuum systems. Future work should validate the design with nonlinear magnetostatic modeling, molecular-flow simulations, and measurements on a complete pump geometry.

title: Direct Validation of Superconductivity through Contact-Free Detection of Persistent Supercurrents Using Room-Temperature Quantum Magnetometry
summary: The accelerated emergence of new materials is driving the search for high temperature superconductors, but rapid experimental validation remains a critical bottleneck, particularly for microscopic samples under high pressure. Here, we demonstrate one-step direct superconductivity validation through room-temperature, contact-free detection of remnant supercurrents. The technique utilizes a cryogen-free optically pumped atomic magnetometer to detect the temperature-dependent magnetic field produced by supercurrents of a superconductor. The superconducting transition is directly identified by the abrupt disappearance of magnetic field from the remnant supercurrent above the transition temperature and the reversal of the supercurrent direction upon reversing the applied magnetic field. Validated on YBCO microcrystals and REBCO tape, this technique detects pico-Tesla magnetic fields from supercurrents induced by the ambient Earth's magnetic field in a millimeter-sized REBCO square disk, as well as from sub-100 micrometer YBCO microcrystals compatible with high-pressure diamond anvil cells. The use of a ferrite flux guide enables sensitive detection from centimeter-scale distances. Requiring no electrical contacts, magnetic coils, or integrated magnetic sensors, this non-invasive, room-temperature platform offers a scalable approach for high-throughput screening and validation of superconductivity.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a contact-free, room-temperature technique for one-step validation of superconductivity by detecting remnant supercurrent magnetic fields using a cryogen-free optically pumped atomic magnetometer, validated on YBCO microcrystals and REBCO tape.
AI.motivation: Rapid experimental validation of newly discovered high temperature superconductors is a critical bottleneck, especially for microscopic samples under high pressure, where existing methods require electrical contacts, integrated sensors, or complex setups that are impractical for high-throughput screening.
AI.method: A cryogen-free optically pumped atomic magnetometer detects the temperature-dependent magnetic field produced by remnant supercurrents. The superconducting transition is identified by the abrupt disappearance of the magnetic field above the transition temperature and the reversal of supercurrent direction upon reversing the applied magnetic field. A ferrite flux guide enables detection from centimeter-scale distances. The platform requires no electrical contacts, magnetic coils, or integrated magnetic sensors.
AI.result: The technique successfully detects pico-Tesla magnetic fields from supercurrents induced by the ambient Earth's magnetic field in a millimeter-sized REBCO square disk, as well as from sub-100 micrometer YBCO microcrystals compatible with high-pressure diamond anvil cells. Validation was performed on YBCO microcrystals and REBCO tape.
AI.conclusion: This non-invasive, room-temperature platform offers a scalable approach for high-throughput screening and validation of superconductivity, addressing the experimental validation bottleneck in the search for new high temperature superconductors.

title: A Langmuir-Like Adsorption Model for MoS2 Gas Sensors: Bridging Theory and Experiment
summary: Gas sensors based on layered TMDCs (transition-metal dichalcogenides) such as MoS2 have attracted considerable attention recently and are considered as a promising alternative to the conventional metal-oxide-based gas sensing devices. Recent studies on TMDC gas sensors have mainly addressed either the theoretical description of adsorption mechanisms or the fabrication of test devices and the investigation of their gas sensing performance. However, a suitable approach for modeling the gas sensing behavior of TMDC devices and for establishing a reliable connection between theoretical results and the response of experimental devices when exposed to gases remains absent. To bridge this gap, in the present work a new Langmuir-based adsorption model, capable of calculating both the sensor sensitivity and selectivity, is developed and applied to MoS2-based gas sensors. It is shown that by using appropriate published data for the adsorption energy and the charge transfer as input data, the reported experimental sensitivities of MoS2 gas sensors can be well reproduced by the model.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a novel Langmuir-based adsorption model for TMDC gas sensors (specifically MoS2) that can calculate both sensor sensitivity and selectivity, bridging the gap between theoretical adsorption studies and experimental device responses.
AI.motivation: While TMDC-based gas sensors have attracted significant attention as alternatives to metal-oxide sensors, previous research has been fragmented—some studies focused on theoretical adsorption mechanisms while others addressed experimental device fabrication and testing. A major gap exists: there is no suitable modeling approach that connects theoretical calculations to the actual gas sensing response of experimental TMDC devices, limiting the ability to predict and understand sensor performance.
AI.method: A new Langmuir-based adsorption model is developed that can compute both sensor sensitivity and selectivity. The model uses published data for adsorption energy and charge transfer as input parameters and is applied to MoS2-based gas sensors.
AI.result: The model successfully reproduces reported experimental sensitivities of MoS2 gas sensors when appropriate published adsorption energy and charge transfer data are used as inputs, demonstrating its validity and predictive capability.
AI.conclusion: The proposed Langmuir-based model provides a reliable bridge between theoretical adsorption studies and experimental device responses for TMDC gas sensors, offering a tool to predict sensor sensitivity and selectivity and potentially guiding future sensor design and optimization.

title: Topological Boundary States and the Edge Chain in Semi-Infinite Two-Dimensional Insulators
summary: We show that it is possible to compute the adiabatically protected edge and corner states of semi-infinite, two-dimensional, topological insulators by considering the first layer of lattice sites, what we call the "edge chain," independently from the bulk. We start by accepting this claim as an ansatz, then, using the Shemesh theorem, we show that the edge states one finds using our procedure are adiabatically protected, provided we restrict ourselves to adiabatic evolutions that do not break chiral symmetry. We show explicit examples of our method in a 2D extension of the SSH model, the SSH3 model, the Haldane model and the Breathing Kagome Lattice.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a method to compute adiabatically protected edge and corner states of 2D topological insulators by considering only the first layer of lattice sites ("edge chain") independently from the bulk. Using the Shemesh theorem, the authors prove these edge states are adiabatically protected under chiral-symmetry-preserving evolutions, and demonstrate the method on the SSH3 model, Haldane model, and Breathing Kagome Lattice.
AI.motivation: To simplify the computation of topologically protected edge and corner states in 2D topological insulators by decoupling the boundary layer from the bulk, which could provide an efficient and tractable approach to characterizing these states.
AI.method: The authors treat the first layer of lattice sites ("edge chain") as independent from the bulk as an ansatz. They then invoke the Shemesh theorem to prove that the edge states obtained from this reduced procedure are adiabatically protected, provided the adiabatic evolution preserves chiral symmetry. The method is validated through explicit examples in multiple models including a 2D SSH extension, SSH3, Haldane, and Breathing Kagome Lattice.
AI.result: The edge states computed via the isolated edge-chain approach are shown to be adiabatically protected when chiral symmetry is maintained. The method is successfully demonstrated across several 2D topological insulator models, confirming the validity of the ansatz.
AI.conclusion: Edge and corner states of 2D topological insulators can be reliably obtained from the first layer of lattice sites alone, without full bulk computation, as long as chiral symmetry is preserved during adiabatic evolution. This offers a simplified yet rigorous framework for analyzing boundary physics of topological materials.

title: Enumerating Chemical Structures, Stereoisomers, and Stereogenic Units with Analytic Combinatorics
comment: Submitted to J. Math. Chem. 27 pages, 7 figures
summary: The enumeration of chemical structures traditionally relies on graph- and group-theoretic techniques, including Pólya theory, in order to account for stereochemical symmetries. These methods require bespoke derivations and methods for each molecular family of interest, and quickly become very intricate for nontrivial classes. In this work, we demonstrate that analytic combinatorics provides a unifying, highly extensible, and relatively simple framework for enumeration problems. Using the symbolic method, we show that classical counting problems, such as the enumeration of acyclic alkanes and other hydrocarbon families, can be naturally solved via concise combinatorial specifications of the class of interest. We first demonstrate the simplicity of this approach by replicating existing results in this framework, requiring significantly less work than previously necessary, and then extend these ideas to more complex problems, counting broader classes of molecules accounting for both tetrahedral and E/Z stereoisomerism, counting the distribution of stereogenic units, and enumerating achiral and meso compounds. All results are made reproducible through CombOL, our open-source software package which automates the translation of combinatorial specifications into generating functions using the symbolic method, and performs both univariate and multivariate enumeration.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates that analytic combinatorics, via the symbolic method, provides a unifying and simpler framework for enumerating chemical structures compared to traditional graph- and group-theoretic approaches like Pólya theory. The authors replicate classical results (e.g., acyclic alkane enumeration) with concise combinatorial specifications and extend the framework to complex problems involving tetrahedral and E/Z stereoisomerism, stereogenic unit distributions, and achiral/meso enumeration, all automated via their open-source CombOL software.
AI.motivation: Traditional enumeration methods for chemical structures rely on bespoke graph-theoretic and group-theoretic derivations (e.g., Pólya theory) that must be re-derived for each molecular family and become highly intricate for nontrivial classes. A simpler, unifying framework is needed.
AI.method: The authors apply analytic combinatorics using the symbolic method, translating combinatorial specifications of molecular classes directly into generating functions. They demonstrate this on classical problems (acyclic alkanes, hydrocarbons) and extend it to broader classes accounting for tetrahedral and E/Z stereoisomerism, stereogenic unit distributions, and achiral/meso enumeration. All computations are automated via CombOL, their open-source software package supporting univariate and multivariate enumeration.
AI.result: The paper replicates existing enumeration results with significantly less effort than traditional methods and extends the framework to more complex problems including tetrahedral and E/Z stereoisomer counting, distributions of stereogenic units, and enumeration of achiral and meso compounds—all made reproducible through the CombOL software package.
AI.conclusion: Analytic combinatorics offers a highly extensible, unifying, and relatively simple framework for chemical enumeration problems, overcoming the complexity and bespoke nature of classical graph- and group-theoretic approaches, with computational automation making results reproducible.

title: Decoherence-controlled collective criticality in a two-dimensional quantum Stag Hunt
summary: Physical decoherence can preserve the microscopic strategic neutrality condition of a quantum game while changing the thermodynamic regime of the corresponding interacting population. We demonstrate this for an Eisert--Wilkens--Lewenstein (\textit{EWL}) Stag Hunt embedded as independent nearest neighbor encounters on a square lattice. For the restricted strategies $\mathsf{Q}=i\mathbb{Z}$ and $\mathsf{D}=i\mathbb{Y}$, noisy two-player payoff matrices are determined for phase damping, depolarization, and amplitude damping and mapped exactly to channel dependent Ising parameters $\mathfrak{J}(Γ,p)$ and $\mathfrak{H}(Γ,p)$. Phase damping and depolarization show the clearest contrast: they share the same microscopic neutrality branch $\mathfrak{H}=0$, while only depolarization suppresses the interaction as $(1-p)^2$. At $β=1$, this produces an exact depolarization-driven square-lattice critical point at $p_{*}\approx 0.233460\ldots$, whereas phase damping remains in the ordered coexistence regime along the same neutrality branch. Monte Carlo finite size scaling is consistent with two-dimensional Ising criticality and distinguishes field driven coexistence below $p_{*}$ from a smooth crossover above it. Amplitude damping additionally reveals a strong dependence on channel placement: the post-strategy neutrality branch reaches $Γ=0$ at $p=1/3$ and then disappears. Resource negativity further shows that microscopic two-qubit entanglement and collective interaction strength are distinct quantities. The resulting extended lattice remains an ordinary classical Ising system.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes quantum games (specifically EWL Stag Hunt) embedded on a square lattice, showing that different physical decoherence channels (phase damping, depolarization, amplitude damping) map exactly to Ising model parameters while preserving strategic neutrality. Depolarization uniquely drives an exact critical point (p*≈0.233460) at β=1, whereas phase damping stays in ordered coexistence; amplitude damping shows strong channel-placement dependence. Monte Carlo scaling confirms 2D Ising criticality, and resource negativity shows microscopic entanglement and collective interaction are distinct quantities.
