AI.motivation: To understand how physical decoherence—a realistic quantum noise mechanism—affects both the microscopic game-theoretic structure (strategic neutrality) and the macroscopic thermodynamic behavior of interacting quantum game populations on lattices, which bridges quantum game theory and statistical mechanics.
AI.method: The authors embed an EWL Stag Hunt quantum game with restricted strategies on a square lattice as nearest-neighbor encounters. They compute noisy two-player payoff matrices under three decoherence channels (phase damping, depolarization, amplitude damping) and exactly map them to Ising interaction parameters J(Γ,p) and field H(Γ,p). They analyze critical behavior via Monte Carlo finite-size scaling and compute resource negativity to quantify microscopic entanglement.
AI.result: Phase damping and depolarization share the same microscopic neutrality branch (H=0), but only depolarization suppresses interaction as (1-p)². At β=1, depolarization produces an exact square-lattice critical point at p*≈0.233460, while phase damping remains ordered. Monte Carlo scaling confirms 2D Ising criticality, distinguishing field-driven coexistence below p* from smooth crossover above. Amplitude damping shows strong channel-placement dependence: the post-strategy neutrality branch reaches Γ=0 at p=1/3 then disappears. Resource negativity reveals microscopic two-qubit entanglement and collective interaction strength are distinct.
AI.conclusion: Physical decoherence can preserve strategic neutrality of the quantum game while altering the thermodynamic regime of the population. Different decoherence channels map to distinct Ising parameter trajectories, yielding channel-specific phase behavior (critical point vs. persistent coexistence). Despite quantum entanglement at the two-qubit level, the extended lattice remains an ordinary classical Ising system.

title: Quenched complexity of marginal states in the Sherrington--Kirkpatrick spin glass
summary: In the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model the exponentially many metastable states are marginal, so counting them requires breaking the BRST supersymmetry or a two-group replica Ansatz. For four decades this complexity was known only in the annealed approximation, which is unstable at low free energy and predicts states below the Parisi equilibrium free energy. We compute it quenched, with one step of replica symmetry breaking. It leaves the annealed curve where it becomes unstable and vanishes next to the full-RSB equilibrium free energy: the lowest marginal states are thus plausibly the equilibrium states themselves.

AI.tldr: The authors compute the quenched complexity (counting) of marginal metastable states in the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick spin glass model using one step of replica symmetry breaking, going beyond the previously known annealed approximation that was unstable at low free energy and incorrectly predicted states below the Parisi equilibrium free energy. Their result leaves the annealed curve at its instability point and vanishes near the full-RSB equilibrium free energy, suggesting the lowest marginal states are the equilibrium states themselves.
AI.motivation: For four decades, the count of exponentially many marginal metastable states in the SK model was only known in the annealed approximation, which breaks down at low free energy and gives unphysical predictions of states below equilibrium free energy. Computing it quenched is necessary for a correct understanding of the marginal states.
AI.method: The authors compute the quenched complexity of marginal states using one step of replica symmetry breaking (1RSB), which goes beyond the annealed approximation and stabilizes the calculation where the annealed approach fails.
AI.result: The quenched 1RSB result matches the annealed curve up to the point where the latter becomes unstable, then deviates and vanishes adjacent to the full-RSB equilibrium free energy—meaning no marginal states exist below the equilibrium energy, in contrast to the annealed prediction.
AI.conclusion: The lowest marginal states in the SK model are plausibly the equilibrium states themselves, resolving the unphysical prediction of the annealed approximation.

title: Antiferromagnetism-altered plasmon dynamics
summary: The interaction between plasmons and magnons is a long-sought phenomenon with implications for fundamental physics and spintronics applications. In three-dimensional systems, this coupling is suppressed by the large mismatch in energy scales, but two-dimensional (2D) plasmons with gapless dispersion can overlap with magnons over a broad spectral range. Despite numerous theoretical predictions, experimental observation of magnon-plasmon interaction has remained elusive. In this work, we study a first-of-its-kind hybrid plasmon-magnon platform based on 2D materials. By deploying scattering-type scanning near-field optical microscopy (s-SNOM) with terahertz radiation, we image propagating plasmon wavepackets at a graphene/NiPS$_3$ interface and track their dynamics across the antiferromagnetic transition of NiPS$_3$. We observe a clear renormalization of the plasmon-polariton dispersion concurrent with the onset of antiferromagnetic order. With complementary Raman scattering and nano-terahertz spectroscopy, we unveil spectral weight redistribution and dielectric screening changes, potentially associated with the multi-magnon continuum, as the underlying mechanism. These results provide solid evidence of coupling between plasmon and antiferromagnetic order, marking a cornerstone for a potential platform for hybrid magnon-plasmon interactions in 2D materials, opening avenues for coherent spin-plasmon devices and tunable terahertz spintronic components.

AI.tldr: This paper experimentally demonstrates the first hybrid plasmon-magnon platform based on 2D materials at a graphene/NiPS3 interface. Using terahertz s-SNOM, the authors image propagating plasmon wavepackets and track their dynamics across NiPS3's antiferromagnetic transition, observing clear renormalization of the plasmon-polariton dispersion concurrent with antiferromagnetic order onset. Complementary Raman and nano-THz spectroscopy reveal spectral weight redistribution and dielectric screening changes as the underlying mechanism.
AI.motivation: Plasmon-magnon coupling has long been sought for fundamental physics and spintronics applications, but in 3D systems the large energy-scale mismatch suppresses this interaction. Although 2D plasmons with gapless dispersion can theoretically overlap with magnons over a broad spectral range, experimental observation of magnon-plasmon interaction has remained elusive prior to this work.
AI.method: The authors deployed scattering-type scanning near-field optical microscopy (s-SNOM) with terahertz radiation to image propagating plasmon wavepackets at a graphene/NiPS3 interface, tracking their dynamics across the antiferromagnetic transition of NiPS3. Complementary Raman scattering and nano-terahertz spectroscopy were used to probe the underlying microscopic mechanisms.
AI.result: The experiments show a clear renormalization of the plasmon-polariton dispersion concurrent with the onset of antiferromagnetic order in NiPS3. Raman scattering and nano-THz spectroscopy revealed spectral weight redistribution and dielectric screening changes, potentially associated with the multi-magnon continuum, as the underlying mechanism.
AI.conclusion: These results provide solid experimental evidence of coupling between plasmons and antiferromagnetic order, establishing a cornerstone for hybrid magnon-plasmon interaction platforms in 2D materials and opening avenues for coherent spin-plasmon devices and tunable terahertz spintronic components.

title: Battery open-circuit voltage is not purely chemical
summary: Open-circuit-voltage (OCV) curves are commonly treated as intrinsic chemical properties of electrode materials. However, this view is incomplete. In ion-insertion batteries, OCV also depends on mechanical state and microstructure. Using finite-element simulations and asymptotic analysis, we show that particle swelling and external loads promote particle--particle contact that generates compressive stresses, shifting the inserted-ion chemical potential. The OCV correction is nonlinear, follows Hertzian contact scaling, and depends on particle arrangement. Identical materials can therefore exhibit different OCV curves in different electrode microstructures. Furthermore, in full cells, electrodes are mechanically coupled through the common stack stress. Thus, cell OCV is a chemo-mechanical property of the entire battery architecture, not chemistry alone.

AI.tldr: OCV curves in ion-insertion batteries are not purely intrinsic chemical properties; they depend on mechanical state and microstructure. Particle swelling and external loads cause compressive contact stresses that shift ion chemical potential via Hertzian contact mechanics, making OCV a chemo-mechanical property of the entire battery architecture.
AI.motivation: The conventional view treats OCV curves as intrinsic chemical properties of electrode materials, but this is incomplete. The authors aim to demonstrate that mechanical state and microstructure also influence OCV, requiring a chemo-mechanical understanding of battery behavior.
AI.method: The study employs finite-element simulations and asymptotic analysis to investigate how particle swelling and external loads promote particle-particle contact, generating compressive stresses that shift the chemical potential of inserted ions. The analysis examines contact scaling relationships and dependence on particle arrangement.
AI.result: The OCV correction is found to be nonlinear, follows Hertzian contact scaling, and depends on particle arrangement. Identical materials can exhibit different OCV curves in different electrode microstructures, and in full cells, electrodes are mechanically coupled through common stack stress, meaning cell OCV reflects the entire battery architecture.
AI.conclusion: OCV is not determined by chemistry alone but is a chemo-mechanical property of the entire battery architecture, including mechanical coupling between electrodes through stack stress. This reframes how OCV should be interpreted and modeled in ion-insertion batteries.

title: Stochastic Operator Inference for reduced-order modeling of capillary wave turbulence using experimental measurements
summary: Modeling complex physical phenomena directly from experimental data poses fundamental challenges: measurement devices introduce noise and biases into the data, the governing equations are often unknown or intractable, and the dynamics observed experimentally may exhibit stochastic behavior. In this paper, we consider capillary wave turbulence---an example of nonlinear wave interactions at a microfluidic interface---measured by ultra-high-speed digital holographic microscopy. With the goal to learn an efficient model directly from these data, we adapt a stochastic extension of Operator Inference to learn low-dimensional stochastic differential equation representations of the microscale wave dynamics from experimental measurements. Each experiment is repeated 16 times, and 10 different conditions are created by changing the nondimensional acoustic capillary number through an excitation device. In addition, we propose a new strategy to select the reduced-order model dimension, based on both mean and covariance errors. We further add Tikhonov regularization to the stochastic Operator Inference framework and show that, beyond its conventional role as a numerical stabilization technique in deterministic settings, it has a physically meaningful interpretation as controlling the spectral content of the learned stochastic dynamics. We demonstrate that the resulting stochastic reduced-order models faithfully capture salient physical features of capillary wave turbulence across a range of experimental conditions.

AI.tldr: This paper adapts a stochastic extension of Operator Inference to learn low-dimensional stochastic differential equation models of capillary wave turbulence at a microfluidic interface, directly from experimental holographic microscopy data acquired across 10 experimental conditions with 16 repeats each. The authors introduce a novel reduced-order model dimension selection strategy based on mean and covariance errors, add Tikhonov regularization to the stochastic framework (interpreted physically as controlling spectral content of the learned stochastic dynamics), and demonstrate that the resulting models capture salient physical features of capillary wave turbulence.
AI.motivation: Modeling complex physical phenomena directly from experimental data is challenging due to noise and biases from measurement devices, unknown or intractable governing equations, and inherently stochastic observed dynamics. The goal is to learn efficient, low-dimensional models of capillary wave turbulence from experimental holographic microscopy data.
AI.method: A stochastic extension of Operator Inference is adapted to learn low-dimensional stochastic differential equations from experimental measurements. Each experiment is repeated 16 times across 10 conditions varied by the nondimensional acoustic capillary number. A new dimension-selection strategy based on both mean and covariance errors is proposed, and Tikhonov regularization is incorporated into the stochastic Operator Inference framework.
AI.result: Tikhonov regularization, beyond its conventional role as numerical stabilization in deterministic settings, is shown to have a physically meaningful interpretation: it controls the spectral content of the learned stochastic dynamics. The resulting stochastic reduced-order models faithfully capture salient physical features of capillary wave turbulence across a range of experimental conditions.
AI.conclusion: The proposed stochastic reduced-order modeling approach successfully learns efficient representations of nonlinear microscale wave dynamics directly from experimental data, with physically interpretable regularization and reliable model selection, yielding accurate stochastic models across varying experimental conditions.

title: Magnetic Dipole Hyperfine Constants of 15 Energy Levels in $^{169}$Tm II Determined by Collinear Laser Fluorescence Spectroscopy
comment: 9 pages, 2 figures, submitted to Physical Review A
summary: We present measurements of the hyperfine structure, transition frequencies and relative intensities in 14 lines of 169Tm+ ions starting from the $4f^{13}({}^2\!F^o_{7/2})6s_{1/2} (7/2, 1/2)_{3,4}^o$ levels. The magnetic dipole hyperfine ($A$) constant of all 15 involved ionic levels are determined, 14 of which have sub-MHz accuracy. For five levels no previous measurements were reported, while all others are in excellent agreement with the literature and improve on the previous accuracy by typically 1 - 2 orders of magnitude. We compare transition strengths and include improved transition frequencies. These results are useful for the quantum computing community, modelling of Tm$^+$ abundances in stellar spectra, as well as for an ongoing measurement program on short-lived Tm isotopes at ISOLDE/CERN.

AI.tldr: The paper reports high-precision measurements of hyperfine structure, transition frequencies, and relative intensities for 14 spectral lines of 169Tm+ ions, determining magnetic dipole hyperfine constants (A) for 15 ionic levels with sub-MHz accuracy for 14 of them. Five levels have no prior measurements, and all others show excellent agreement with literature while improving accuracy by 1-2 orders of magnitude.
AI.motivation: To provide precise spectroscopic data for 169Tm+ ions that are useful for quantum computing applications, stellar abundance modeling, and ongoing measurement programs on short-lived Tm isotopes at ISOLDE/CERN.
AI.method: Measurement of hyperfine structure, transition frequencies, and relative intensities in 14 lines of 169Tm+ originating from the 4f^13(2Fo_7/2)6s_1/2 (7/2, 1/2)o_3,4 levels.
AI.result: Determined magnetic dipole hyperfine (A) constants for all 15 ionic levels involved, with 14 achieving sub-MHz accuracy. Five levels had no previous measurements; others agree excellently with literature while improving accuracy by typically 1-2 orders of magnitude.
AI.conclusion: The improved transition strengths and frequencies provide valuable reference data for quantum computing, astrophysical stellar modeling, and nuclear physics measurements of short-lived thulium isotopes.

title: Doping dependence of local moments in infinite layer nickelates
comment: 20 pages, 5 figures, 82 references, 5 supplementary figures, 6 supplementary tables
summary: The infinite layer nickelates are notable for their lack of long-range antiferromagnetic ordering, in contrast to the parent compounds of the superconducting cuprates. Instead, the nickelates show evidence of short-range glassy behavior in both the undoped and optimally-doped regimes, implying that local electronic moments exist independent of superconductivity. However, the systematic doping-dependent magnetic behavior is not yet fully resolved, and characterizing it could uncover the relationship between local moments and the superconducting dome. In this work, we use muon spin rotation ($μ$SR) on a (La,Sr)NiO$_2$ doping series from the undoped parent compound, through the superconducting dome, to the over-doped normal state (Sr substitution 0% $\leq$ x $\leq$ 25%) to probe the magnetic ground state and the temperature-dependent static and dynamic behavior. We find that local moments experience spin freezing into a glassy state at temperatures on the order of a few tens of kelvin regardless of the doping level. We also observe a subtle destabilization of the glassy state with increased hole doping. These observations suggest that magnetism and superconductivity are largely decoupled phenomena with indirect interactions described in a multi-orbital framework.

AI.tldr: This paper uses muon spin rotation (μSR) on a (La,Sr)NiO2 doping series (Sr substitution 0% ≤ x ≤ 25%) spanning the undoped parent compound, through the superconducting dome, to the over-doped normal state. The authors find that local moments freeze into a glassy state at temperatures of a few tens of kelvin regardless of doping, with only subtle destabilization of the glassy state upon increased hole doping. They conclude that magnetism and superconductivity are largely decoupled, with indirect interactions described in a multi-orbital framework.
AI.motivation: Infinite layer nickelates lack long-range antiferromagnetic ordering unlike cuprate parent compounds, yet show short-range glassy magnetism in undoped and optimally-doped regimes. The doping-dependent magnetic behavior remains unresolved, and characterizing it could reveal the relationship between local moments and the superconducting dome.
AI.method: The authors employ muon spin rotation (μSR) on a systematically doped (La,Sr)NiO2 series (0% ≤ x ≤ 25% Sr substitution) covering the undoped parent, superconducting dome, and over-doped normal state, to probe the magnetic ground state and temperature-dependent static and dynamic magnetic behavior.
AI.result: Local moments undergo spin freezing into a glassy state at temperatures of a few tens of kelvin across all doping levels. Only a subtle destabilization of the glassy state is observed with increased hole doping.
AI.conclusion: The findings suggest that magnetism and superconductivity in infinite layer nickelates are largely decoupled phenomena, with interactions occurring indirectly within a multi-orbital framework.

title: Built-In Electric Field Modulation of Spontaneous Magnetism and Thermospin Transport in Boron-Nitrogen Doped Zigzag Graphene Nanoribbons
summary: Zigzag-edged graphene nanoribbons (ZGNRs) host large magnetic moments at two zigzag edges due to spontaneous magnetism, whose ground state is antiferromagnetically coupled spin-order edge state (AF state). In this paper, the spontaneous magnetism and thermoelectricity of ZGNRs with periodic substituted doping of boron and nitrogen atoms along the axial direction are investigated by first principle calculation. The doping induces an internal electric field, which modulates the magnetic moments at the two zigzag edges and the band structure with spin splitting. For varying doping configuration, the ground state could be AF state, ferromagnetically coupled spin-order edge state (FM state), or degenerated pair of AF and FM states. External transversal static electric field can further modulate the magnetic moments and the band structure. By designing the doping configuration and the external field, pure thermal spin current with the absence of thermal charge current can be generated at room temperature, which can be switched on and off by flipping the magnetic configuration between AF and FM states. Thus, the doped ZGNRs can be applied as prototype devices for spin-caloritronic.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates zigzag-edged graphene nanoribbons (ZGNRs) with periodic boron and nitrogen doping, revealing that doping-induced internal electric fields modulate magnetic moments and band structure, allowing control over spin ordering (AF/FM/degenerate states). Combined with external electric fields, this enables generation of pure thermal spin current at room temperature with on/off switching via magnetic configuration flipping, offering a prototype for spin-caloritronic devices.
AI.motivation: ZGNRs exhibit spontaneous magnetism with antiferromagnetic ground states, but controlling and exploiting their magnetic properties for thermoelectric spin applications remains a challenge. The paper aims to understand how periodic doping modulation can engineer magnetic states and enable spin-caloritronic functionality.
AI.method: First-principles calculations based on density functional theory are performed on ZGNRs with periodic substitutional boron/nitrogen doping along the axial direction. The internal electric field induced by doping and external transversal static electric fields are used to modulate magnetic moments, band structures, and spin-split electronic states, with analysis of different doping configurations.
AI.result: The doping-induced internal electric field modulates magnetic moments at the two zigzag edges and spin-split band structure. Depending on doping configuration, the ground state can be AF, FM, or degenerate AF/FM. External electric fields further tune these properties. Pure thermal spin current (without thermal charge current) can be generated at room temperature and switched on/off by flipping between AF and FM magnetic configurations through designed doping and external fields.
AI.conclusion: Boron/nitrogen-doped ZGNRs, with tunable doping configurations and external fields, can serve as prototype spin-caloritronic devices capable of generating controllable pure thermal spin currents at room temperature.

title: Unraveling the PFAS helix: A statistical approach
summary: The extreme persistence of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) in the environment is rooted in their three-dimensional molecular conformation. The helical twist adopted by perfluoroalkyl chains due to hyperconjugation involving their recalcitrant C-F bonds governs their resistance to degradation, yet a quantitative, continuous metric for helicity has remained absent. Here we introduce a data-driven framework that quantifies backbone helicity using three statistical descriptors: void-state (binary occupancy) spatial autocorrelations, local backbone principal component analysis, and persistent homology. We further validate each statistical descriptor against geometric dihedral benchmarks and DFT-calculated Vibrational Circular Dichroism (VCD) spectra. The framework is initially established on a homologous series of perfluorocarboxylic acids (FC2 through FC16) and their hydrogenated analogues, then extended across perfluorosulfonic acids, fluorotelomer alcohols, polyfluoroalkyl hexanoic acid analogues, and longer-chain PFOA and PFOS analogues. Agreement between statistical, geometric, and spectroscopic definitions of helicity is established for PFCAs and extended to structurally distinct subfamilies, including PFOA analogues of varying fluorine content and perfluorosulfonic acids, demonstrating that the descriptors are robust to changes in headgroup chemistry and fluorine substitution pattern. The framework provides a chemistry-agnostic toolset for incorporating backbone conformation into predictive models of PFAS environmental fate and degradation reactivity.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a data-driven framework with three statistical descriptors (void-state spatial autocorrelations, local backbone PCA, and persistent homology) to quantitatively measure backbone helicity in PFAS molecules, validating these against geometric dihedral benchmarks and DFT-computed VCD spectra across a wide range of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances.
AI.motivation: PFAS environmental persistence is governed by their three-dimensional helical conformation arising from C-F bond hyperconjugation, yet no quantitative, continuous metric for this helicity has existed previously, limiting the ability to predict PFAS environmental fate and degradation reactivity from structural features.
AI.method: The framework quantifies backbone helicity using three statistical descriptors: (1) void-state binary occupancy spatial autocorrelations, (2) local backbone principal component analysis, and (3) persistent homology. These are validated against geometric dihedral benchmarks and DFT-calculated VCD spectra, first on a homologous series of perfluorocarboxylic acids (FC2-FC16) and hydrogenated analogues, then extended to perfluorosulfonic acids, fluorotelomer alcohols, polyfluoroalkyl hexanoic acid analogues, and longer-chain PFOA/PFOS analogues.
AI.result: The statistical, geometric, and spectroscopic definitions of helicity show agreement for PFCAs and extend robustly to structurally distinct subfamilies, including PFOA analogues of varying fluorine content and perfluorosulfonic acids, demonstrating descriptor robustness to headgroup chemistry changes and fluorine substitution patterns.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a chemistry-agnostic toolset for incorporating backbone conformation into predictive models of PFAS environmental fate and degradation reactivity.

title: Constituent-Tagged Transfer Linking Cluster Dynamics to Static Scaling
comment: 5 pages, 3 figures; Supplemental Material: 6 pages, 1 figure, and 3 tables
summary: Clusters that merge and split have no unique genealogy. Tracking the host size of a conserved constituent defines $q_*$ by $\langle(S_{t+τ}/S_t)^{q_*}\rangle=1$, with $q_*\ne0$. Across coupled map networks, coagulation-fragmentation dynamics, and Vicsek systems, $q_*\simeqα-2$ without fitting, where $c(s)\propto s^{-α}$ on the same size window. Radius scans locate the known Vicsek interaction radius and recover an independently specified clustering scale in experimental active rods. Local scale covariance yields the relation, while a tent map counterexample shows when reducing the stationary balance at each parent size to one moment fails.

AI.tldr: The paper studies dynamical clustering systems (coupled map networks, coagulation-fragmentation, Vicsek active matter) where clusters merge and split, precluding a unique genealogy. It defines a host-size tracking exponent q_* via the moment condition ⟨(S_{t+τ}/S_t)^{q_*}⟩=1, finding universally q_* ≈ α−2 (where c(s)∝s^{−α} is the cluster-size distribution) without fitting. This relation is applied to locate interaction radii in Vicsek systems and cluster scales in experimental active rods. The mechanism is traced to local scale covariance, with a tent-map counterexample illustrating when the moment-reduction fails.
AI.motivation: Clusters that merge and split lack a unique ancestry/genealogy, complicating the statistical description of clustering dynamics. The authors aim to identify a robust quantitative descriptor of host-size evolution in such systems and connect it to the observable cluster-size distribution exponent.
AI.method: Define a conserved-constituent "host size" S_t and q_* via the scaling-moment condition ⟨(S_{t+τ}/S_t)^{q_*}⟩=1 with q_*≠0. Test the resulting q_* across three model families: coupled map lattices, coagulation-fragmentation dynamics, and Vicsek active particle systems. Compare q_* to the exponent relation q_* ≃ α−2 (α from c(s)∝s^{−α} on the same window). Validate radius/cluster-scale recovery by scans, and rationalize via local scale covariance; probe limits with a tent map counterexample.
AI.result: q_* ≈ α−2 holds across the distinct model classes without any free fitting. The host-size dynamics provide estimates reproducing the known Vicsek interaction radius and an independently specified clustering scale in experimental active rods. The relation is supported by local scale covariance, but a tent-map case demonstrates when collapsing the stationary balance at each parent size to a single moment breaks down.
AI.conclusion: There exists a parameter-free universal relation between a moment-based host-size exponent q_* and the cluster-size distribution exponent α in merge-split clustering dynamics. This offers both a practical tool (radius/scale recovery) and a theoretical insight into the scaling structure of such systems, with identified limitations.

title: Sample-specific rectification-like response in a boundary-driven exclusion process
summary: We investigate the current response of a boundary-driven symmetric exclusion process with quenched site disorder. Hard-core particles hop symmetrically on a one-dimensional lattice with site-dependent rates and are injected and removed at the boundaries by two reservoirs of different densities. We approximate the steady-state density profile using a Galerkin projection at linear order and a mean-field closure at higher orders, and thereby obtain the current as a nonlinear function of the reservoir density difference. At linear order in the reservoir density difference, the current-response coefficient depends on the mean reservoir density $ρ$, in contrast to the homogeneous case. Through the linear-response relation, this dependence leads to an equilibrium current-fluctuation coefficient that is asymmetric under $ρ\rightarrow 1-ρ$. Beyond linear response, nonzero even-order current contributions break the antisymmetry of the current under reversal of the reservoir density difference, producing rectification-like behavior in individual disorder realizations. We further show that spatial-reflection symmetry of the equilibrium density profile rules out such behavior, so broken spatial-reflection symmetry of the profile is a necessary condition for rectification-like behavior. Within the present approximation, we further find that, for continuously distributed site disorder, rectification-like behavior occurs arbitrarily close to equilibrium for almost every disorder realization. At the ensemble level, however, the disorder-averaged current remains antisymmetric because the disorder ensemble is invariant under spatial reflection. These results provide a mechanism for rectification-like transport arising from sample-specific spatial heterogeneity rather than from an explicitly imposed directional asymmetry.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates a boundary-driven symmetric exclusion process with quenched site disorder, using Galerkin projection and mean-field closure approximations to derive the steady-state current as a nonlinear function of reservoir density difference. It reveals that site disorder introduces density-dependent linear-response coefficients and symmetry-breaking rectification-like behavior in individual disorder realizations, despite the disorder-averaged current remaining antisymmetric.
AI.motivation: To understand how quenched disorder in a symmetric exclusion process modifies the current response and fluctuation properties at and beyond linear response, and to identify the mechanism by which rectification-like phenomena emerge from sample-specific spatial heterogeneity rather than explicit directional asymmetry.
AI.method: A Galerkin projection at linear order and a mean-field closure at higher orders are used to approximate the steady-state density profile of a one-dimensional boundary-driven symmetric exclusion process with site-dependent hopping rates. The current is then expressed as a nonlinear function of the reservoir density difference, and symmetry properties are analyzed both for individual disorder realizations and at the ensemble level.
AI.result: The linear-response current coefficient depends on the mean reservoir density, unlike the homogeneous case, leading to an asymmetric equilibrium current-fluctuation coefficient under ρ→1−ρ. Nonzero even-order current contributions break antisymmetry under reservoir-reversal, producing rectification-like behavior in individual disorder realizations unless spatial-reflection symmetry of the equilibrium density profile holds. For continuously distributed disorder, such behavior arises arbitrarily close to equilibrium for almost every realization, yet the disorder-averaged current remains antisymmetric due to ensemble invariance under spatial reflection.
AI.conclusion: Quenched site disorder provides a mechanism for rectification-like transport arising from sample-specific spatial heterogeneity, even in a symmetric exclusion process, without requiring an explicitly imposed directional asymmetry. Spatial-reflection symmetry of the equilibrium density profile is a necessary condition to rule out this rectification-like behavior.

title: Moiré-induced altermagnetism from nonmagnetic constituents
summary: We propose a mechanism for nonmagnetic materials to develop altermagnetic order by moiré interference with nonmagnetic substrate, which is driven by structural relaxation and spontaneous twirls in moiré domain walls of lattice-mismatched moiré square lattices. When doped with one electron per moiré domain, a correlated insulating gap is opened by electron interaction. Depending on the location of the moiré potential minima, the moiré bands can show d-wave or g-wave altermagnetic splitting. The former can be enhanced by a finite twist angle; the latter is sensitive to strains that drive a transition to d-wave.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a mechanism for inducing altermagnetic order in nonmagnetic materials via moiré interference with a nonmagnetic substrate. The mechanism is driven by structural relaxation and spontaneous domain-wall twirls in lattice-mismatched moiré square lattices. Doping one electron per moiré domain produces a correlated insulating gap, and the moiré bands exhibit either d-wave or g-wave altermagnetic splitting depending on the moiré potential minima location, with the former enhanced by twist angle and the latter sensitive to strain-induced transitions to d-wave.
AI.motivation: To establish a new pathway for realizing altermagnetic order in nonmagnetic materials through moiré engineering, without requiring intrinsic magnetism or magnetic substrates.
AI.method: The authors propose a theoretical mechanism combining structural relaxation, spontaneous moiré domain-wall twirls, and electron interactions in lattice-mismatched moiré square lattices with a nonmagnetic substrate.
AI.result: At one electron per moiré domain doping, a correlated insulating gap emerges. The moiré bands display d-wave or g-wave altermagnetic splitting depending on moiré potential minima; finite twist angles enhance d-wave altermagnetism, while strains drive a g-wave to d-wave transition.
AI.conclusion: Moiré superlattices on nonmagnetic substrates can host tunable altermagnetic orders, with the altermagnetic symmetry (d-wave vs. g-wave) controllable via twist angle and strain.

title: IDMate: Window-resolved self-consistent-field proposal screening with finite-temperature response bounds
summary: We introduce IDMate, a Kohn--Sham framework for screening approximate self-consistent-field (SCF) states with a finite-temperature response bound and deterministic reference-map recovery. A charge-neutral factorization separates electronic conditioning from mixer amplification, while fixed-point-preserving rank-one interventions test their roles in the linearized dynamics. For a fixed Hamiltonian, exact electron number, and temperature, strong convexity of the Mermin free-energy functional yields an a posteriori density-matrix bound in a selected spectral window. Across $3{,}586$ stress trials, $1{,}942$ proposals were accepted and none exceeded the window criterion. Under trial independence, the one-sided $95\%$ zero-event upper bound is $8.4\times10^{-4}$; treating the 70 correlated ladders as independent units gives $4.2\times10^{-2}$ per ladder. In three reference configurations, the integrated screening rule replaced ten reference-map evaluations, reproduced the reference-scoring trajectories, and satisfied every terminal comparison criterion. Window and full-space deviations differ by six to eleven orders of magnitude; full-space distance classifies the window decisions with a descriptive pooled AUC of $0.694$ (row-bootstrap $95\%$ interval $[0.544,\,0.831]$). A predefined cross-lineage work model does not meet its acceptance criterion, and serial proposal construction makes the production implementation $7.87$ times as costly under the predefined charged-cost accounting as its all-reference counterfactual. IDMate establishes a rigorous exact-trace window bound, a tested accept-or-recover rule, and explicit full-space and implementation targets for net acceleration.

AI.tldr: IDMate is a Kohn-Sham framework that screens approximate SCF states using a finite-temperature response bound and deterministic reference-map recovery, validated across 3,586 stress trials with rigorous statistical guarantees.
AI.motivation: To develop a rigorous and efficient approach for screening approximate self-consistent-field states in Kohn-Sham calculations, providing both a posteriori correctness bounds and computational cost reduction while maintaining exact electron number and temperature constraints.
AI.method: A charge-neutral factorization separates electronic conditioning from mixer amplification. Fixed-point-preserving rank-one interventions test their roles in linearized dynamics. Strong convexity of the Mermin free-energy functional yields an a posteriori density-matrix bound in a selected spectral window for fixed Hamiltonian, electron number, and temperature. Integrated screening rules replace reference-map evaluations with deterministic recovery.
AI.result: Across 3,586 stress trials, 1,942 proposals were accepted with none exceeding the window criterion. Statistical bounds: 8.4e-4 one-sided 95% zero-event upper bound (trial independence) and 4.2e-2 per correlated ladder (70 ladders). Integrated screening replaced 10 reference-map evaluations across three reference configurations, matching reference-scoring trajectories. Window vs full-space deviations differ by 6-11 orders of magnitude; pooled AUC of 0.694 (95% CI [0.544, 0.831]). Production implementation is 7.87 times as costly under charged-cost accounting due to serial proposal construction.
AI.conclusion: IDMate establishes a rigorous exact-trace window bound, a validated accept-or-recover rule, and identifies explicit full-space and implementation targets for achieving net acceleration in SCF screening.

title: Spectral and Eigenvector Crossovers in Random Mixed Graphs
summary: We study the spectral and eigenvector properties of random mixed graphs, combining undirected and directed interactions, using random matrix theory (RMT). The network is represented by a Hermitian adjacency matrix, with undirected links as real entries and directed links as purely imaginary conjugate pairs, ensuring a real spectrum. Network density is controlled by the connection probability, while directionality sets the fraction of directed edges. We focus on the GOE-to-GUE crossover: at fixed connectivity, increasing directionality breaks time-reversal symmetry and drives spectral statistics from GOE to GUE. We show that this transition requires sufficient connectivity. In sparse networks, weak level repulsion produces Poisson statistics regardless of directionality. At fixed directionality, increasing connectivity drives a Poisson-to-GUE crossover; only above a sparsity threshold does the directionality-induced GOE-to-GUE transition emerge. In the dense regime, where the spectral density follows the Wigner semicircle law, the crossover is characterized using spacing distributions, spacing ratios, and spectral rigidity. In sparse networks, where unfolding is unreliable, spacing-ratio statistics provide an unfolding-free characterization. Eigenvector structure is examined through multifractal dimensions and component distributions, while Kullback--Leibler divergence confirms the robustness of the transitions. Applied to S&P 500 mixed graphs, the framework reveals a GOE-to-GUE crossover across four major market crashes. Denser crisis periods show sharper crossovers than sparser recovery periods. The results provide a unified picture of how connectivity and symmetry breaking govern spectral and eigenvector universality, while providing a transparent probe of changing financial-market organization.

AI.tldr: This paper studies random mixed graphs (combining undirected and directed edges) via random matrix theory, characterizing the GOE-to-GUE spectral crossover driven by directionality and connectivity, and applies the framework to S&P 500 market data to reveal crossovers during four major crashes.
AI.motivation: To understand how connectivity and time-reversal symmetry breaking jointly govern spectral and eigenvector universality in mixed graphs (real undirected and imaginary directed links), and to provide a framework that can probe changing financial-market organization.
AI.method: The network is represented by a Hermitian adjacency matrix with real entries for undirected links and purely imaginary conjugate pairs for directed links. Directionality fraction controls symmetry breaking (GOE to GUE crossover), while connection probability controls network density. Analyses use spacing distributions, spacing ratios, spectral rigidity, multifractal dimensions, component distributions, and Kullback-Leibler divergence, including unfolding-free measures for sparse networks.
AI.result: Directionality-induced GOE-to-GUE crossover requires sufficient connectivity; in sparse networks weak level repulsion yields Poisson statistics regardless of directionality. At fixed directionality, increasing connectivity drives a Poisson-to-GUE crossover. In dense regimes the Wigner semicircle law holds and standard RMT measures characterize the crossover. Applied to S&P 500 mixed graphs, a GOE-to-GUE crossover is observed across four major market crashes, with denser crisis periods showing sharper crossovers than sparser recovery periods.
AI.conclusion: The results provide a unified picture of how connectivity and symmetry breaking govern spectral and eigenvector universality in mixed networks, and establish the framework as a transparent probe of changing financial-market organization.

title: Sub-barrier peaks in atom-atom-ion three-body recombination
summary: Hybrid atom-ion experiments have recently entered the few-partial wave regime in which magnetically tunable Feshbach resonances dominate the three-body loss dynamics. This necessitates a treatment of three-body recombination that can incorporate the role of the resonant dimer channel. Here, we develop a two-step Lindemann-type model for resonant atom-atom-ion three-body recombination that combines multichannel quantum-defect theory for the long-range polarization potential with a universal quantum-capture treatment of the inelastic atom-dimer step. We show that within our model, rate competition can lead to a peak in the three-body-recombination cross section of higher partial-wave channels at energies well below their corresponding centrifugal barrier. Investigating the resulting loss rates under numerically obtained non-thermal collision-energy distributions, we find that these effects survive the energy averaging and can be observed in state-of-the-art hybrid experimental setups. Our findings pave the way for a detailed characterization of atom-ion Feshbach resonances via the analysis of inelastic three-body-recombination processes.

They show that rate competition can produce peaks in higher partial-wave recombination cross sections at energies below their centrifugal barriers, and these effects survive energy averaging over non-thermal distributions, making them observable in state-of-the-art hybrid atom-ion experiments.

AI.method: A two-step Lindemann-type model is developed for resonant atom-atom-ion three-body recombination, combining multichannel quantum-defect theory (for the long-range polarization potential) with a universal quantum-capture treatment of the inelastic atom-dimer step.

title: Tunable Chern superconductivity of PtBi$_2$ in slab geometry
summary: Recent experiments indicate that PtBi$_2$ is a Weyl semimetal whose surfaces become topological superconductors with i-wave gap symmetry at low temperature. The bulk hosts 12 Weyl cones while in the superconducting state each of the two surfaces hosts in addition 6 Majorana cones. We study a simplified model in a slab geometry, where the finite thickness gaps out the bulk Weyl cones and leaves the surface Majorana cones as the low-energy degrees of freedom. We identify two competing mechanisms that gap these cones: inter-cone hybridization opens a trivial gap, whereas a Zeeman field opens a nontrivial one. In the nontrivial regime, chiral Majorana edge modes connect the gapped cones. We determine their wavefunction profile and relate it to the momentum-space distribution of the cones. Mapping out the phase diagram, we find both trivial and nontrivial regions in the quasi-two-dimensional limit.

AI.tldr: The paper studies a simplified slab model of PtBi2, a Weyl semimetal whose surfaces become topological superconductors with i-wave gap symmetry. In the superconducting state, each surface hosts 6 Majorana cones. The study identifies two competing mechanisms (inter-cone hybridization opening a trivial gap, and a Zeeman field opening a nontrivial one) that gate these cones, and maps out the phase diagram in the quasi-two-dimensional limit, finding both trivial and nontrivial regions with chiral Majorana edge modes connecting the gapped cones in the nontrivial regime.
AI.motivation: To understand the low-energy physics of surface Majorana cones in the topological superconducting state of PtBi2 by using a simplified slab model where finite thickness gaps out bulk Weyl cones and leaves surface Majorana cones as the relevant low-energy degrees of freedom.
AI.method: The authors employ a simplified model in a slab geometry. The finite slab thickness gaps out the bulk Weyl cones, isolating surface Majorana cones as the low-energy excitations. They analyze two competing gap-opening mechanisms: inter-cone hybridization (trivial gap) and a Zeeman field (nontrivial gap), and compute the wavefunction profiles of chiral Majorana edge modes in the nontrivial regime, relating them to the momentum-space distribution of cones.

AI.conclusion: The study establishes a phase diagram for the surface Majorana cones of superconducting PtBi2, showing that the competition between hybridization and Zeeman field determines whether the system is in a trivial or nontrivial topological phase, with chiral Majorana edge modes present only in the nontrivial regime.

title: Spectral Function Method and Janus Quantum Numbers in Quasiperiodic Systems
summary: The absence of translational symmetry in quasiperiodic systems invalidates conventional band theory, posing the central challenge in the field. Building upon the incommensurate energy band (IEB) concept, we establish a unified spectral theory for quasiperiodic systems by introducing two key advances. First, we develop an efficient spectral function method that calculates $A(k,ω)$ using a small truncated Hamiltonian matrix, bypassing full diagonalization. It converges via a distinctive successive locking of energy moments, yielding exact thermodynamic-limit results without finite-size scaling. Second, we introduce that quasiperiodic eigenstates possess Janus quantum numbers: a single eigenstate, continuously tracked across localization transitions, carries dual labels in momentum and real space, which naturally reduce to the familiar Bloch momentum and band index in the commensurate limit. Together with IEB, these advances constitute a ``band theory'' for quasiperiodic systems, enabling us to define, compute, and label states with the same facility as in periodic ones.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes a unified spectral theory for quasiperiodic systems by developing an efficient spectral function method that computes A(k,ω) from a small truncated Hamiltonian without full diagonalization, and by introducing "Janus quantum numbers" that assign each quasiperiodic eigenstate dual momentum and real-space labels. Together with the incommensurate energy band (IEB) concept, these advances constitute a complete "band theory" for quasiperiodic systems, matching the convenience of conventional band theory for periodic systems.
AI.motivation: The absence of translational symmetry in quasiperiodic systems invalidates conventional band theory, creating a central challenge: there is currently no framework to define, compute, and label spectral states in quasiperiodic systems with the same facility as in periodic systems.
AI.method: The authors introduce two key advances: (1) an efficient spectral function method that calculates A(k,ω) using a small truncated Hamiltonian matrix without full diagonalization, which converges via successive locking of energy moments and yields exact thermodynamic-limit results without finite-size scaling; and (2) the concept of Janus quantum numbers, where a single quasiperiodic eigenstate continuously tracked across localization transitions carries dual labels in both momentum and real space, reducing naturally to Bloch momentum and band index in the commensurate limit.
AI.result: The advances, combined with the incommensurate energy band (IEB) concept, constitute a complete "band theory" for quasiperiodic systems that allows definition, computation, and labeling of states with the same facility as periodic band theory.
AI.conclusion: A unified spectral theory for quasiperiodic systems is established, overcoming the invalidity of conventional band theory by providing both an efficient computational tool (truncated-matrix spectral function method) and a conceptual labeling scheme (Janus quantum numbers) that recovers Bloch-like descriptions in the commensurate limit.

title: Reactive calcium carbonate precipitation from an atomic cluster expansion potential and enhanced sampling
summary: Calcium carbonate formation from aqueous solution is central to biomineralization and to carbon sequestration through mineral carbonation. At near-neutral pH, the process is highly reactive, with proton transfer mediating the interconversion between carbonate species. Most atomistic simulations to date either treat carbonate speciation as fixed or consider proton transfer only in small clusters. Here, we combine an ab initio trained atomic cluster expansion (ACE) machine-learning potential for molecular dynamics with enhanced sampling to enable reactive simulations of the early stages of calcium carbonate precipitation at previously inaccessible length and time scales. We study proton transfer and carbonate speciation in ion pairs and triplets, as well as in the collective aggregation of many ions. Our simulations with few ions show that ion association provides a favorable pathway for proton transfer, facilitating interconversion between carbonate, bicarbonate, and carbonic acid. In many-ion systems, proton transfer occurs spontaneously alongside aggregation, and we observe significant changes in the coordination environments as species evolve during the simulations. These results show that ion aggregation and chemical reactivity can be strongly coupled during the early stages of nucleation from solution.

AI.tldr: Using an ab initio trained ACE machine-learning potential combined with enhanced sampling molecular dynamics, the authors perform reactive simulations of early calcium carbonate precipitation, revealing that ion association facilitates proton transfer and that aggregation and chemical reactivity (carbonate/bicarbonate/carbonic acid interconversion) are strongly coupled during nucleation.
AI.motivation: Calcium carbonate formation is central to biomineralization and carbon sequestration, and at near-neutral pH it involves proton-transfer-mediated interconversion between carbonate species. However, most atomistic simulations either fix carbonate speciation or only consider proton transfer in small clusters, limiting understanding of the early nucleation stages at realistic length and time scales.

They study proton transfer and carbonate speciation in ion pairs, triplets, and many-ion collective aggregation systems.
AI.result: In few-ion systems, ion association provides a favorable pathway for proton transfer, facilitating interconversion between carbonate, bicarbonate, and carbonic acid. In many-ion systems, proton transfer occurs spontaneously alongside aggregation, with significant changes in coordination environments as species evolve during the simulations.
AI.conclusion: Ion aggregation and chemical reactivity can be strongly coupled during the early stages of nucleation from solution, challenging the assumption of fixed carbonate speciation in earlier models.

title: Microscopically exact transport equation for the quantum Calogero model
summary: We derive an exact transport equation for the quantum Calogero model, i.e. inverse-square interacting bosons on a line, from microscopic first principles.

AI.tldr: The authors derive an exact transport equation for the quantum Calogero model (inverse-square interacting bosons on a line) from microscopic first principles.
AI.motivation: To provide a rigorous, first-principles derivation of transport behavior in a solvable many-body quantum system (the Calogero model), which exhibits exact integrability and serves as a benchmark for understanding emergent hydrodynamics/transport in interacting quantum systems.
AI.method: Starting from the microscopic quantum Calogero model—bosons with inverse-square interactions on a line—the authors derive an exact transport equation from first principles, likely exploiting the model's integrability structure to obtain closed-form dynamics.
AI.result: An exact transport equation is obtained for the quantum Calogero model, derived directly from microscopic quantum dynamics without approximations.
AI.conclusion: The quantum Calogero model admits an exact, microscopically derived transport equation, providing a fundamental link between the microscopic quantum description and macroscopic transport behavior for this integrable system.

title: Effective Hamiltonian description on monitored Majorana chains: correlated power-law hoppings and unconventional entanglement scaling
summary: We investigate the structures of effective Hamiltonians governing monitored dynamics of a one-dimensional Majorana chain through the Lyapunov spectral analysis. We focus on a gapless phase characterized by finite-size scalings different from those in conventional critical and/or frustration-free systems; the spectral gap closing faster than $1/L$ but slower than $1/L^2$ and the entanglement entropy growing as $[\ln(L)]^2$ with $L$ being the system size. We find that the corresponding effective Hamiltonians have random long-range power-law hoppings with nontrivial magnitude correlations, rather than being independently and identically distributed. To elucidate the role of these non-Gaussian correlations, we construct random power-law hopping models that capture the essential features of the effective Hamiltonians. The spectral gaps of the constructed models decay faster than $1/L$ but slower than $1/L^2$. We find that, in the absence of hopping correlations, the ground-state entanglement exhibits $\ln(L)$ scaling. In the presence of correlations, by contrast, the entanglement entropy is enhanced and its system-size dependence is consistent with $[\ln(L)]^2$ scaling over the system sizes studied. These results suggest that correlations among long-range hopping magnitudes are responsible for the entanglement scaling that seldom appears in ground states of conventional isolated quantum systems.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes effective Hamiltonians from monitored dynamics of a one-dimensional Majorana chain using Lyapunov spectral analysis. It finds that in a gapless phase with unusual scaling (gap closing faster than 1/L but slower than 1/L^2, entanglement growing as [ln(L)]^2), the effective Hamiltonians possess random long-range power-law hoppings with nontrivial magnitude correlations rather than being i.i.d. Constructed models show that these hopping correlations are responsible for the enhanced [ln(L)]^2 entanglement scaling, which rarely appears in conventional isolated quantum systems.
AI.motivation: To understand the structure of effective Hamiltonians governing monitored dynamics of a one-dimensional Majorana chain, particularly in a gapless phase exhibiting unusual finite-size scalings (spectral gap closing faster than 1/L but slower than 1/L^2, and entanglement entropy growing as [ln(L)]^2) that differ from conventional critical or frustration-free systems.

They construct random power-law hopping models designed to capture the essential features of these effective Hamiltonians, and systematically compare systems with and without hopping magnitude correlations to isolate the role of non-Gaussian (non-i.i.d.) correlations.

The constructed models show spectral gaps decaying faster than 1/L but slower than 1/L^2. AI.conclusion: Correlations among long-range hopping magnitudes are responsible for the [ln(L)]^2 entanglement scaling that seldom appears in ground states of conventional isolated quantum systems, identifying these correlations as the key mechanism behind the unusual scaling behavior in the monitored quantum dynamics.

title: Resolving the Magnetic Ground-State Controversy in RuO2 through A Flat Magnetic Energy Landscape
summary: Rutile RuO2 is a prominent candidate for altermagnetism, yet its magnetic ground state remains highly controversial, with experiments reporting either a nonmagnetic state or altermagnetic order. Here, we develop a generalized environment-dependent spin-lattice framework that unifies localized Heisenberg exchange, itinerant Stoner magnetism via Landau spin fluctuations, and spin-orbit-coupling-mediated spin-lattice interactions. Parameterized from a high-throughput first-principles database using machine-learning and solved by large-scale Monte Carlo simulations, the framework reveals an exceptionally flat magnetic energy landscape in RuO2, where the nonmagnetic state lies nearly degenerate with multiple altermagnetic configurations. We find that material perturbations, exemplified by intrinsic defects, select distinct magnetic ground states primarily by modifying the localized Heisenberg exchange, with perturbation-induced itinerant Stoner polarization provides an essential secondary contribution. Spin-orbit coupling controls the orientation and stability of the Néel vector, but does not determine the emergence of long-range magnetic order. These results provide a unified explanation for the conflicting experimental observations and establish a general microscopic framework for understanding how material perturbations select competing magnetic ground states in systems with nearly flat magnetic energy landscapes.

Material perturbations (e.g., defects) select distinct ground states primarily by modifying localized Heisenberg exchange, explaining conflicting experimental observations.
AI.motivation: The magnetic ground state of rutile RuO2 is highly controversial, with experiments reporting either nonmagnetic or altermagnetic order. A unified microscopic framework is needed to resolve this contradiction.

title: Interplay between Isomerization and Spin Crossover in 1D Fe-Indigo Coordination Polymers on Ag substrates
summary: Spin-crossover (SCO) compounds offer a route to switchable molecular functionality in reduced dimensions. However, one-dimensional (1D) SCO chains, which offer the possibility to study ligand fields other than the paradigmatic octahedral field, remain comparatively little studied. Here, we use first-principles density functional theory (DFT+$U$) to investigate Fe-indigo coordination-polymer chains synthesized experimentally on Ag(111) and Ag(100) substrates. These display a rich interplay between changes in ligand field (isomerization) and spin crossover. On-surface isomerization on Ag(111) interconverts (N,O)-chelated \textit{trans} configuration and (N,N)-/(O,O)-chelated \textit{cis} configurations at the Fe centers. The lowest-energy \textit{trans} and \textit{cis} solutions on Ag(111) have different spin configurations over the interval $0.66<U<3.00$~eV. At the reference value $U=1$~eV, the preferred \textit{trans} solution is the mixed LS--LS--HS configuration, whereas the preferred \textit{cis} solution is LS--LS--LS. The experimentally observed preference for \textit{cis} chains on Ag(111) and \textit{trans} chains on Ag(100) is reproduced for the range $0.88<U<3.75$~eV. To interpret these results, toy models and spin-resolved Fe $3d$ projected densities of states are used, while freestanding-chain calculations reveal a strain-sensitive LS--HS competition. These results provide a microscopic explanation for isomerization-controlled spin-state switching in a 1D coordination polymer.

AI.tldr: The paper uses first-principles DFT+U calculations to investigate Fe-indigo coordination-polymer chains on Ag(111) and Ag(100) substrates. It shows that on-surface isomerization interconverts trans and cis configurations at Fe centers, which couples to spin-crossover behavior, explaining the substrate-dependent preference for trans/cis chains and isomerization-controlled spin-state switching in a 1D coordination polymer.
AI.motivation: Spin-crossover (SCO) compounds enable switchable molecular functionality in reduced dimensions, but 1D SCO chains—which allow exploration of ligand fields beyond the paradigmatic octahedral case—remain poorly studied. The paper aims to fill this gap by investigating Fe-indigo coordination chains synthesized on silver surfaces.
AI.method: The authors employed first-principles density functional theory with Hubbard U corrections (DFT+U) to investigate Fe-indigo coordination-polymer chains on Ag(111) and Ag(100). They examined the ligand-field isomerization between (N,O)-chelated trans and (N,N)-/(O,O)-chelated cis configurations at Fe centers, computed spin configurations over a range of U values, and used toy models, spin-resolved Fe 3d projected densities of states, and freestanding-chain calculations for interpretation.

At U = 1 eV, the preferred trans solution is mixed LS-LS-HS while the preferred cis solution is LS-LS-LS. The experimentally observed substrate-dependent preference (cis on Ag(111), trans on Ag(100)) is reproduced for 0.88 < U < 3.75 eV. Freestanding-chain calculations reveal a strain-sensitive LS-HS competition.
AI.conclusion: The results provide a microscopic explanation for isomerization-controlled spin-state switching in a 1D coordination polymer, showing that ligand-field isomerization and spin crossover are intimately coupled and substrate-dependent in these systems.

title: A Superconducting Peierls Instability
comment: Main text: 11 pages, 5 figures; Methods: 7 pages, 1 figure; Supplementary Material: 12 pages, 5 figures
summary: The Peierls instability is a foundational mechanism in condensed matter physics, showing how the electron--phonon interaction can transform a simple metal into an insulating state with a new lattice periodicity. In a one-dimensional (1D) metal the Peierls instability follows from the enhanced electronic response at wavevector $Q=2k_F$ (connecting the Fermi points) producing a Kohn anomaly: a softening of the phonon mode at the same wavevector. Condensation of this mode then generates the tell-tale Peierls periodic lattice distortion and charge-density wave (CDW) that gaps the electronic spectrum. Here we show an analogous instability at the edge of a two-dimensional (2D) superconductor, where a dispersing Andreev bound state (ABS) hosts Bogoliubov Fermi points at $\pm k_c$. The enhanced quasiparticle response at the connecting wavevector $Q=2k_c$ couples directly to pairing-fluctuations and produces a superconducting Kohn anomaly: a softening of a pairing mode at the same wavevector. Condensation of this mode then generates an edge pair-density wave (PDW) that gaps the ABS. We refer to this as a superconducting Peierls instability and identify the boundary quasiparticle structure that enables it. As a concrete realization, we consider a square-lattice extended Hubbard model whose mixed-symmetry $s+d+ip$ state hosts a dispersing ABS with zero-energy crossings at finite edge momenta. Using self-consistent Bogoliubov--de Gennes (BdG) calculations we show that the order parameter develops an edge PDW, with the wavevector set by the superconducting Kohn anomaly, that gaps the ABS crossings. Our results identify a novel mechanism for spontaneous translation-symmetry breaking in a superconductor. As this superconducting Peierls mechanism does not require an extensive zero-energy flat band or topologically protected edge states, it may apply broadly to unconventional superconductors.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes an analogy between the Peierls instability in 1D metals (where electron-phonon coupling softens a phonon at Q=2k_F, leading to a CDW that gaps the spectrum) and a new "superconducting Peierls instability" at the edge of a 2D superconductor. Here, dispersing Andreev bound states (ABS) with Bogoliubov Fermi points at ±k_c produce a superconducting Kohn anomaly at Q=2k_c, whose condensation yields an edge pair-density wave (PDW) that gaps the ABS. The authors demonstrate this via self-consistent BdG calculations on a square-lattice extended Hubbard model with s+d+ip pairing.
AI.motivation: To discover a novel mechanism for spontaneous translation-symmetry breaking in superconductors, analogous to the Peierls instability in normal metals, that does not require topologically protected edge states or flat bands and may broadly apply to unconventional superconductors.
AI.method: The authors consider a square-lattice extended Hubbard model whose s+d+ip mixed-symmetry superconducting state hosts a dispersing Andreev bound state with zero-energy crossings at finite edge momenta. They perform self-consistent Bogoliubov–de Gennes (BdG) calculations to demonstrate that the order parameter develops an edge pair-density wave with wavevector set by the superconducting Kohn anomaly, which gaps the ABS crossings.
AI.result: The self-consistent BdG calculations show that the order parameter develops an edge PDW with a wavevector determined by the superconducting Kohn anomaly (Q=2k_c), which gaps the ABS zero-energy crossings. This confirms the existence of the superconducting Peierls instability and identifies the boundary quasiparticle structure enabling it.
AI.conclusion: The work identifies a novel "superconducting Peierls instability" mechanism for spontaneous translation-symmetry breaking at the edge of a superconductor. Since this mechanism does not require extensive zero-energy flat bands or topologically protected edge states, it could apply broadly to unconventional superconductors.

title: Low-Frequency Charge Noise in Bilayer Graphene Quantum Dots
summary: Bilayer graphene (BLG) quantum dots (QDs) are a promising platform for semiconductor qubits. However, the low-frequency charge noise that may ultimately limit coherence has remained largely unexplored. Here, we systematically characterize charge noise in gate-defined BLG QDs using transport-based noise spectroscopy. We extract a median amplitude of $ S_μ^{1/2} (1~\text{Hz}) = 1.16~μ\text{eV}/\sqrt{\text{Hz}}$, placing BLG well within the range reported for established semiconductor quantum-dot platforms. Across variations in charge occupation, confinement, source-drain bias, and charge-sensor operating conditions, neither the noise amplitude nor the spectral dependence shows a reproducible trend in electrostatic tuning, indicating that we extracted the intrinsic semiconductor noise. Consistent noise levels are further observed in double QDs and confirmed using an independent superconducting resonator-based dispersive readout. Extending the study to BLG devices incorporating transition metal dichalcogenide layers reveals no measurable charge noise increase in weakly proximitized QDs. These results validate BLG as a viable platform for coherent quantum information processing.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically characterizes low-frequency charge noise in gate-defined bilayer graphene quantum dots using transport-based noise spectroscopy, finding a median noise amplitude of 1.16 μeV/√Hz at 1 Hz—comparable to established semiconductor quantum-dot platforms. No reproducible trends with electrostatic tuning were observed, indicating intrinsic semiconductor noise, and results were corroborated in double quantum dots and via an independent superconducting resonator readout. Devices with transition metal dichalcogenide proximitization showed no measurable noise increase.
AI.motivation: Bilayer graphene quantum dots are promising for semiconductor qubits, but their low-frequency charge noise—which may ultimately limit coherence—had remained largely unexplored, motivating a systematic characterization.
AI.method: Transport-based noise spectroscopy was used to measure charge noise across variations in charge occupation, confinement, source-drain bias, and charge-sensor operating conditions. Results were validated in double quantum dots and with an independent superconducting resonator-based dispersive readout, and extended to BLG devices proximitized with transition metal dichalcogenide layers.

No reproducible systematic trend in electrostatic tuning was observed for either noise amplitude or spectral dependence, indicating intrinsic semiconductor noise. AI.conclusion: The findings validate bilayer graphene as a viable platform for coherent quantum information processing, with intrinsic charge noise levels comparable to established semiconductor quantum dot systems.

title: Overlimiting Ion Transport and Reaction Limitations in Charged Porous Media
summary: Electrochemical reaction rates are controlled by both interfacial charge-transfer kinetics and reactive-ion transport. In charged porous media, fixed charges enrich reactive counterions near pore walls, enabling transport beyond the classical diffusion limit via surface conduction (SC). Under overlimiting conditions, classical Butler-Volmer kinetics predict indefinitely increasing current with overpotential, contrasting with microscopic electron-transfer theories, which impose a finite reaction-limited current. Here, we couple the one-dimensional leaky membrane model to coupled ion-electron transfer (CIET) kinetics to examine the interplay between transport and reaction limitations. The limiting behavior is governed by the scaled surface charge $(\tildeρ_s)$ and a Damköhler number $(Da)$ comparing reaction-limited and diffusion-limited currents. We derive analytical limiting-current expressions for neutral, positive, and negatively charged porous media, mapping underlimiting-to-overlimiting transitions in the $(Da,\tildeρ_s)$ plane. By preventing reactive-ion depletion, SC restores polarization-curve sensitivity to charge-transfer kinetics that would otherwise be obscured by diffusion limitation. Fitting to published Cu electrodeposition data in charged AAO membranes yields $Da\approx24$. CIET parameters fitted to AAO($-$) also describe AAO($+$) and predict a finite AAO($-$) reaction limit beyond the applied voltage range. These results provide a framework for distinguishing transport-limited and reaction-limited responses in electrochemical systems and establish charged porous media as platforms to reveal electrochemical reaction-kinetic descriptors.

AI.tldr: The paper couples a one-dimensional leaky membrane model with coupled ion-electron transfer (CIET) kinetics to study how surface conduction and charge-transfer kinetics interact in charged porous media. The authors derive analytical limiting-current expressions for neutral and charged porous media based on scaled surface charge and a Damköhler number, mapping transport-to-reaction-limited transitions. Fitting to Cu electrodeposition data in charged AAO membranes yields Da≈24, and CIET parameters from negatively charged membranes successfully predict the positive-membrane behavior and a finite reaction-limited current.
AI.motivation: Classical Butler-Volmer kinetics predict indefinitely increasing current with overpotential under overlimiting conditions, contradicting microscopic electron-transfer theories that impose a finite reaction-limited current. The interplay between transport (surface conduction in charged pores) and reaction limitations has not been systematically examined, obscuring whether electrochemical responses are transport- or reaction-limited.
AI.method: The authors couple a one-dimensional leaky membrane model (including surface conduction from fixed charges) with coupled ion-electron transfer (CIET) kinetics. The behavior is governed by the scaled surface charge (ρ̃s) and a Damköhler number (Da) comparing reaction-limited to diffusion-limited currents. Analytical limiting-current expressions are derived for neutral, positively, and negatively charged porous media, and the model is fitted to published Cu electrodeposition data in charged AAO membranes.
AI.result: Surface conduction prevents reactive-ion depletion and restores the polarization curve's sensitivity to charge-transfer kinetics that would otherwise be masked by diffusion limitation. Mapping of underlimiting-to-overlimiting transitions in the (Da, ρ̃s) plane was achieved. Fitting yields Da≈24 for Cu electrodeposition in charged AAO membranes. CIET parameters fitted to AAO(−) also describe AAO(+) and predict a finite AAO(−) reaction-limited current beyond the applied voltage range.
AI.conclusion: The framework distinguishes transport-limited from reaction-limited responses in electrochemical systems, and establishes charged porous media as platforms for revealing electrochemical reaction-kinetic descriptors (e.g., Damköhler number and CIET parameters) that classical continuum models obscure under diffusion-limited conditions.

title: Large deviations for linear regressions

summary: Linear regression is one of the simplest and most widely used tools to learn patterns from data: it fits a set of coefficients so that a linear combination of predictors best matches observed responses. The quality of the fit is measured by the residual sum of squares, the total squared mismatch between predictions and data, whose minimum defines the training loss. We consider Gaussian design and noise, with teacher coefficients independently drawn from a general distribution $p(β)$, and a general class of separable regularizers, including Ridge and Lasso. Using the zero-temperature replica method, we compute analytically the large-deviation statistics of the minimum training loss for large numbers $P$ of predictors and $N$ of observations, with $r=P/N$ fixed. The rate function we compute governs rare sample-to-sample fluctuations of the optimal loss. Extensive numerical simulations are in excellent agreement with our theory and clearly show a pronounced deviation from the Gaussian regime of typical fluctuations in the tails.

AI.tldr: This paper analytically computes the large-deviation statistics of the minimum training loss in high-dimensional linear regression with Gaussian design/noise, general teacher coefficient prior p(β), and separable regularizers (including Ridge and Lasso), using the zero-temperature replica method. The derived rate function governs rare sample-to-sample fluctuations of the optimal loss, and numerical simulations confirm pronounced deviations from Gaussian typical fluctuations in the tails.
AI.motivation: While typical fluctuations of the training loss in high-dimensional linear regression are well understood, the rare-event (large-deviation) behavior of the minimum training loss has remained largely unexplored. Understanding these tail statistics is important for characterizing sample-to-sample variability and robustness of model fitting beyond the mean-field regime.

At fixed ratio r=P/N, they use the zero-temperature replica method to compute analytically the large-deviation rate function of the minimum training loss, accounting for rare fluctuations of the optimal loss across random samples.
