title: Symmetry-breaking line defects embedded to a 3D $O(N)$ critical bulk
summary: While spontaneous breaking of a discrete symmetry in one-dimensional classical systems with short-range interactions is absent, it is expected that a line defect embedded in a bulk criticality exhibits a stable discrete symmetry spontaneous breaking. Here, we investigate the behavior of a pinning-field line defect immersed in a 3D bulk that remains tuned to the $O(N)$ Wilson-Fisher critical point. Employing the fuzzy sphere technique, we provide convincing evidence of the existence of stable defect conformal fixed points, and we demonstrate their renormalization group stability by showing no relevant operator and less effective degrees of freedom than that at bulk fixed point via $g$-function. Moreover, we investigate the defect domain wall operator for various $N$, and we identify that it becomes irrelevance for $N\gtrsim 3$ but it is relevant for $N<3$.These evidence indicate that a one-dimensional defect coupled to a critical bulk cannot support a stable symmetry spontaneously broken defect fixed point due to domain wall proliferation for $N<3$ Wilson-Fisher universality, while in the case of $N \gtrsim 3$ a symmetry broken defect is possible.

AI.tldr: This paper studies a pinning-field line defect (1D) embedded in a 3D O(N) Wilson-Fisher critical bulk using the fuzzy sphere technique. They find stable defect conformal fixed points for various N, and show via g-function analysis that defect degrees of freedom are less than the bulk fixed point. Analysis of the defect domain wall operator reveals it is relevant for N<3 but irrelevant for N≳3, implying discrete symmetry-broken defect fixed points are unstable for N<3 (due to domain wall proliferation) but stable for N≳3.
AI.motivation: While discrete symmetry cannot be spontaneously broken in (1+1)D classical systems with short-range interactions, it is predicted that a line defect in a critical bulk might host stable symmetry breaking. This work aims to test this prediction by studying a 1D defect coupled to a 3D O(N) Wilson-Fisher critical bulk, which serves as an effective 2D (defect) critical system coupled to a higher-dimensional environment.
AI.method: The authors use the fuzzy sphere technique (a numerical conformal field theory method based on regularizing the theory on a sphere with fuzzy non-commutative geometry) to study a pinning-field line defect embedded in a 3D O(N) Wilson-Fisher critical bulk. They compute the defect g-function to compare effective degrees of freedom and analyze renormalization group stability by checking for relevant operators. They also investigate the defect domain wall operator's relevance as a function of N.
AI.result: Evidence for stable defect conformal fixed points is found. The g-function shows fewer effective degrees of freedom at the defect than at the bulk fixed point, confirming RG stability with no relevant operators. The defect domain wall operator is relevant for N<3 but becomes irrelevant for N≳3, determining the stability of symmetry-broken defect phases as a function of N.
AI.conclusion: A one-dimensional defect coupled to an O(N) Wilson-Fisher critical bulk cannot host a stable spontaneously symmetry-broken defect fixed point for N<3 due to domain wall proliferation. However, for N≳3, a symmetry-broken defect fixed point is possible and stable.

title: An Ultrathin Laterally Conductive Mesh Interphase Enables Spatially Extended Zinc Deposition for Aqueous Zinc Batteries
summary: Zn metal anodes often suffer from nonuniform interfacial reactions during cycling, resulting in uneven deposition and dendrite growth. Existing artificial interphases can mitigate side reactions or regulate nucleation, but rarely achieve regulation of the interfacial electron/field distribution to sustain uniform deposition at the evolving Zn/electrolyte interface. Here, we develop an Au mesh interphase (AuMI), an ultrathin two-dimensional Au aerogel network that couples lateral electron redistribution with open pathways for ions. During Zn plating/stripping, the conductive AuMI distributes electron transport across the Zn surface, while its porous mesh preserves Zn$^{2+}$ access, enabling more uniform interfacial reactions. Experiments and simulations show that AuMI homogenizes the interfacial electric field and current distribution, promotes more uniform Zn plating/stripping, and limits dendrite growth. As a result, this regulated interfacial reaction mode enables AuMI Zn symmetric cells to operate stably for 3000 h at 1 mA cm$^{-2}$/1 mAh cm$^{-2}$ and for 1100 h at 10 mA cm$^{-2}$/10 mAh cm$^{-2}$, while AuMI Zn||NVO (NaV$_3$O$_8$\cdot$1.5H$_2$O) full cells retain 80.8 % capacity after over 5000 cycles at 1 A g$^{-1}$. These findings highlight the importance of combining ultrathin architecture, lateral electron transport, and open Zn2+ access in artificial interphases for stable aqueous Zn metal anodes.

AuMI enables 3000 h stability at 1 mA cm⁻² and 1100 h at 10 mA cm⁻² in symmetric cells, and 80.8% capacity retention over 5000 cycles in Zn||NVO full cells.
AI.motivation: Zn metal anodes suffer from nonuniform interfacial reactions causing uneven deposition and dendrite growth. Existing artificial interphases only mitigate side reactions or regulate nucleation but rarely achieve simultaneous regulation of interfacial electron/field distribution at the evolving Zn/electrolyte interface, which is needed for sustained uniform deposition.

The conductive AuMI distributes electron transport across the Zn surface while its porous structure preserves Zn²⁺ access. Experiments and simulations were used to characterize interfacial electric field homogenization and current distribution, along with electrochemical testing in symmetric and full cells.

AuMI Zn symmetric cells operated stably for 3000 h at 1 mA cm⁻²/1 mAh cm⁻² and 1100 h at 10 mA cm⁻²/10 mAh cm⁻². AuMI Zn||NVO full cells retained 80.8% capacity after over 5000 cycles at 1 A g⁻¹.
AI.conclusion: Combining ultrathin architecture, lateral electron transport, and open Zn²⁺ access in artificial interphases is critical for stable aqueous Zn metal anodes, highlighting the design principle of coupling electron/field regulation with ion accessibility for next-generation interphase engineering.

title: Weak-coupling theory of half-metals and other fractional metallic phases in biased doped Bernal bilayer graphene
summary: The paper presents a theoretical study of many-body electronic phases in doped and electrically biased Bernal-stacked (AB) bilayer graphene. We develop a variational mean-field theory with no fitted parameters. For the electron-electron interaction, we employ a parameter-free random-phase approximation to model the short-range screened Coulomb repulsion. The remaining long-range Coulomb potential energy is dictated by the geometry of the sample, behaving as a parallel-plate capacitor. We formulate the theory directly in terms of the experimentally controlled displacement field $\frak D$ rather than the interaction-renormalized interlayer potential difference. It makes our theory better suited for direct comparison with experiment. The resulting phase diagram is quite rich. It hosts several fractional-metal states connected by first- and second-order transitions. At higher bias and doping, three distinct fractional metallic states emerge. We classify these phases by the number of doped sectors and the symmetry of the order parameters. Our results - obtained without any parameter fitting - reproduce key qualitative and quantitative features of recent experiments. This includes the energy scale associated with the loss of fractional metallic order. At lower bias and doping, the model stabilizes a broad spectrum of fractional-metal phases with more exotic symmetry-breaking patterns. This suggests that further experimental exploration of the latter regime is warranted.

AI.motivation: To provide a theory with no fitted parameters that can be directly compared with experiments on biased Bernal-stacked bilayer graphene, particularly in understanding fractional metallic phases and their energy scales.
AI.method: A variational mean-field theory with no fitting parameters, employing a parameter-free random-phase approximation for short-range screened Coulomb repulsion while treating long-range Coulomb interactions as a parallel-plate capacitor potential dictated by sample geometry. The theory is formulated directly in terms of the experimentally controlled displacement field (rather than the interaction-renormalized interlayer potential difference).

At higher bias and doping, three distinct fractional metallic states emerge, classified by the number of doped sectors and symmetry of order parameters. At lower bias and doping, a broader spectrum of fractional-metal phases with more exotic symmetry-breaking patterns is stabilized. The results reproduce key qualitative and quantitative experimental features, including the energy scale of fractional-metallic order loss.
AI.conclusion: The parameter-free theory successfully captures experimental observations in biased bilayer graphene and predicts additional fractional-metal phases at lower bias and doping, suggesting that further experimental exploration of this regime is warranted.

title: Stochastic Tensor Contraction for Efficient MP2 Exchange
summary: Second-order Moller--Plesset perturbation theory (MP2) is one of the simplest correlated wave-function methods, but its conventional $O(N^5)$ cost limits its application to large systems. Stochastic tensor contraction (STC) has recently appeared as a general technique to evaluate high-order tensor contractions in quantum chemistry. Here, we apply STC to the exchange contribution of Laplace-transformed MP2, which is the source of $O(N^5)$ scaling in the formulation. The resulting STC exchange algorithm has an $O(N^3)$ deterministic setup cost and an $O(N^2)$ stochastic cost at fixed absolute error. The estimator is unbiased and provides a way to specify the target stochastic error by estimating the number of required samples before the full calculation. We implement the algorithm using a hybrid deterministic--stochastic evaluation strategy, with grouped index sampling, to reduce the computational prefactor. Over a range of benchmark molecules containing up to $\sim 7000$ basis functions, the stochastic exchange evaluation takes as little as $1/270$ of the time of a complete DF-MP2 calculation on the same system. Within the Laplace-transformed formulation, the $O(N^4)$ scaling direct contribution is thus the only significant cost. Our results further substantiate the power of STC to serve as a general tensor-contraction engine for quantum chemistry.

AI.tldr: The paper applies stochastic tensor contraction (STC) to the exchange contribution of Laplace-transformed MP2, reducing its O(N^5) scaling to O(N^3) deterministic setup and O(N^2) stochastic cost. Using a hybrid deterministic-stochastic strategy with grouped index sampling, the method achieves up to 270x speedup in exchange evaluation compared to full DF-MP2 on benchmark molecules with ~7000 basis functions.
AI.motivation: MP2 is a widely used correlated wave-function method, but its conventional O(N^5) computational cost limits application to large molecular systems. The exchange contribution in Laplace-transformed MP2 is the primary source of this scaling, so reducing its cost is key to enabling MP2 for larger systems.
AI.method: The authors apply stochastic tensor contraction (STC) to evaluate the exchange contribution of Laplace-transformed MP2. The approach features an unbiased estimator with O(N^3) deterministic setup cost and O(N^2) stochastic cost at fixed absolute error. The number of required samples can be pre-estimated before full calculation, and a hybrid deterministic-stochastic evaluation strategy with grouped index sampling is used to lower the computational prefactor.
AI.result: On benchmark molecules with up to ~7000 basis functions, the stochastic exchange evaluation takes as little as 1/270 of the time of a complete density-fitted MP2 (DF-MP2) calculation on the same system. This leaves the O(N^4)-scaling direct contribution as the only significant cost in the Laplace-transformed formulation.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate that STC serves as an effective general tensor-contraction engine for quantum chemistry, substantially reducing the cost of the exchange term in MP2 and extending the applicability of MP2 to larger molecular systems.

title: Death by mutants: unusual multicritical dynamics in a two-species model for absorbing state transitions
summary: We explore the phases and active-to-absorbing state phase transitions (AAPT) in a two-species model, where the species A and its mutant B are {\em asymmetrically} or {\em nonreciprocally} coupled. We identify a multicritical point that connects the global absorbing state of both the species and its mutant, with a uniform active state. The critical dynamics at this multicritical point is studied within the lowest order perturbation theory. This asymmetric coupling between species A and mutant B leads to unequal and distinct upper critical dimensions $d_c^A$ and $d_c^B$ respectively for A and B dynamics. We show that the multicritical point in this model is characterised by an unusual breakdown of scale-invariance by fluctuation-induced logarithmic modulations with power law behaviour of the order parameter and correlation lengths of the species A at all dimensions $d<d_c^A$. Above $d_c^A$, conventional scale-invariance is restored. The dynamics of the mutant species B belongs to the DP universality class with an upper critical dimension of $d_c^B=4$

AI.tldr: This paper studies active-to-absorbing state phase transitions in a two-species model with asymmetric (nonreciprocal) coupling between a species A and its mutant B. The authors identify a multicritical point connecting a global absorbing state to a uniform active state. The asymmetric coupling yields distinct upper critical dimensions for the two species (dc^A and dc^B). At the multicritical point below dc^A, scale invariance breaks down via fluctuation-induced logarithmic modulations, while the mutant B dynamics belongs to the directed percolation (DP) universality class with dc^B=4.
AI.motivation: To understand how nonreciprocal or asymmetric coupling between two species (a host species and its mutant) alters phase structure and critical behavior in non-equilibrium absorbing-state transitions, particularly whether novel universality classes and unusual critical phenomena emerge from such couplings.
AI.method: Analytical study of a two-species model with asymmetric coupling using renormalization-group/lowest-order perturbation theory. The analysis identifies a multicritical point and computes critical dynamics, upper critical dimensions for each species separately, and examines the scaling behavior of order parameters and correlation lengths.
AI.result: A multicritical point connects the global absorbing state with a uniform active state. The asymmetric coupling produces unequal upper critical dimensions dc^A and dc^B for A and B, respectively. Below dc^A, species A exhibits a breakdown of scale-invariance with fluctuation-induced logarithmic modulations superimposed on power-law behaviors of the order parameter and correlation lengths; conventional scale invariance is recovered above dc^A. Species B's dynamics belong to the directed percolation universality class with dc^B=4.
AI.conclusion: Nonreciprocal coupling between species and mutant leads to novel multicritical behavior where scale invariance is anomalously broken below an upper critical dimension, yet the mutant species still belongs to the standard directed percolation universality class. This reveals that asymmetry in coupling can fundamentally alter critical dynamics of one species while preserving conventional universality for the other.

title: Studying line defect at Deconfined Quantum Criticality via fuzzy sphere regularization
summary: The interplay between bulk critical fluctuations and nontrivial topology can enrich defect physics and give rise to novel defect universality classes. Understanding the fate of such defects therefore constitutes an important open problem. In this work, we studied a particularly simple setting: a (0+1)-dimensional pinning-field defect coupled to a (2+1)-dimensional deconfined quantum critical bulk. Using the fuzzy-sphere regularization, we numerically investigated the defect operator spectrum and extracted several universal quantities characterizing the defect conformal fixed point, including the scaling dimensions of defect-changing(creating) operators and the defect \(g\)-function. These results establish the first numerical characterization of line-defect conformal data at deconfined quantum criticality and may stimulate further investigations of defect critical phenomena in topological quantum critical matter.

AI.tldr: The authors numerically study a (0+1)-dimensional pinning-field defect coupled to a (2+1)-dimensional deconfined quantum critical bulk using the fuzzy-sphere regularization, extracting universal defect conformal data including scaling dimensions of defect-changing/creating operators and the defect g-function—establishing the first numerical characterization of line-defect conformal data at deconfined quantum criticality.
AI.motivation: Understanding how bulk critical fluctuations interact with nontrivial topology to modify defect physics is an open problem. This work aims to probe whether defects at deconfined quantum critical points form novel universality classes distinct from conventional critical phenomena.
AI.method: The authors employ a (0+1)-dimensional pinning-field defect coupled to a (2+1)-dimensional deconfined quantum critical bulk, regularized using the fuzzy-sphere approach. They numerically investigate the defect operator spectrum and compute universal quantities characterizing the defect conformal fixed point, including scaling dimensions of defect-changing(creating) operators and the defect g-function.
AI.result: The numerical simulations yield the defect operator spectrum and several universal quantities at the defect conformal fixed point, establishing the first numerical characterization of line-defect conformal data at deconfined quantum criticality.
AI.conclusion: The results provide the first numerical access to defect conformal data in deconfined quantum critical systems, opening the door for further investigations of defect critical phenomena in topological quantum critical matter.

title: Thermal history controls the optoelectronic response of lead halide perovskites through structure and dynamics
summary: Lead halide perovskites are promising optoelectronic materials for photovoltaics, light emission and detection. Their efficiencies in PV now approach the detailed-balance limit, leaving stability as the principal barrier. The intrinsic instabilities studied to date centre on ionic motion within a fixed, homogeneous lattice. Here we identify a further source of intrinsic structural instability, hidden in the lattice dynamics. Mapping caesium, methylammonium and formamidinium-based compositions with Cl, Br, I and mixed X-sites through all accessible phases, using single crystal X-ray and neutron diffuse scattering, machine-learning-assisted molecular dynamics, a phenomenological octahedral tilt model and hyperspectral photoluminescence, we find that nearly every composition hosts equilibrium local structural fluctuations: dynamic nanodomains of correlated octahedral tilts, a few nanometres in size, that locally break the crystallographic symmetry. Three complementary levers control them. The A-site cation sets their symmetry, shape and anisotropy, from sparse, isotropic and tetragonal in formamidinium-based compositions to dense, anisotropic and orthorhombic in nominally cubic caesium-based ones, the most locally disordered we studied. The halide controls the dynamic disorder and the phase-transition sequence. Thermal history is the third: different ramp rates drive nominally identical compositions into distinct crystallographic phases, each with its own hidden local order. In MAPbI3, the heating rate alone changes the photoluminescence quantum efficiency across the phase transition. Because these transitions lie within device operating ranges, from terrestrial thermal cycling to the extremes of space, thermal history may shape the local structure, and hence the optoelectronic response, throughout fabrication and operation, establishing it as a design variable alongside composition.

AI.tldr: Lead halide perovskites harbor a previously unrecognized source of intrinsic structural instability: equilibrium dynamic nanodomains of correlated octahedral tilts (a few nm in size) that locally break crystallographic symmetry across nearly all compositions. These are controlled by three levers—A-site cation (symmetry/shape/anisotropy), halide (dynamic disorder and phase-transition sequence), and thermal history (ramp rate selects distinct crystallographic phases with different local order)—and can alter photoluminescence quantum efficiency, making thermal history a design variable alongside composition.
AI.motivation: Lead halide perovskites approach the detailed-balance efficiency limit in photovoltaics, leaving stability as the principal obstacle. Prior studies of intrinsic instability focused only on ionic motion within a fixed, homogeneous lattice, missing additional structural instability sources that could affect device performance and longevity.
AI.method: The authors combined single-crystal X-ray and neutron diffuse scattering, machine-learning-assisted molecular dynamics, a phenomenological octahedral tilt model, and hyperspectral photoluminescence to map Cs, MA and FA-based compositions with Cl, Br, I and mixed X-sites across all accessible phases.
AI.result: Nearly every composition hosts equilibrium local structural fluctuations: dynamic nanodomains of correlated octahedral tilts (~nm scale) that locally break crystallographic symmetry. A-site cation sets symmetry/shape/anisotropy (from sparse isotropic tetragonal in FA to dense anisotropic orthorhombic in nominally cubic Cs—the most locally disordered). Halide controls dynamic disorder and phase-transition sequence. Thermal history is a third lever: different ramp rates drive identical compositions into distinct phases, and in MAPbI3 heating rate alone changes PL quantum efficiency across the phase transition.
AI.conclusion: Because these phase transitions lie within device operating ranges (from terrestrial thermal cycling to space extremes), thermal history can shape local structure and thus optoelectronic performance throughout fabrication and operation. Thermal history should therefore be treated as a design variable alongside compositional tuning for lead halide perovskites.

title: Wavefunctions for Anyon Superconductors
summary: Anyon superconductivity arises from the condensation of mobile anyons rather than from a conventional Cooper instability, yet a systematic wavefunction description remains lacking. We develop a hierarchy-wavefunction construction for superconducting states derived from parent topological orders and identify their off-diagonal long-range order, condensate charge, chiral central charge, and residual topological order through the plasma analogy and topological field theories. We construct Abelian and non-Abelian examples descending from the semion state, a $ν=2/3$ hierarchy state, the $ν=1/3$ Laughlin state, $ν=1$ integer quantum Hall state, and Pfaffian state. Remarkably, for the semion case, the superconducting many-semion wavefunction is equivalent to a state of fermionized anyons filling two effective Landau levels, recovering Laughlin's original construction of semion superconductor. Finally, we show that hierarchy wavefunctions emerge naturally in the dilute, long-distance limit of the anyon-Hilbert-space formulation, which applies to ideal Chern bands and moiré bands of twisted bilayer MoTe$_2$. Our results establish a unified wavefunction-level framework linking anyon condensation, superconducting order, and topological field theory.

AI.tldr:
This paper develops a hierarchy-wavefunction construction for anyon superconductivity, establishing a unified framework linking anyon condensation, superconducting order, and topological field theory through off-diagonal long-range order, condensate charge, chiral central charge, and residual topological order.

The work constructs both Abelian and non-Abelian examples down from parent topological orders (semion, ν=2/3 hierarchy, ν=1/3 Laughlin, ν=1 IQH, and Pfaffian states), notably recovering Laughlin's original construction of the semion superconductor, and shows these wavefunctions emerge in the dilute limit applicable to ideal Chern bands and twisted bilayer MoTe₂.
AI.motivation: While anyon superconductivity is known to arise from the condensation of mobile anyons rather than a conventional Cooper instability, a systematic wavefunction-level description has been lacking. The paper aims to fill this gap by providing a unified formulation connecting anyon condensation, superconducting order, and topological field theory at the wavefunction level.

They use the plasma analogy and topological field theories to diagnose off-diagonal long-range order, condensate charge, chiral central charge, and residual topological order. They also establish the connection to the anyon-Hilbert-space formulation in the dilute, long-distance limit relevant to ideal (moiré) Chern bands.

title: Generalized s-d model for Wannier-Mott excitons in layered magnetic semiconductors
summary: The recent discovery of excitons coupled to the magnetic order, and the consequent strong magneto-optic responses, in some van der Waals magnetic semiconductors has triggered intense activity at the interface of magnetism and semiconductor optics. Here, we present an analytically tractable minimal model that describes magnetic order, electrons, holes, and excitons within a unified framework, thereby capturing a wide range of phenomena. It treats the magnetic order and itinerant carriers to be comprised by distinct electronic orbitals that are mutually coupled via orbital-dependent onsite exchange, similar to the treatment of metallic magnets using an s-d model. Investigating CrSBr bilayer as a case study, we benchmark our model and its predictions against recent experimental and ab-initio results finding good agreement as well as new insights enabled by the model's simplicity. Examining the optical selection rules, we find the conservation of a quantum number formed from a combination of spin and layer pseudospin to be a useful guiding principle, even in noncollinear magnetic configurations. Our analysis finds a series of bright and dark excitonic states in such layered A-type antiferromagnets. The presented framework should be valuable in achieving intuitive understanding of recently discovered excitonic phenomena and guiding the discovery of other excitonic states in layered magnetic semiconductors.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an analytically tractable minimal model unifying magnetic order, electrons, holes, and excitons in van der Waals magnetic semiconductors, benchmarked against CrSBr bilayer experiments and ab-initio results.
AI.motivation: Recent discovery of excitons coupled to magnetic order with strong magneto-optic responses in van der Waals magnetic semiconductors has motivated a need for an intuitive, unified theoretical framework to understand these phenomena.
AI.method: Develops a minimal analytical model analogous to the s-d model for metallic magnets, treating magnetic order and itinerant carriers as distinct electronic orbitals coupled via orbital-dependent onsite exchange. The model is benchmarked against CrSBr bilayer as a case study.
AI.result: The model shows good agreement with experimental and ab-initio results for CrSBr. It reveals a conserved quantum number combining spin and layer pseudospin that guides optical selection rules even in noncollinear magnetic configurations, and identifies a series of bright and dark excitonic states in layered A-type antiferromagnets.
AI.conclusion: The presented framework provides an intuitive understanding of recently discovered excitonic phenomena and offers guiding principles for discovering new excitonic states in layered magnetic semiconductors.

title: Diabatic Seam Space Sampling for Hydrogen Tunneling Systems with Nuclear-Electronic Orbital Theory
summary: Hydrogen tunneling is central to many chemical and biological processes. Herein, we introduce the vibronic-SHAKE (V-SHAKE) approach to comprehensively sample energy-conserving molecular configurations enabling hydrogen tunneling. A constrained form of nuclear-electronic orbital multistate density functional theory (NEO-MSDFT) dynamics, where the tunneling hydrogen nucleus is quantized, is used to sample geometries in the diabatic seam space corresponding to the intersection of the reactant and product NEO-DFT diabatic vibronic surfaces. V-SHAKE is applied to hydrogen and deuterium tunneling in 4-cyanobutanolate and Z-4-hydroxybut-3-en-2-one. The vibronic coupling is found to vary significantly in the diabatic seam space, mainly due to changes in the donor-acceptor distance. The reaction coordinate and gradient of the vibronic coupling at the minimum energy crossing point are nearly orthogonal and are dominated by motions stabilizing the product relative to the reactant or decreasing the donor-acceptor distance, respectively. V-SHAKE provides fundamental insights and validation for assumptions underlying rate theories.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces vibronic-SHAKE (V-SHAKE), a new method for sampling energy-conserving molecular configurations that enable hydrogen tunneling, using constrained nuclear-electronic orbital multistate density functional theory (NEO-MSDFT) dynamics. The method quantizes the tunneling hydrogen nucleus to sample geometries in the diabatic seam space (intersection of reactant and product NEO-DFT diabatic vibronic surfaces). Applied to hydrogen/deuterium tunneling in 4-cyanobutanolate and Z-4-hydroxybut-3-en-2-one, it reveals that vibronic coupling varies significantly in the seam space mainly due to donor-acceptor distance changes, and that the reaction coordinate and vibronic coupling gradient at the minimum energy crossing point are nearly orthogonal, dominated by product-stabilizing motions and donor-acceptor distance reduction, respectively.
AI.motivation: Hydrogen tunneling is central to many chemical and biological processes, yet comprehensive sampling of molecular configurations that enable tunneling has been lacking. There is a need to go beyond simplified assumptions in rate theories and to map the diabatic seam space where hydrogen tunneling occurs.
AI.method: V-SHAKE employs a constrained form of nuclear-electronic orbital multistate density functional theory (NEO-MSDFT) dynamics in which the tunneling hydrogen nucleus is quantized. The approach samples energy-conserving geometries within the diabatic seam space—the intersection of reactant and product NEO-DFT diabatic vibronic surfaces—enabling systematic exploration of tunneling-competent configurations.
AI.result: V-SHAKE was applied to hydrogen and deuterium tunneling in 4-cyanobutanolate and Z-4-hydroxybut-3-en-2-one. Vibronic coupling was found to vary significantly across the diabatic seam space, primarily driven by changes in the donor-acceptor distance. At the minimum energy crossing point, the reaction coordinate and the gradient of the vibronic coupling are nearly orthogonal: the reaction coordinate is dominated by motions stabilizing the product relative to the reactant, while the vibronic coupling gradient is dominated by motions decreasing the donor-acceptor distance.
AI.conclusion: V-SHAKE provides fundamental insights into hydrogen tunneling and offers validation for the assumptions underlying rate theories, establishing a framework for comprehensively sampling tunneling-competent molecular configurations in quantum nuclear dynamics.

title: Accelerating stochastic processes through nonequilibrium driving: Thermodynamic constraints on the maximum speed-up
summary: We derive a new set of bounds controlling the speed-up of the survival rate of trajectory-dependent observables induced by the application of a perturbation. Via the study of survival probabilities in two different contexts, continuous-time Markov jump processes and overdamped diffusions, we obtain different fashions of the bound on the achievable boost. These bounds, obtained by a nonlinear response theory of constrained path probabilities, are explicitly linked to thermodynamics. For arbitrary time-dependent survival rates, we find a linear bound that depends on both the perturbation strength and the entropy production rate prior to the perturbation. For rare processes characterized by a constant survival rate, the bound is exponential and is determined by the excess heat generated by the perturbation. We exemplify the inequalities on two prototypical model systems, namely, a unicyclic network and forced diffusion in a bistable potential.

AI.tldr: The paper derives new bounds on how much a perturbation can accelerate the survival rate of trajectory-dependent observables in stochastic systems, linking these bounds to thermodynamic quantities such as entropy production and excess heat.
AI.motivation: To understand the fundamental thermodynamic limits on how much a perturbation can enhance the survival probability of rare or trajectory-dependent events, connecting kinetic acceleration to thermodynamic costs.
AI.method: The authors employ nonlinear response theory of constrained path probabilities for two stochastic frameworks: continuous-time Markov jump processes and overdamped diffusions. They derive bounds on survival-rate speed-up—a linear bound for arbitrary time-dependent survival rates (depending on perturbation strength and prior entropy production rate) and an exponential bound for rare processes with constant survival rates (determined by excess heat).
AI.result: Two distinct bounds are obtained: a linear bound for general time-dependent survival rates tied to the entropy production rate, and an exponential bound for constant-rate rare processes linked to excess heat. The inequalities are validated on a unicyclic network and forced diffusion in a bistable potential.
AI.conclusion: The derived thermodynamic bounds provide a general framework connecting the achievable speed-up of survival probabilities to dissipation, offering practical limits for accelerating rare events in stochastic systems.

title: Such stuff as magic is made on: compact operator algebra, stabilizer polytope and the structure of reduced density matrices in a Kitaev spin liquid
summary: Quantum many-body systems exhibit rich and complex behaviour. Magic has recently emerged as a powerful new diagnostic for probing such systems, complementing other key features such as many-body entanglement. Here, starting from an investigation of the onset of magic within subsystems of a larger many-body quantum system, we show that intricate structures emerge which shed important light on the underlying many-body physics. Focusing on the Kitaev honeycomb model, we first identify the temperature below which local subsystems acquire magic. Remarkably, we find that the optimal magic witnesses active at the onset of magic reveal compact operator spaces that continue to capture the local thermal states throughout their subsequent evolution. For the six-site hexagonal marginal, this connection can be made stronger: the same operator space emerges independently from the symmetries of the local marginal and forms the symmetry-resolved plaquette algebra. When these symmetries are realized exactly, the local state lies entirely within this algebra and the reduced robustness of magic is equal to the full robustness of magic. The same reduced description can also be applied to other local quantum resources, which we illustrate using genuine multipartite entanglement. Furthermore, the operator spaces possess a rich algebraic structure in the form of finite-dimensional Euclidean Jordan algebras, with a natural interpretation in terms of bond and bond-cycle operators. Our general methodology therefore show how the onset of local magic can reveal a compact, physically meaningful operator structure underlying the finite-temperature Kitaev spin liquid, and opens up a new avenue towards reduced descriptions of quantum resources in many-body systems.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the onset of "magic" (a quantum resource measure) in local subsystems of the Kitaev honeycomb model, revealing that the operator spaces active at the magic onset form compact Euclidean Jordan algebras that faithfully capture local thermal states. For the six-site hexagonal marginal, these spaces coincide with the symmetry-resolved plaquette algebra, where reduced robustness of magic equals full robustness. The framework extends to other quantum resources like genuine multipartite entanglement.
AI.motivation: Magic has emerged as a powerful new diagnostic for probing many-body quantum systems, complementing entanglement. However, little is known about how magic emerges locally within finite-temperature many-body systems, and whether the onset of local magic can reveal underlying operator structures of physical relevance in quantum spin liquids.
AI.method: The authors investigate the Kitaev honeycomb model and identify the critical temperature below which local subsystems acquire magic. They analyze the operator spaces supporting the optimal magic witnesses at onset, study their evolution with temperature, and examine the six-site hexagonal marginal where the operator space coincides with a symmetry-resolved plaquette algebra. They also characterize the algebraic structure of these spaces as finite-dimensional Euclidean Jordan algebras associated with bond and bond-cycle operators, and extend the reduced description to other resources such as genuine multipartite entanglement.
AI.result: They find that (i) the optimal magic witnesses at onset reveal compact operator spaces that continue to capture local thermal states throughout their evolution; (ii) for the six-site hexagonal marginal the same operator space emerges from the local marginal symmetries, forming the symmetry-resolved plaquette algebra; (iii) when symmetries are exactly realized, the local state lies entirely within this algebra and reduced robustness of magic equals full robustness; (iv) the operator spaces form finite-dimensional Euclidean Jordan algebras with an interpretation in terms of bond and bond-cycle operators; (v) the reduced description applies to other resources, e.g., genuine multipartite entanglement.
AI.conclusion: The onset of local magic reveals a compact, physically meaningful operator structure underlying the finite-temperature Kitaev spin liquid, opening a new avenue toward reduced descriptions of quantum resources in many-body systems.

title: A Strategy Toward Room Temperature Topological Hall Effect via Local Moment Magnetism
summary: Topological spin textures in local moment systems hold great promise for technological applications due to their large magnetic moments, strong spin-orbit coupling (SOC), and high tunability. Finding new spin textures that are stable near room temperature is paramount to maximizing their potential for applications. Here, we provide a strategy for realizing topological spin textures at high temperatures by identifying rare earth ($R$) magnets ordering at or near room temperature. We demonstrate the feasibility of this strategy in one of these magnets, hexagonal Gd$_5$Pb$_3$, which orders at $T_C$ = 285 K. The indication for topological spin textures comes from topological Hall effect (THE), which, in Gd$_5$Pb$_3$, occurs between $T$ = 100 - 200 K, an order of magnitude higher temperature than in other reported $R$-based systems. Our results present an opportunity to explore the role of SOC, anisotropic exchange, geometric frustration, and magnetic interactions in stabilizing topological spin textures, and provide a pathway toward realizing them near room temperature in $R$-based magnets.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a strategy for realizing topological spin textures at high temperatures in rare-earth (R) magnets and demonstrates it in hexagonal Gd5Pb3, which orders at TC = 285 K. Topological Hall effect (THE) is observed between 100-200 K—an order of magnitude higher than in other R-based systems—offering a pathway toward room-temperature topological spin textures.
AI.motivation: Topological spin textures in local-moment systems have high application potential due to large magnetic moments, strong spin-orbit coupling, and tunability, but finding textures stable near room temperature remains a key challenge for practical use.
AI.method: The strategy involves identifying rare-earth magnets that order magnetically at or near room temperature, then probing for topological spin textures via the topological Hall effect (THE) as an experimental signature. Feasibility is demonstrated in hexagonal Gd5Pb3 (TC = 285 K).
AI.result: Gd5Pb3 exhibits topological Hall effect between 100-200 K, which is an order of magnitude higher in temperature than previously reported in other rare-earth-based systems, indicating the presence of topological spin textures at elevated temperatures.
AI.conclusion: The work provides an experimental pathway toward achieving topological spin textures near room temperature in rare-earth-based magnets and opens opportunities to investigate the roles of spin-orbit coupling, anisotropic exchange, geometric frustration, and magnetic interactions in stabilizing these textures.

title: Generative Nested Sampling of Atomistic Thermodynamic Landscapes
summary: Nested sampling (NS) resolves the thermodynamics of an atomistic system from a single simulation, but its practical reach is limited by the Markov-chain updates needed to decorrelate walkers within each likelihood-constrained ensemble. Flow-based NS has removed this bottleneck for gravitational-wave (GW) inference, yet its transfer to atomistic systems is not merely a change of application. Comparing a GW150914-like binary-black-hole likelihood with an eight-particle two-dimensional Lennard-Jones (LJ) system of comparable dimensionality, we show that the two landscapes differ fundamentally: atomistic multimodality is discrete and combinatorial, generated by particle permutations separated by hard collision walls, and its coordinate coupling is dense and collective, whereas the GW posterior exhibits smooth degeneracies and localized parameter coupling. Guided by this diagnosis, we introduce NS-Flows: a single conditional normalizing flow, conditioned on the NS energy bound and trained on a sliding window of recent live sets, that replaces MCMC by direct parallel draws corrected by importance-weighted rejection resampling. Live sets supply data self-consistently, allowing flow training without structured priors or a pre-existing dataset. For LJ disks in PBC, the algorithm reduces energy evaluations by over two orders of magnitude and wall-clock time by roughly one third, an advantage that becomes increasingly favorable as the cost of the potential grows. The flow's generation efficiency further acts as a physical diagnostic: it varies non-monotonically along the annealing trajectory, is lowest in the dense disordered regime, and is quantitatively captured by the constrained ensemble's internal mode complexity together with target drift across the training window, identifying liquid-like ensembles, rather than prior-target separation, as the hard case for current flow architectures.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces NS-Flows, a conditional normalizing flow-based nested sampling algorithm for atomistic systems. It diagnoses why flow-based NS cannot directly transfer from gravitational-wave inference to molecular systems (due to discrete combinatorial multimodality from particle permutations and dense collective coupling), then uses a single flow conditioned on the NS energy bound and trained on sliding live sets to replace MCMC. For Lennard-Jones disks in periodic boundary conditions, it reduces energy evaluations by over two orders of magnitude and wall-clock time by ~1/3, while flow generation efficiency serves as a physical diagnostic of ensemble complexity.
AI.motivation: Nested sampling resolves the thermodynamics of atomistic systems from one simulation, but is bottlenecked by costly MCMC decorrelation of walkers within likelihood-constrained ensembles. While flow-based NS has removed this bottleneck for gravitational-wave inference, a direct transfer to atomistic systems fails because the two posterior landscapes are fundamentally different in their multimodality and coupling structure, so a new approach tailored to atomistic systems is needed.
AI.method: The authors first compare a GW150914-like BBH likelihood with an 8-particle 2D Lennard-Jones system of comparable dimensionality, diagnosing fundamental landscape differences (discrete combinatorial multimodality from particle permutations separated by hard collision walls vs. smooth degeneracies; dense collective coordinate coupling vs. localized coupling). They then introduce NS-Flows: a single conditional normalizing flow conditioned on the NS energy bound and trained on a sliding window of recent live sets, which replaces MCMC with direct parallel draws corrected by importance-weighted rejection resampling. Live sets supply training data self-consistently, requiring no structured priors or pre-existing datasets.
AI.result: For LJ disks in periodic boundary conditions, NS-Flows reduces energy evaluations by over two orders of magnitude and wall-clock time by roughly one third, with advantages growing as potential costs increase. Flow generation efficiency varies non-monotonically along the annealing trajectory, is lowest in the dense disordered regime, and is quantitatively predicted by the internal mode complexity of the constrained ensemble plus target drift across the training window. Liquid-like ensembles—not prior-target separation—are identified as the hard case for current flow architectures.
AI.conclusion: Flow-based nested sampling can be effectively adapted to atomistic systems when the architecture (single conditional flow trained self-consistently on sliding live sets) accounts for the distinctive discrete-combinatorial, densely-coupled multimodality of molecular landscapes. Beyond algorithmic gains, the flow's generation efficiency doubles as a physical diagnostic that reveals which thermodynamic regimes (dense liquid-like ensembles) challenge current flow models.

title: Real-space Floquet topology written by the orbital angular momentum of light
summary: Floquet engineering usually treats light as a uniform control field that changes the topology of an entire driven material. Here we show that structured light carrying orbital angular momentum (OAM) enables a different regime, in which topology is written directly in real space. For ultrathin topological insulator films, circularly polarized Laguerre--Gaussian beams generate a radial Floquet mass whose sign changes define a topological annulus bounded by two concentric chiral ring modes. The transition is helicity selective: below a thickness-dependent critical frequency, left-circularly polarized light drives mass inversion, whereas right-circularly polarized light increases the gap and leaves the film trivial. Independently, the OAM quantum number shifts and reshapes the annulus without changing the frequency, intensity, or helicity. In the decoupled-surfaces limit, the same mechanism produces a purely Floquet-induced topological mass and a vortex-core zero mode. These results identify photon OAM as a control parameter for nonequilibrium topology and provide a route to programmable topological landscapes in quantum materials.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using structured light carrying orbital angular momentum (OAM), specifically circularly polarized Laguerre-Gaussian beams, to engineer topology directly in real space within ultrathin topological insulator films. This generates a radial Floquet mass that creates a topological annulus bounded by two concentric chiral ring modes, with helicity-selective transitions and OAM-tunable landscape geometry.
AI.motivation: Traditional Floquet engineering uses uniform light fields to globally change the topology of a driven material. The authors aim to enable spatially structured topological control by using light that varies in space (via OAM), allowing topology to be written locally rather than uniformly.
AI.method: The approach uses circularly polarized Laguerre-Gaussian beams impinging on ultrathin topological insulator films. The spatially varying phase/intensity profile of the OAM-carrying beam induces a position-dependent (radial) Floquet mass term. Analysis considers thickness-dependent critical frequencies, helicity dependence, and the decoupled-surfaces limit.
AI.result: The radial Floquet mass changes sign across the beam, defining a topological annulus bounded by two concentric chiral ring modes. The effect is helicity-selective: below a critical frequency related to film thickness, left-circular polarization drives mass inversion while right-circular increases the gap. The OAM quantum number independently shifts and reshapes the annulus. In the decoupled-surfaces limit, a purely Floquet-induced topological mass and vortex-core zero mode emerge.
AI.conclusion: Photon orbital angular momentum is identified as a new control parameter for nonequilibrium topology, offering a route to programmable topological landscapes in quantum materials.

title: Competing lattice structures induced by Sn substitution in CsV$_3$Sb$_5$
summary: Understanding the effect of chemical substitution on competing phases of kagome metals is crucial for disentangling the interplay between local structural distortions and electronic instabilities. In \cvs, Sn substitution strongly modifies the electronic phase diagram, yet the microscopic mechanism driving this remains unclear. Here, we combine $^{121}$Sb nuclear quadrupole resonance (NQR) measurements and density functional theory calculations to investigate the atomic-scale effects of Sn substitution in CsV$_3$Sb$_{5-x}$Sn$_x$. At low Sn concentrations, the observed satellite NQR peaks exhibit signatures of local structural distortion induced by Sn substitution, qualitatively consistent with our computational analysis. These impurity-induced features persist across the entire experimentally investigated doping range, up to $x$ = 0.65, and remain observable up to room temperature. For $x=1$, the fully doped idealized case, the estimated dynamical instabilities of the kagome lattice suggest the stabilization of two nearly energy-degenerate equilibrium structures characterized by V-trimers, distinguished by a zero- or $π$-phase shift between adjacent layers along the $c$-axis. Together, these results show that Sn substitution drives a complex interplay between local impurity-induced distortions and competing structural instabilities in vanadium-based kagome compounds.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how Sn substitution affects CsV$_3$Sb$_5$ kagome metals using $^{121}$Sb NQR and DFT calculations, finding that Sn induces local structural distortions at low concentrations (persisting up to x=0.65 and room temperature), while at the fully doped x=1 limit, dynamical instabilities stabilize two nearly degenerate equilibrium structures characterized by V-trimers with either zero- or π-phase shifts between layers.
AI.motivation: Understanding how chemical substitution affects competing phases in kagome metals is crucial for disentangling the interplay between local structural distortions and electronic instabilities. While Sn substitution strongly modifies the electronic phase diagram of CsV$_3$Sb$_5$, the microscopic mechanism driving this remains unclear.
AI.method: The authors combine $^{121}$Sb nuclear quadrupole resonance (NQR) measurements with density functional theory (DFT) calculations to probe atomic-scale effects of Sn substitution across the CsV$_3$Sb$_{5-x}$Sn$_x$ series.
AI.result: (1) At low Sn concentrations, satellite NQR peaks reveal signatures of local structural distortion induced by Sn substitution, consistent with computational predictions. (2) These impurity-induced features persist across the full experimentally studied doping range (up to x=0.65) and remain observable up to room temperature. (3) For the idealized fully doped case (x=1), dynamical instability analysis of the kagome lattice suggests stabilization of two nearly energy-degenerate equilibrium structures with V-trimers, distinguished by zero- or π-phase shifts between adjacent layers along the c-axis.
AI.conclusion: Sn substitution in CsV$_3$Sb$_5$ drives a complex interplay between local impurity-induced distortions and competing structural instabilities in vanadium-based kagome compounds.

title: Grain boundary evolution in nanoparticles
summary: Grain boundary evolution is a key dynamical process that enables structural rearrangements in nanoparticles and drives them towards low energy configurations. Grain boundaries can also enhance catalytic properties, making it important to understand the elementary processes underlying their evolution for grain boundary engineering in nanoparticles. Compared with bulk materials, nanoparticles have additional rotational and translational degrees of freedom, can accommodate structural changes through shape relaxation, and grain boundaries terminate at free surfaces. However, the atomic-scale mechanisms of GB evolution under these less constrained conditions remain comparatively less understood than in bulk materials. Here, using atomistic simulations, we focus on low energy $\Sigma3$ (coherent twin boundary) and $\Sigma11$ grain boundaries, which are among the persistent compact GB structures that emerge during nanoparticle structural evolution. We identify two fundamental atomic displacements, column shift (C) and screw shift (S), that recur during the evolution of these grain boundaries and their junctions. These displacements occur through different atomic pathways and combine in different ways to generate grain boundary migration, structural transformations, and junction evolution. In particular, the same initial and final grain boundary configurations can be connected through different atomic pathways, and a column shift can occur either as a full shift or through disconnection kinks. C and S remain identifiable even when the grain boundary character changes, for example during a $\Sigma11$ to $\Sigma3$ transformation. An understanding of these elementary GB processes can help identify strategies to control grain boundary evolution and thereby engineer GB structures in nanoparticles.

AI.tldr: This paper uses atomistic simulations to investigate grain boundary (GB) evolution in nanoparticles, focusing on low-energy Σ3 and Σ11 GBs. The authors identify two fundamental atomic displacement mechanisms—column shift (C) and screw shift (S)—that drive GB migration, structural transformations, and junction evolution in nanoparticles, where GBs have fewer constraints than in bulk materials.
AI.motivation: Grain boundary evolution is essential for structural rearrangements in nanoparticles and can enhance catalytic properties. Understanding the elementary atomic-scale processes underlying GB evolution in nanoparticles—which have extra rotational/translational degrees of freedom and where GBs terminate at free surfaces—remains less understood than in bulk materials, yet is crucial for GB engineering.
AI.method: The authors employ atomistic simulations to study low-energy Σ3 (coherent twin) and Σ11 grain boundaries in nanoparticles. They analyze the atomic trajectories to identify recurring elementary displacement modes—column shift (C) and screw shift (S)—and characterize how these displacements combine via different atomic pathways to produce GB migration, structural transformations, and junction evolution.
AI.result: Two fundamental atomic displacements (C and S) are identified as recurring elementary processes during GB evolution in nanoparticles. These can operate via different atomic pathways, combine in various ways to drive GB migration and junction evolution, and remain identifiable even when GB character transforms (e.g., Σ11 to Σ3). A column shift may occur as a full shift or via disconnection kinks, and equivalent initial/final GB states can be connected by distinct pathways.
AI.conclusion: Understanding these elementary GB processes—column shifts and screw shifts—provides a framework for controlling GB evolution and offers strategies for engineering grain boundary structures in nanoparticles to optimize their properties.

title: Frenkel line of Yukawa fluids within the self-consistent relaxation theory
summary: For a simple model fluid, the Yukawa fluid, the condition for dynamic crossover, known as the Frenkel line, is defined. The condition is related to the fact that the roton minimum in the dispersion relation of longitudinal acoustic-like excitations exists only when the collective vibrational dynamics of particles dominates in the liquid. Based on the self-consistent relaxation theory for the Yukawa fluid, thermodynamic states are determined in which the roton minimum disappears. The obtained values of the state parameters for the Frenkel line are consistent with the results of studies in which the position of this line on the phase diagram of the Yukawa fluid was determined using molecular dynamics simulations. It is shown that the Frenkel line in this system can be determined directly from the structural characteristic -- the static structure factor. A physical interpretation of the roton minimum frequency for the simple liquids near the Frenkel line is proposed.

AI.tldr: The paper derives the Frenkel line—the dynamic crossover condition—for the Yukawa fluid using self-consistent relaxation theory. The condition is linked to the existence of the roton minimum in longitudinal acoustic-like dispersion relations, which only persists when collective vibrational dynamics dominate. The predicted thermodynamic states agree with molecular dynamics simulations, and it is shown that the Frenkel line can be identified directly from the static structure factor. A physical interpretation of the roton minimum frequency near the Frenkel line is proposed.
AI.motivation: To establish a rigorous analytic/structural criterion for locating the Frenkel line (liquid-like to gas-like dynamic crossover) in simple fluids such as the Yukawa fluid, rather than relying solely on empirical definitions or extensive molecular dynamics simulations.
AI.method: The authors employ self-consistent relaxation theory for the Yukawa fluid to compute thermodynamic states where the roton minimum in the longitudinal acoustic-like dispersion relation vanishes. They compare the resulting Frenkel line parameters to prior molecular dynamics results and further propose determining the line from the static structure factor. They also offer a physical interpretation of the roton minimum frequency.
AI.result: Thermodynamic states where the roton minimum disappears are identified, giving values for the Frenkel line that are consistent with molecular dynamics simulations. The Frenkel line can be determined directly from the static structure factor. A physical interpretation for the roton minimum frequency near the Frenkel line is provided.
AI.conclusion: The Frenkel line for the Yukawa fluid is theoretically and structurally characterized: it corresponds to the disappearance of the roton minimum, marks the crossover from collective vibrational to non-collective dynamics, and is accessible via the static structure factor without full dynamical simulations.

title: Coherent interaction of WS$_2$ and quasi-2D perovskite excitons over micrometer distances via a cavity field
summary: The coherent coupling of cavity-confined photons and excitonic matter resonances leads to the formation of cavity polaritons, hybrid light-matter quasi-particles. If multiple exciton resonances couple to the same photonic mode, the resulting polariton constitutes a coherent interaction between matter resonances that can be spatially separated without any direct electronic coupling. In this work, we demonstrate the formation of such a coherent coupling at room temperature using an open optical cavity containing two distinct van der Waals materials - monolayer WS2 and layered quasi-2D halide perovskites (HaPs) - separated by $1.5 μ\rm m$. The system forms three polariton branches, with the middle branch possessing nearly equal fractions of both excitons and the photonic mode. White-light reflectivity and luminescence measurements are in good agreement with simulations using a coupled harmonic oscillator and a microscopic Wannier-Hopfield framework. Our results lay the foundation to combine highly complementary degrees of freedom in 2D materials in an in-situ tunable fashion to enable new polaritonic functionalities.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates room-temperature coherent coupling between excitons in two distinct van der Waals materials (monolayer WS2 and layered quasi-2D halide perovskites) via a shared cavity photonic mode. The system forms three polariton branches where the middle branch contains nearly equal excitonic and photonic fractions. Experimental reflectivity and luminescence measurements match simulations from coupled oscillator and Wannier-Hopfield models.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that spatially separated excitonic resonances in different van der Waals materials can be coherently coupled through a shared photonic cavity mode at room temperature, without any direct electronic coupling, enabling new polaritonic functionalities by combining complementary degrees of freedom from distinct 2D materials.
AI.method: An open optical cavity confining light is used to couple monolayer WS2 and layered quasi-2D halide perovskites (HaPs) separated by 1.5 μm. The hybridized system is characterized via white-light reflectivity and luminescence measurements, and the results are simulated using a coupled harmonic oscillator model and a microscopic Wannier-Hopfield framework.
AI.result: Three polariton branches form at room temperature, with the middle branch having nearly equal fractions of both exciton species and the photonic mode. Experimental reflectivity and photoluminescence data agree well with model simulations.
AI.conclusion: Coherent polaritonic coupling between different van der Waals materials is achievable at room temperature via a shared cavity photon mode, even with spatial separation and no direct electronic coupling. This provides an in-situ tunable platform to combine complementary degrees of freedom in 2D materials, enabling new polaritonic functionalities.

title: Optimal Control of Periodic Nonequilibrium Mechanochemical Systems via Automatic Differentiation
summary: Biological molecular machines are mesoscopic systems that act repeatedly and periodically to perform important cellular tasks while contending with strong fluctuations and operating in an overdamped regime. Optimal control theory is a tool that can be used to understand the design principles behind efficient operation of these machines; however, most studies on optimal control of classical mesoscopic systems have focused on control problems that do not repeat periodically. Here, we automatically differentiate Fokker-Planck simulations to design efficient nonequilibrium control strategies for simple models of periodic molecular machines with and without explicit changes in the machine's chemical state. The designed protocols and theoretical analysis provide insight into the design principles governing efficient driving in these nonequilibrium systems. Designed control protocols should seek to reduce mechanical heat by rotating the entire angular probability distribution at a constant speed without changing its shape, and should reduce chemical heat by reducing the proportion of chemical transitions with large heat.

AI.tldr: The paper uses automatic differentiation of Fokker-Planck simulations to design optimal nonequilibrium control protocols for periodic molecular machines, revealing that efficient driving involves rotating the angular probability distribution at constant speed to minimize mechanical heat and reducing the proportion of high-heat chemical transitions to minimize chemical heat.
AI.motivation: Biological molecular machines operate periodically in overdamped regimes with strong fluctuations, and existing optimal control studies for classical mesoscopic systems have largely ignored periodic operation. Understanding design principles for efficient periodic molecular machines is essential.
AI.method: Automatic differentiation of Fokker-Planck simulations is applied to design efficient nonequilibrium control strategies for periodic molecular machine models, both with and without explicit changes in chemical state.
AI.result: Designed protocols reveal that mechanical heat is minimized by rotating the entire angular probability distribution at constant speed without shape change, while chemical heat is minimized by reducing the proportion of chemical transitions that carry large heat.
AI.conclusion: The findings provide design principles for efficient driving of periodic molecular machines, distinguishing between mechanical and chemical heat reduction strategies in these nonequilibrium systems.

title: Non-Resonant Impulsively Stimulated Raman Scattering by a Terahertz Field: a Case Study of 1T-TaS2
summary: Time-domain ultrafast and nonlinear terahertz spectroscopy techniques are recently applied to many condensed matter systems for investigating their collective excitations. In centrosymmetric systems, these collective modes are typically Raman-active and therefore do not couple directly to the terahertz electric field. The mechanism by which light-matter interaction realizes in these studies has not been explicitly discussed in detail. In this work, we perform terahertz pump - optical probe and terahertz third harmonic generation investigations on 1T-TaS2, a material exhibiting a rich charge-density-wave (CDW) phase diagram including the commensurate, nearly-commensurate and incommensurate CDW phases. The transition between these distinct states leaves a clear signature on the dynamical Raman response. We investigate how the Raman-active phonons couple to a broadband monocycle terahertz field as well as a narrowband multicycle terahertz field. Our results indicate that a modified impulsively stimulated Raman scattering mechanism involving two-photon absorption, also known as non-resonant Raman scattering, underlies the coherent excitation and observation of the lattice modes. These results are relevant for future spectroscopy investigation and coherent control of collective modes using low-energy terahertz field as well as cavity electrodynamical dressing of solids.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates how Raman-active phonons in 1T-TaS2 (a charge-density-wave material) couple to terahertz fields via a modified impulsively stimulated Raman scattering mechanism involving two-photon absorption, despite these modes being nominally non-centrosymmetric-inactive in the THz regime.
AI.motivation: Ultrafast terahertz spectroscopy is increasingly used to study collective excitations in condensed matter, but in centrosymmetric systems the relevant modes are Raman-active and do not couple directly to the THz electric field. The underlying light-matter coupling mechanism has not been explicitly examined, motivating this study.
AI.method: The authors performed terahertz pump–optical probe spectroscopy and terahertz third-harmonic generation measurements on 1T-TaS2 across its commensurate, nearly-commensurate, and incommensurate charge-density-wave phases, comparing excitation with broadband monocycle and narrowband multicycle THz fields.
AI.result: The dynamical Raman response clearly changes across CDW phase transitions. Raman-active phonons couple to both broadband and narrowband THz fields, and the results establish that a modified impulsively stimulated Raman scattering mechanism involving two-photon (non-resonant) absorption governs the coherent excitation and detection of lattice modes.
AI.conclusion: The findings clarify the mechanism of THz excitation of Raman-active collective modes in centrosymmetric systems and are relevant for future THz spectroscopy, coherent control of collective modes, and cavity-electrodynamical dressing of solids.

title: Polaron Self-Trapping Rates from First Principles
summary: Polaron formation, also known as self-trapping, is a process akin to nonradiative carrier capture at point defects or impurities. In this work, we develop the formalism to determine how long it takes to form a small hole or electron polaron from first principles. We employ an accurate, fully first-principles approach based on a Koopmans compliant hybrid functional. The self-trapping rate is the product of two components: the nonradiative capture coefficient, which we evaluate using a one-dimensional approximation, and the maximum density of polaron sites, whose physics we elucidate based on finite-size interactions present in supercells. We apply our methodology to several technologically relevant materials known to host hole polarons, Ga$_2$O$_3$, Al$_2$O$_3$, BeO, KBr, MgO, NaCl, SiO$_2$, SnO$_2$, TiO$_2$, and ZnO, and to an electron polaron in rutile TiO$_2$. We also study an emerging semiconductor, rutile GeO$_2$, where we find that polaron formation could hamper $p$-type conductivity. The calculated self-trapping lifetimes span 7 orders of magnitude, from $10^{-1}$ to $10^6$~ps, in agreement with experiments where available, and providing detailed insight into the dynamics of carrier localization and relaxation in solids.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a first-principles formalism to compute the time required for small polaron formation (self-trapping) in solids, combining a nonradiative capture coefficient evaluated via a one-dimensional approximation with the maximum density of polaron sites derived from finite-size supercell interactions. The method is applied to hole polarons in ten materials and an electron polaron in rutile TiO2, yielding self-trapping lifetimes spanning 10^-1 to 10^6 ps, consistent with experiments.
AI.motivation: Polaron formation (self-trapping) is a fundamental process analogous to nonradiative carrier capture at defects, yet no rigorous first-principles framework existed to determine the timescale of small polaron formation. Understanding this kinetics is critical for carrier dynamics and transport in materials, especially for evaluating p-type conductivity limitations in emerging semiconductors.
AI.method: The self-trapping rate is formulated as the product of two components: (1) the nonradiative capture coefficient evaluated using a one-dimensional approximation, and (2) the maximum density of polaron sites, whose physical origin is clarified via finite-size interactions in supercell calculations. Total energies are computed using an accurate Koopmans-compliant hybrid functional within a fully first-principles framework.
AI.result: Calculated self-trapping lifetimes span seven orders of magnitude (10^-1 to 10^6 ps) across hole polarons in Ga2O3, Al2O3, BeO, KBr, MgO, NaCl, SiO2, SnO2, TiO2, ZnO, and an electron polaron in rutile TiO2. The results agree with available experimental data. For rutile GeO2, polaron formation is predicted to hamper p-type conductivity.
AI.conclusion: The developed formalism provides a quantitative, first-principles description of polaron self-trapping kinetics with predictive power across a wide range of materials, offering detailed insight into carrier localization and relaxation dynamics. The finding for GeO2 highlights the potential practical impact of polaron formation on charge transport in emerging semiconductors.

title: Performance of Nanoring-based Transparent Conductors: a Computational Investigation
summary: Metallic nanoring networks can serve as promising flexible transparent electrodes. These materials are crucial components in a wide range of applications, including solar cells, touchscreens and displays. In this work, a computational investigation considers in detail (i) the electrical conductance and optical performance of nanoring networks and (ii) the breakdown of these networks due to electrical damage. The electrical resistance of both the nanorings and the contacts between the rings (junctions) is taken into account. In part (i), the effects of 5 parameters on the electrical sheet resistance and optical transparency are presented. It is shown that several parameter combinations achieve better performance in comparison to indium tin oxide, currently the most widely used transparent electrode. In part (ii), due to electrical damage, the nanoring systems display the formation of a crack, running parallel to the vertical terminals, where a voltage difference is applied. The network degradation is measured by its sheet resistance, and a universal effect is observed: networks with varying filling factors exhibit the same degradation profile.

AI.tldr: This paper computationally investigates metallic nanoring networks as flexible transparent electrodes, examining both their electrical/optical performance and their degradation due to electrical damage. Networks with certain parameter combinations outperform indium tin oxide, and electrically damaged networks show universal degradation profiles regardless of filling factor.
AI.motivation: Metallic nanoring networks hold promise as flexible transparent electrodes for applications like solar cells, touchscreens, and displays, where alternatives to indium tin oxide (ITO) are needed.
AI.method: A computational investigation analyzes (i) electrical conductance and optical performance of nanoring networks, considering resistance from both nanorings and ring-to-ring junctions, examining 5 parameters affecting sheet resistance and optical transparency; and (ii) breakdown behavior due to electrical damage, studying crack formation and measuring network degradation via sheet resistance.

title: Unravelling the Li-Haldane Conjecture with the Projected Ensemble
summary: The entanglement spectra of fractional quantum Hall states contain universal fingerprints of their underlying topological order, as posited by the Li-Haldane conjecture. In this work, we uncover a finer universal structure within the entanglement spectra unravelled by projective measurements. Concretely, we study the projected ensemble of fractional quantum Hall states, defined as the collection of quantum states on a subsystem conditioned on measurement outcomes of its complement. We find that this ensemble exhibits a hidden hierarchy inside the Li-Haldane edge manifold: by conditioning on measurement outcomes, the entanglement spectrum's support is split into measurement-dependent sectors whose ranks we demonstrate are fixed by conformal field theory counting, an observation we dub the measurement-resolved Li-Haldane conjecture. For the non-Abelian Moore-Read state, this hierarchy is particularly rich: each parity-resolved edge manifold contains internal subspaces whose dimensions reproduce the conformal field theory counting of the opposite-parity sector. This structure persists even in realistic Coulomb-interacting ground states, establishing the projected ensemble as a sharp new probe of topological order beyond what the entanglement spectrum alone can detect.

The authors uncover a "measurement-resolved Li-Haldane conjecture": conditioning on measurement outcomes splits the entanglement spectrum into sectors whose ranks are fixed by conformal field theory (CFT) counting. For the non-Abelian Moore-Read state, each parity-resolved edge manifold contains internal subspaces reproducing the CFT counting of the opposite-parity sector. This structure persists in realistic Coulomb-interacting ground states, establishing the projected ensemble as a new probe of topological order beyond the entanglement spectrum alone.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to go beyond the traditional entanglement spectrum analysis of FQH states (based on the Li-Haldane conjecture) to uncover finer universal fingerprints of topological order. They propose that projective measurements and the resulting projected ensemble can reveal structure hidden within the entanglement spectrum that conventional analysis cannot detect.
AI.method: The authors construct the projected ensemble of FQH states, which is the collection of quantum states on a subsystem conditioned on all possible measurement outcomes of the complementary subsystem. They analyze the measurement-induced sectorization of the entanglement spectrum's support and compare the ranks/dimensions of these measurement-dependent sectors against predictions from conformal field theory counting. The framework is applied to both ideal and realistic Coulomb-interacting ground states, including the non-Abelian Moore-Read state where a parity-resolved hierarchy of edge manifold internal subspaces is examined.
