For the Moore-Read state, each parity-resolved edge manifold contains internal subspaces whose dimensions reproduce the CFT counting of the opposite-parity sector, constituting a rich internal structure. This measurement-resolved structure persists even in realistic Coulomb-interacting ground states.
AI.conclusion: The measurement-resolved Li-Haldane conjecture establishes the projected ensemble as a sharp, novel probe of topological order in FQH systems, capable of revealing universal structure beyond what the entanglement spectrum alone can detect. This opens a new avenue for characterizing topological phases via projective-measurement-based diagnostics.

title: Hidden Magnetic Octupolar Order driven by Spin-Orbit coupling in KFeF$_3$
summary: Phase transitions are typically driven by symmetry-breaking structural distortions that lift electronic degeneracies, yet in some cases, these transitions may be driven by a hidden order without conventional structural signatures. Here, we demonstrate that the 3$d$ perovskite, KFeF$_3$, hosts such a hidden instability. Using a combination of high-resolution powder diffraction, magnetometry, symmetry-based analysis and first principles calculations, we reveal that while the 90 K cubic to rhombohedral transition arises from conventional magnetostriction accompanying antiferromagnetic order, a second transition at 40 K lowers the symmetry to monoclinic without any detectable Jahn-Teller distortion or translational symmetry-breaking. Symmetry-based Landau analysis supports a hidden zone centered magnetic octupole order parameter, whose improper coupling accounts for the weak ferromagnetism and pronounced symmetry-breaking strain. Density functional calculations show that spin-orbit coupling suppresses the competing Jahn-Teller instability, and thereby favors higher rank magnetic multipolar degrees of freedom. These findings establish KFeF$_3$ as a model system in which the competing energy scales between spin-orbit coupling and orbital degeneracy result in the emergence of hidden, multipolar order. We show that the control of such magnetic, multipolar order could, in principle, provide a route to induce altermagnetism.

AI.tldr: KFeF3 exhibits a hidden magnetic octupolar order at 40 K, distinct from conventional magnetostriction-driven transitions, establishing it as a model system where spin-orbit coupling competes with orbital degeneracy to produce multipolar order, potentially enabling altermagnetism.
AI.motivation: To identify and characterize hidden order phase transitions that occur without conventional structural signatures (Jahn-Teller distortion or translational symmetry-breaking), and to understand how competing energy scales between spin-orbit coupling and orbital degeneracy give rise to such unusual multipolar ordering.
AI.method: Combines high-resolution powder diffraction, magnetometry, symmetry-based Landau analysis, and first-principles density functional theory (DFT) calculations to investigate the structural and magnetic transitions in KFeF3, including analysis of magnetic octupolar order parameters and strain coupling.
AI.result: The 90 K cubic-to-rhombohedral transition arises from conventional magnetostriction with antiferromagnetic order. A second transition at 40 K lowers symmetry to monoclinic without detectable Jahn-Teller distortion or translational symmetry-breaking, explained by a hidden zone-centered magnetic octupole order parameter whose improper coupling accounts for weak ferromagnetism and symmetry-breaking strain. DFT shows spin-orbit coupling suppresses competing Jahn-Teller instability and favors higher-rank magnetic multipolar order.
AI.conclusion: KFeF3 is established as a model system for hidden multipolar order driven by competing spin-orbit coupling and orbital degeneracy energy scales, with potential implications for controlling magnetic multipolar order to induce altermagnetism.

title: Interplay of B-Site Off-Centering and Molecular Orientations in the Mixed Hybrid Perovskite MAGe1xSnxI3
summary: B-site mixing is a common strategy for tuning properties of halide perovskites. In the lead-free system MAGe1-xSn_xI3, it brings tilting and off-centering into competition. Using large-scale molecular dynamics driven by a machine-learned interatomic potential, we map the structural behavior across the full composition range. MAGeI3 exhibits strong polar B-site off-centering that remains nearly constant up to the cubic transition, together with methylammonium (MA) orientational order that weakens progressively on heating. By contrast, MASnI3 combines octahedral tilting with weaker, predominantly antipolar off-centering. Ge-like behavior persists upon alloying and gives way to Sn-like behavior only beyond roughly 65 % Sn. In the high-temperature phases, the B-site cations remain locally off-centered but directionally disordered. On the Ge-rich side, the distorted inorganic framework biases the soft MA orientational landscape toward a restricted set of preferred directions. This coupling shows how the composition of the inorganic sublattice can tune molecular ordering in lead-free hybrid perovskites.

AI.motivation: B-site mixing is a common strategy for tuning the properties of halide perovskites, but the competition between octahedral tilting and B-site off-centering in lead-free mixed systems like MAGe1-xSnxI3 is not well understood across the full composition range.
AI.method: Large-scale molecular dynamics simulations driven by a machine-learned interatomic potential were used to map structural behavior across the full MAGe1-xSnxI3 composition range.
AI.result: MAGeI3 shows strong polar B-site off-centering nearly constant up to the cubic transition with progressively weakening MA orientational order on heating. MASnI3 combines octahedral tilting with weaker, predominantly antipolar off-centering. Ge-like behavior persists upon alloying and transitions to Sn-like behavior only beyond ~65% Sn. In high-temperature phases, B-site cations remain locally off-centered but directionally disordered, and on the Ge-rich side the distorted inorganic framework biases MA orientations toward restricted preferred directions.
AI.conclusion: The composition of the inorganic sublattice can tune molecular (MA) ordering in lead-free hybrid perovskites, as demonstrated by the coupling between the distorted inorganic framework on the Ge-rich side and the soft MA orientational landscape.

title: The Casimir free energy of peptide films on a silicon substrate: Impact of dielectric-to-metal transition in silicon and nanoparticles in peptide
summary: Using the Lifshitz theory of the van der Waals and Casimir forces, we calculate the Casimir free energy of thin peptide films deposited on silicon substrates. The Casimir free energy is found as a function of film thickness for different fractions of water in the film, in the presence of either nonmagnetic or magnetic nanoparticles, and under the impact of irradiation of a silicon substrate with laser pulses or dopants resulting in the dielectric-to-metal phase transition. It is shown that for a dielectric silicon there is the borderline value of the film thickness, such that the Casimir free energy is negative and contributes to the film stability for thicker films, but is positive and makes the film less stable for thinner ones. According to our results, the borderline value of peptide film thickness decreases with increasing volume fractions of water and in the film. This decrease is more pronounced for the magnetic nanoparticles and becomes stronger with increasing their radius. The borderline value of peptide film thickness is found as a function of the fraction of water in the film. If the silicon substrate is in metallic state, the Casimir free energy of peptide coating is always positive, which makes it less stable. Possible applications of the obtained results in organic electronics and biomedicine are discussed.

AI.tldr: The paper uses Lifshitz theory to compute the Casimir free energy of thin peptide films on silicon substrates, examining how film thickness, water content, nanoparticles (magnetic or nonmagnetic), and silicon substrate phase (dielectric vs. metallic) affect film stability. A borderline film thickness exists for dielectric silicon where the Casimir energy transitions from stabilizing (negative) to destabilizing (positive); this borderline decreases with water content and is more affected by magnetic nanoparticles. Metallic silicon always yields positive Casimir energy, destabilizing the coating.
AI.motivation: To understand and predict the role of quantum vacuum (Casimir) forces in the stability of thin organic (peptide) coatings on silicon substrates, which is relevant for applications in organic electronics and biomedicine where precise control of film stability is critical.
AI.method: The Lifshitz theory of van der Waals and Casimir forces is used to calculate the Casimir free energy as a function of peptide film thickness. Parameters varied include the volume fraction of water in the film, the presence and radius of nonmagnetic vs. magnetic nanoparticles, and the dielectric-to-metal phase transition of the silicon substrate induced by laser pulses or dopants.
AI.result: For dielectric silicon, a borderline film thickness exists: above it the Casimir free energy is negative (stabilizing) and below it positive (destabilizing). This borderline value decreases with increasing water fraction and decreases more strongly for magnetic nanoparticles with larger radii. For metallic silicon, the Casimir free energy is always positive, making the film less stable regardless of thickness. The borderline thickness is mapped as a function of water fraction.
AI.conclusion: Casimir forces can significantly influence the stability of thin peptide coatings, with tunability via film composition (water/nanoparticles) and substrate electronic state (dielectric vs. metallic). The findings have potential applications in organic electronics and biomedicine, where controlling coating stability is important.

title: Fermi-Point Topology Determines Emergent Conformal Criticality in Extended Quantum Spin Chains
summary: Quantum criticality in one-dimensional quantum systems is characterized by emergent conformal field theories (CFTs), whose central charge counts independent gapless degrees of freedom. Establishing a microscopic connection between this universal conformal structure and the momentum-space topology of the underlying quasiparticle spectrum remains challenging. Here, we uncover a direct correspondence between Fermi-point topology, conformal criticality, and quantum entanglement in an extended quantum spin chain with competing cluster interactions, exchange anisotropy, and a transverse magnetic field. We show that interaction- and field-driven Lifshitz transitions generate conformal critical phases with effective central charges $c_{\rm eff}=1/2$, $1$, $3/2$, $2$, and $3$, including a multicritical point where Ising and Luttinger-liquid sectors coexist. Importantly, the central charge is not determined simply by the number of lattice gap closings or Fermi points, but by the number and conformal content of independent low-energy continuum sectors after accounting for lattice symmetries, reciprocal-lattice identifications, and mode equivalences. Thus, Lifshitz transitions may leave the conformal anomaly unchanged or modify the central charge depending on whether spectral reconstruction generates new independent continuum sectors. Real- and momentum-space entanglement spectra provide complementary microscopic signatures, revealing both the conformal content and momentum-space organization of critical modes. Our results establish a microscopic framework linking Fermi-point topology to emergent CFTs and show how interaction-driven spectral reconstruction can generate higher-central-charge criticality and unconventional multicritical behavior.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes a direct correspondence between Fermi-point topology, conformal criticality, and quantum entanglement in an extended quantum spin chain with competing cluster interactions, exchange anisotropy, and a transverse magnetic field. The authors show that Lifshitz transitions generate conformal critical phases with effective central charges ranging from c_eff=1/2 to 3, including a multicritical point where Ising and Luttinger-liquid sectors coexist. Crucially, the central charge is determined not by the number of lattice gap closings or Fermi points alone, but by the number and conformal content of independent low-energy continuum sectors after accounting for lattice symmetries, reciprocal-lattice identifications, and mode equivalences.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to bridge the gap between the universal conformal structure (characterized by central charge) of one-dimensional quantum critical systems and the momentum-space topology of their underlying quasiparticle spectra—an established but poorly understood microscopic connection.
AI.method: The paper analyzes an extended quantum spin chain that includes competing cluster interactions, exchange anisotropy, and a transverse magnetic field. It employs real- and momentum-space entanglement spectra as complementary probes to reveal both the conformal content and momentum-space organization of critical modes, while tracking interaction- and field-driven Lifshitz transitions that reshape the quasiparticle spectrum.
AI.result: The study identifies conformal critical phases with effective central charges c_eff = 1/2, 1, 3/2, 2, and 3, including a multicritical point featuring coexisting Ising and Luttinger-liquid sectors. The central charge is found to depend on the number of independent low-energy continuum sectors beyond simple Fermi-point counting, after accounting for lattice symmetries, reciprocal-lattice identifications, and mode equivalences. Lifshitz transitions may either preserve the conformal anomaly or modify the central charge depending on whether spectral reconstruction creates new independent continuum sectors. Real- and momentum-space entanglement spectra provide complementary microscopic signatures of these effects.
AI.conclusion: The results establish a microscopic framework linking Fermi-point topology to emergent CFTs, demonstrating how interaction-driven spectral reconstruction can generate higher-central-charge criticality and unconventional multicritical behavior in one-dimensional quantum systems.

title: Electron-phonon coupled hydrodynamics in semimetal TaAs_2
summary: Hydrodynamic corrections to diffusive transport can arise when momentum-conserving collisions between quasiparticles become prominent, and they have been documented for both electrons and phonons. An emerging frontier topic is coupled electron-phonon (e-ph) hydrodynamics. Here, through electrical and thermal transport measurements on TaAs2 crystals with different impurity levels, we document the emergence of an e-ph bifluid in the temperature window of 5 to 15 K. Within this range, the lattice thermal conductivity exhibits a faster-than-T^3 temperature dependence, as a consequence of non-monotonic and purity-dependent phonon mean free paths, a signature of phonon Poiseuille flow. However, strong e-ph coupling impedes the emergence of a ballistic regime. This is corroborated by the observation of quantum oscillations in the lattice thermal conductivity. Prominent phonon-mediated momentum exchange between electrons amplifies the violation of the Wiedemann-Franz law and yields a two-order-of-magnitude discrepancy between quantum and transport lifetimes, a signature of electron hydrodynamics in semimetals. Our results imply that in semimetals with optimized e-ph coupling, thanks to matching between the cryogenic phonon wave?length and the Fermi wavelength, momentum and energy flow between the electron and phonon reservoirs as frequently as within each reservoir.

AI.tldr: The paper reports the emergence of a coupled electron-phonon (e-ph) bifluid in TaAs2 crystals in the 5-15 K temperature range, evidenced by phonon Poiseuille flow (non-monotonic, purity-dependent phonon mean free paths and faster-than-T^3 lattice thermal conductivity) and electron hydrodynamic signatures (strong violation of the Wiedemann-Franz law, two-order-of-magnitude discrepancy between quantum and transport lifetimes). Strong e-ph coupling suppresses the phonon ballistic regime, and the findings suggest momentum and energy exchange between electron and phonon reservoirs occurs as frequently as within each reservoir due to matched cryogenic phonon and Fermi wavelengths.
AI.motivation: To explore the emerging frontier of coupled electron-phonon hydrodynamics and demonstrate its existence in semimetals, moving beyond separately documented electron and phonon hydrodynamic transport.
AI.method: Electrical and thermal transport measurements were performed on TaAs2 crystals with different impurity levels. Lattice thermal conductivity, phonon mean free paths, quantum oscillations in thermal conductivity, Wiedemann-Franz law violations, and quantum versus transport lifetime discrepancies were analyzed across the 5-15 K temperature region.
AI.result: An e-ph bifluid emerges in the 5-15 K window, evidenced by faster-than-T^3 lattice thermal conductivity from non-monotonic and purity-dependent phonon mean free paths (phonon Poiseuille flow), suppressed phonon ballistic regime due to strong e-ph coupling, quantum oscillations in lattice thermal conductivity, amplified Wiedemann-Franz law violations, and a two-order-of-magnitude discrepancy between quantum and transport lifetimes.
AI.conclusion: In semimetals with optimized e-ph coupling, where cryogenic phonon wavelength matches the Fermi wavelength, momentum and energy flow between electron and phonon reservoirs as frequently as within each reservoir, demonstrating fully coupled e-ph hydrodynamic transport.

title: Hierarchy of topological superconductivity generated via heterostructures of unconventional $p$-wave magnets
comment: 6 Pages + 5 PDF Figures (Main Text) and 6 Pages (Supplementary Material); Comments are welcome
summary: A theoretical framework is proposed to engineer both first and second-order topological superconducting phases in a two-dimensional (2D) heterostructure, consisting of a quantum spin Hall insulator (QSHI) and an unconventional $p$-wave magnet in presence of proximity-induced $s$-wave superconducting pairing. Our analysis establishes that the transitions between the trivial and topological superconducting (TSC) phases can be regulated though the parameters of $p$-wave magnet. Presence of chiral symmetry leads to the characterization of both types of TSC phases by the respective invariants, one-dimensional winding number and quadrupolar winding number. These results are supplemented by an analytical effective low-energy edge theory that yields a deeper insight into the emergence of the different topological phases of the system. Bulk pairing analysis reveals the competition between the effective $(p_x+p_y)$ and $(p_x+ip_y)$ type pairings that are governed by the intrinsic spin-orbit coupling inherited to the QSHI and spin-split bands of the $p$-wave magnet, respectively.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a theoretical framework for engineering both first and second-order topological superconducting phases in a 2D heterostructure combining a quantum spin Hall insulator with a p-wave magnet under proximity-induced s-wave superconductivity, characterized by winding numbers and supported by an effective edge theory.
AI.motivation: To establish a theoretical basis for realizing and controlling both first and second-order topological superconducting phases in a tunable 2D heterostructure, with phase transitions regulated by p-wave magnet parameters.
AI.method: The framework uses a 2D heterostructure of a quantum spin Hall insulator and a p-wave magnet with proximity-induced s-wave pairing. Topological characterization employs one-dimensional and quadrupolar winding numbers under chiral symmetry, supplemented by an analytical effective low-energy edge theory and bulk pairing analysis examining competition between (p_x+p_y) and (p_x+ip_y) type pairings.
AI.result: The analysis shows transitions between trivial and topological superconducting phases can be regulated via p-wave magnet parameters, with both TSC phases characterized by distinct topological invariants. The effective edge theory provides insight into emergent topological phases, and bulk pairing reveals competition between pairing types governed by spin-orbit coupling and spin-split bands.
AI.conclusion: The proposed heterostructure offers a controllable platform for engineering higher-order topological superconductivity, with phase transitions tunable through p-wave magnet parameters and clear topological invariants distinguishing the phases.

title: Equivalence classes of finite-time transitions in optimal control and non-equilibrium relaxation
summary: We present a theory for the optimal control of stochastic systems in structured environments, represented by penalty terms in the cost functional. We show that such control problems generically feature sharp finite-time transitions associated with a qualitative change in the control strategy at a critical time. Starting from an overdamped Langevin equation and a quadratic cost functional, we show that all resulting problems fall into three canonical equivalence classes (parabolic, hyperbolic, and elliptic), distinguished by the sign of the determinant of the control Hamiltonian. For each class, we obtain the optimal protocol, the cost function, and the critical time in closed form, and show that the transition exhibits features of a continuous phase transition at mean-field level. We then establish a mapping between the optimal control cost and the large-deviation rate function governing non-equilibrium relaxation after a potential quench. The mapping covers the parabolic and hyperbolic classes, while the elliptic class has no simple relaxation counterpart. This correspondence implies that recently discovered finite-time dynamical phase transitions, which are exponentially costly to sample directly, are accessible through ordinary averages over optimally controlled trajectories. To validate our theoretical findings, we report three experiments with optically trapped colloidal particles: a control transition for the mean stochastic work, and the finite-time dynamical phase transitions in free diffusion and in harmonic relaxation.

All problems fall into three canonical equivalence classes (parabolic, hyperbolic, elliptic) distinguished by the sign of the control Hamiltonian determinant. Exact closed-form solutions for the optimal protocol, cost function, and critical time are derived for each class, with the transition resembling a continuous phase transition at mean-field level. The authors establish a mapping between optimal control cost and large-deviation rate functions for non-equilibrium relaxation (covering parabolic and hyperbolic classes), implying finite-time dynamical phase transitions are accessible through ordinary averages over optimally controlled trajectories. Three experiments with optically trapped colloidal particles validate the findings.
AI.motivation: To develop a unified theoretical framework for optimal control of stochastic systems in structured environments, and to reveal that such control problems generically feature finite-time dynamical phase transitions that are otherwise exponentially costly to sample directly. The paper also aims to establish a bridge between optimal control theory and large-deviation theory for non-equilibrium statistical mechanics.
AI.method: The authors start from an overdamped Langevin equation with a quadratic cost functional and classify all resulting control problems into three canonical equivalence classes based on the sign of the determinant of the control Hamiltonian (parabolic, hyperbolic, elliptic). For each class, they solve for the optimal protocol, cost function, and critical time in closed form. They establish a mapping between the optimal control cost and the large-deviation rate function for non-equilibrium relaxation after a potential quench. Experimental validation is performed using three optically trapped colloidal particle experiments: control transition for mean stochastic work, and finite-time dynamical phase transitions in free diffusion and harmonic relaxation.

The transition displays features of continuous phase transitions at mean-field level. A mapping between optimal control cost and large-deviation rate functions covers the parabolic and hyperbolic classes (but not elliptic), demonstrating that finite-time dynamical phase transitions, previously exponentially costly to sample, are accessible through ordinary averages over optimally controlled trajectories. The elliptic class, lacking a simple relaxation counterpart, indicates boundaries to this correspondence.

title: Ground-State Phase Diagram, Higher-Winding Topology, and Lifshitz Criticality in an Anisotropic Four-Spin XX Chain
summary: We investigate the quantum critical and topological properties of a spin-$1/2$ XX chain with anisotropic four-spin cluster interactions in a transverse magnetic field. The interplay of exchange anisotropy, cluster interactions, and the external field produces a rich phase diagram with multiple gapped topological phases and distinct quantum critical boundaries. We identify several Lifshitz-type transitions arising from reconstructions of the low-energy Fermi-point structure, including an unconventional multicritical point where distinct critical branches intersect and the momentum-space topology undergoes a singular reorganization. In the isotropic limit, a conventional Lifshitz transition emerges through the merging and annihilation of Fermi points, revealing distinct mechanisms of Fermi-point reconstruction within the same model. The gapped phases are characterized by quantized winding numbers $ν=0,\pm1,-2,$ and $\pm3$, with the higher-winding phases induced by the extended cluster interactions. The $ν=\pm3$ phases exhibit a richer topological structure than conventional short-range Kitaev-type chains and are separated from other sectors by field- and interaction-driven gap closings. These topological distinctions are further reflected in characteristic degeneracy patterns of the lowest levels of the bulk entanglement spectrum. Our results demonstrate that anisotropic multispin interactions provide a versatile route to realizing higher-winding topological phases and unconventional multicriticality in one-dimensional quantum systems.

AI.tldr: This paper studies a spin-1/2 XX chain with anisotropic four-spin cluster interactions in a transverse magnetic field, revealing a rich phase diagram with multiple gapped topological phases (winding numbers ν=0, ±1, -2, ±3), Lifshitz-type transitions, and an unconventional multicritical point. Higher-winding topological phases arise from extended cluster interactions and are distinguished by entanglement spectrum degeneracy patterns.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to understand how anisotropic multispin (cluster) interactions combined with exchange anisotropy and an external field can generate higher-winding topological phases and unconventional multicriticality in one-dimensional quantum spin systems, extending beyond conventional short-range Kitaev-type chains.
AI.method: The study analyzes a spin-1/2 XX chain with anisotropic four-spin cluster interactions in a transverse field. The authors examine low-energy Fermi-point structure reconstructions to identify Lifshitz-type transitions, compute quantized winding numbers to classify gapped topological phases, and analyze the bulk entanglement spectrum degeneracy patterns of the lowest levels to characterize topological distinctions.
AI.result: The model exhibits multiple gapped topological phases with winding numbers ν=0, ±1, -2, and ±3, where the ±3 phases are richer than conventional short-range Kitaev chains. Several Lifshitz transitions arise from Fermi-point reconstructions, including an unconventional multicritical point with singular reorganization of momentum-space topology. In the isotropic limit, a conventional Lifshitz transition occurs via merging and annihilation of Fermi points.

title: Orbital-Free DFT-Assisted Machine-Learned Molecular Dynamics for Electric-Field-Driven Ionic Transport
summary:
We propose an orbital-free density functional theory (OFDFT)-assisted machine-learned molecular dynamics method in which field-independent interatomic forces are evaluated using a machine-learned potential and atomic charges that depend on the local environment are obtained from OFDFT calculations. The atomic charges obtained by Bader partitioning of the OFDFT electron density are multiplied by the electric-field vector and added to the forces from the machine-learned potential. This approach enables molecular dynamics simulations under an electric field at a lower computational cost than Kohn-Sham DFT (KSDFT)-based molecular dynamics.
  As a proof of concept, the method was applied to beta-Li3PS4 bulk and an S8/Li3PS4 heterostructure under periodic boundary conditions. For Li3PS4 bulk, OFDFT yielded Li charges and a total charge of the PS4 unit consistent with those obtained using KSDFT. In the heterostructure, Li ions migrated from the Li3PS4 region into the S-rich region within a simulation time of approximately 170 ps. Accompanying this migration, the mean Bader charge of the S atoms that initially formed S8 rings changed from nearly neutral to negative. A comparison with KSDFT for a representative interfacial structure also confirmed that the negative charging of the S atoms upon the arrival of Li and the magnitude of the Li charges were qualitatively reproduced. These results demonstrate the possibility of treating field-driven ionic transport and changes in interfacial charge states using a universal machine-learned potential without training an additional material-specific charge-prediction model.

AI.tldr: The authors propose an orbital-free DFT (OFDFT)-assisted machine-learned molecular dynamics method that combines field-independent interatomic forces from a machine-learned potential with environment-dependent atomic charges derived from OFDFT via Bader partitioning, enabling low-cost electric-field MD simulations without KSDFT. Validated on beta-Li3PS4 and S8/Li3PS4 heterostructure, it reproduces Li migration into S-rich regions and corresponding negative charging of S atoms.
AI.motivation: To enable molecular dynamics simulations under electric fields at a lower computational cost than Kohn-Sham DFT-based methods, while avoiding the need to train material-specific charge-prediction models.
AI.method: Field-independent interatomic forces are computed using a machine-learned potential, while local-environment-dependent atomic charges are obtained by Bader partitioning of OFDFT electron densities; the charge times the electric-field vector is added to the ML potential forces.
AI.result: For Li3PS4 bulk, OFDFT charges match KSDFT. In the S8/Li3PS4 heterostructure, Li ions migrated into the S-rich region within ~170 ps, and S atoms initially forming S8 rings became negatively charged, consistent with KSDFT reference results for a representative interfacial structure.
AI.conclusion: The method demonstrates the feasibility of treating field-driven ionic transport and interfacial charge-state changes using a universal machine-learned potential without training an additional material-specific charge-prediction model.

title: Strongly anisotropic non-Kramers electron spin as a quantum coherence probe of angular fluctuations
summary: Strongly anisotropic non-Kramers rare-earth ions combine giant longitudinal g-factors with a vanishing transverse component imposed by time-reversal symmetry, a combination that makes their spin transitions exquisitely sensitive to the orientation of the applied magnetic field. We show that this sensitivity carries a dual identity: it is simultaneously an overlooked decoherence channel and the basis for a spin-coherence-based angular probe. Using pulsed electron paramagnetic resonance at X-band, we report the first measurements of the quantum coherence of Tb$^{3+}$ in a native-doped CaWO$_4$ crystal (15 ppb) and map the Hahn-echo coherence time $T_2$ as a function of temperature (2 to 10 K) and resonant field ($10^3$ to $10^4$ G). A parameter-free model combining spin-lattice relaxation, instantaneous diffusion and spectral diffusion from all independently quantified impurities overestimates $T_2$ by an order of magnitude at low temperature and wrongly predicts the field dependence of $T_2$, inconsistent with the observed monotonic decrease of $T_2$ with $B_r$. A two-parameter extension, including dynamical angular fluctuations of the crystal axis, reproduces the full dataset across multiple setups and laboratories. Two controlled experiments nominally identical except for different mechanical configuration of the setup establish the mechanical origin of the dominant contribution. The two-parameter extension corresponds to an angular amplitude noise spectral density of overall order 36 n°/$\sqrt{Hz}$ from global external vibrations (ranging from 10 to 66 n°/$\sqrt{Hz}$ depending on the exact setup mechanical configuration) estimated at $\sim$ 2.5 kHz plus a temperature-dependent contribution assumed to come from local phonon-driven angular jitter. It identifies and highlights a decoherence pathway of practical relevance to any anisotropic solid-state spin system.

AI.tldr: This paper reports the first pulsed EPR coherence measurements of Tb3+ in native-doped CaWO4 and reveals that the strong magnetic anisotropy of non-Kramers ions makes their spin coherence exquisitely sensitive to angular fluctuations of the crystal axis relative to the applied field. A standard decoherence model overestimates T2 by an order of magnitude; a two-parameter extension incorporating dynamical angular jitter (global vibrations at ~2.5 kHz, ~36 n°/√Hz, plus a temperature-dependent phonon-driven term) reproduces all data. This identifies mechanical/angular noise as a previously overlooked decoherence channel relevant to any anisotropic solid-state spin system.
AI.motivation: Non-Kramers rare-earth ions with strong anisotropy have spin transitions that are extremely sensitive to the orientation of the applied magnetic field. The authors aim to investigate whether this sensitivity has a dual role: both as a potential decoherence channel and as the basis for an angular (spin-coherence-based) probe.
AI.method: Pulsed electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) at X-band on Tb3+ in a native-doped CaWO4 crystal (15 ppb). Hahn-echo T2 mapped as a function of temperature (2–10 K) and resonant field (10^3–10^4 G). A parameter-free model (spin-lattice relaxation, instantaneous diffusion, spectral diffusion) was compared to data, then extended by two parameters: global external vibrational angular noise (~36 n°/√Hz at ~2.5 kHz) and a temperature-dependent local phonon-driven angular jitter. Controlled experiments with different mechanical setup configurations were used to test the mechanical origin.
AI.result: The parameter-free model overestimates T2 by an order of magnitude at low temperature and incorrectly predicts its field dependence (data show monotonic decrease of T2 with resonant field). The two-parameter extension reproduces the full dataset across multiple setups and laboratories. Controlled experiments differing only in mechanical configuration establish the mechanical origin of the dominant decoherence contribution.
AI.conclusion: Dynamical angular fluctuations of the crystal axis constitute a significant, previously overlooked decoherence pathway for strongly anisotropic spin systems. This is simultaneously a practical limitation and an exploitable resource, enabling spin-coherence-based angular sensing. The finding generalizes to any anisotropic solid-state spin system relevant to quantum technologies.

title: Universal Driven Critical Dynamics of Entanglement Entropy
summary: The Kibble-Zurek mechanism (KZM) and finite-time scaling (FTS) provide a foundational framework for driven critical dynamics, yet their predictive power has been largely confined to local observables. Here, we establish a universal finite-time scaling theory for the nonequilibrium dynamics of quantum entanglement. Using unbiased quantum Monte Carlo simulations, we investigate the corner entanglement entropy of (2+1)-dimensional interacting Dirac fermions driven from ordered phases toward a quantum critical point. We find that the corner entanglement accurately obeys a universal driven scaling governed by the driving rate and system size, persisting whether the initial ordered state is fully gapped or hosts gapless Goldstone modes. Crucially, this dynamical entanglement exhibits a logarithmic dependence on the driving rate, from which the universal corner coefficient of the underlying conformal field theory can be robustly extracted far from equilibrium. These results generalize the KZM from local observables to the intrinsic nonlocal quantum information measures, offering a practical blueprint for characterizing quantum criticality and entanglement on programmable quantum simulators.

Using quantum Monte Carlo simulations of (2+1)-dimensional interacting Dirac fermions, it shows corner entanglement entropy obeys universal driven scaling with a logarithmic dependence on the driving rate, from which the conformal field theory corner coefficient can be extracted far from equilibrium.
AI.motivation: The Kibble-Zurek mechanism and finite-time scaling have been powerful frameworks for driven critical dynamics, but their predictive power has been limited to local observables. Extending these concepts to nonlocal quantum information measures like entanglement entropy is essential for a complete understanding of driven critical phenomena.
AI.method: The authors employ unbiased quantum Monte Carlo simulations to study the corner entanglement entropy of (2+1)-dimensional interacting Dirac fermions driven from ordered phases toward a quantum critical point. They investigate both gapped ordered states and states hosting gapless Goldstone modes as initial conditions.
AI.result: The corner entanglement entropy obeys a universal driven scaling governed by driving rate and system size, regardless of whether the initial ordered state is fully gapped or hosts gapless Goldstone modes. The dynamical entanglement shows a logarithmic dependence on the driving rate, enabling robust extraction of the universal corner coefficient of the underlying conformal field theory far from equilibrium.
AI.conclusion: These findings generalize the Kibble-Zurek mechanism from local observables to intrinsic nonlocal quantum information measures, providing a practical blueprint for characterizing quantum criticality and entanglement on programmable quantum simulators.

title: SALTED: a symmetry-adapted machine-learning program for predicting electron-densities in molecules and materials
summary: SALTED provides an open-source Python package for machine learning the quantum-mechanical electron density, $n(\mathbf{r})$, in molecular and condensed-phase systems based on input atomic coordinates and species. The program adopts a linear atom-centered decomposition of the electron density, which makes it highly transferable across diverse atomistic configurations sharing similar chemical environments. Because of this representation choice, SALTED is naturally interfaced with state-of-the-art electronic-structure programs based on atomic orbitals, namely CP2K, FHI-aims, and PySCF, from which reference electron-density data can be generated and used to train a model. The learning algorithm is based on a symmetry-adapted extension of Gaussian process regression, making SALTED especially efficient in small-data regimes. Thanks to the implementation of vector-field kernel functions, SALTED can also learn the first-order response of the electron density to applied electric fields, $\partial n(\mathbf{r})/\partial \mathbf{E}$. The application of SALTED within computational workflows has already shown its utility in a wide variety of contexts, including the calculation of polarization vectors and polarizability tensors, the accurate evaluation of Coulomb forces in QM/MM molecular-dynamics simulations, and electronic-structure studies of large-scale 2D materials.

AI.tldr: SALTED is an open-source Python package for machine learning quantum-mechanical electron densities using a linear atom-centered decomposition, interfaced with electronic-structure programs and based on symmetry-adapted Gaussian process regression, capable of learning electron density responses to electric fields.
AI.motivation: To provide a scalable, transferable, and open-source tool for predicting quantum-mechanical electron densities from atomic coordinates and species, bridging machine learning with electronic-structure methods while enabling efficient small-data learning and electric-field response prediction.
AI.method: Adopts a linear atom-centered decomposition of the electron density for transferability across chemical environments; interfaces with atomic-orbital-based electronic-structure codes (CP2K, FHI-aims, PySCF); uses a symmetry-adapted extension of Gaussian process regression with vector-field kernel functions to predict density and its first-order response to applied electric fields.
AI.result: Demonstrated utility across applications including polarization vectors, polarizability tensors, Coulomb forces in QM/MM molecular-dynamics simulations, and electronic-structure studies of large-scale 2D materials.
AI.conclusion: SALTED is a broadly applicable machine-learning framework for electron-density prediction with demonstrated value across molecular and condensed-phase systems, small-data regimes, and electric-field response calculations.

title: Extrinsic orbital Edelstein effect from asymmetric scattering
comment: 19 pages, 4 figures. We invite comments and feedback
summary: The generation and manipulation of orbital angular momentum (OAM) by an external electric field constitute one of the central themes of orbitronics. In particular, the electrically induced nonequilibrium OAM polarization, known as the orbital Edelstein effect (OEE), has attracted considerable attention in recent years. While the intrinsic band-geometric mechanism and the role of conventional symmetric impurity scattering in the OEE are well understood, the contribution from disorder-induced asymmetric scattering remains unclear. Here, we develop a semiclassical theory that separates the OEE into intrinsic, Drude, side-jump, and third- and fourth-order skew-scattering channels. Unlike the Drude channel, the intrinsic, side-jump, and skew-scattering responses survive only in systems with broken time-reversal symmetry. We find that in a magnetized Rashba two-dimensional electron gas (2DEG), these disorder-induced mechanisms can substantially exceed the intrinsic contribution. Remarkably, we find that for a system with Rashba coupling of $1$ $eV Å$, the orbital magnetization is about one order of magnitude larger than the spin magnetization for the chosen parameters, highlighting the crucial role of orbital degrees of freedom in the Edelstein effect.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a semiclassical theory of the orbital Edelstein effect (OEE) that decomposes it into intrinsic, Drude, side-jump, and skew-scattering contributions, revealing that disorder-induced asymmetric scattering mechanisms can substantially exceed the intrinsic contribution in a magnetized Rashba 2DEG, with orbital magnetization an order of magnitude larger than spin magnetization.
AI.motivation: While the intrinsic band-geometric mechanism and symmetric impurity scattering contributions to the orbital Edelstein effect are well understood, the role of disorder-induced asymmetric scattering (i.e., skew scattering) in the OEE remains unclear. This gap motivates the development of a theory that systematically separates and quantifies all scattering-related contributions.
AI.method: The authors develop a semiclassical theory that decomposes the orbital Edelstein effect into intrinsic, Drude, side-jump, and third- and fourth-order skew-scattering channels. The theory is applied to a magnetized Rashba two-dimensional electron gas (2DEG) to evaluate the relative magnitudes of these contributions.
AI.result: The intrinsic, side-jump, and skew-scattering responses survive only in systems with broken time-reversal symmetry, unlike the Drude channel. In a magnetized Rashba 2DEG, disorder-induced mechanisms can substantially exceed the intrinsic contribution. For Rashba coupling of 1 eV Å, the orbital magnetization is about one order of magnitude larger than the spin magnetization for the chosen parameters.
AI.conclusion: Disorder-induced asymmetric scattering mechanisms play a crucial role in the orbital Edelstein effect, potentially dominating over the intrinsic contribution. The large orbital-to-spin magnetization ratio highlights the central importance of orbital degrees of freedom in the Edelstein effect in strongly spin-orbit coupled systems.

title: Thermodynamic Concentration Inequalities: Controlling Uncertainty in Finite-Time and Small-Sample Thermodynamic Inference
summary: We derive nonasymptotic upper bounds on the probability that a generalized current of a geometrically ergodic diffusion observed for any amount of time, or its sample mean over any arbitrary sample size, deviates from the stationary mean by more than any given amount. The concentration-of-measure behavior of generalized currents is universally governed by the relaxation time of the underlying dynamics, the locally observed dissipation rate, and the intrinsic local fluctuations of the observable. We uncover stark qualitative and quantitative differences in fluctuations in and out of thermodynamic equilibrium. We further obtain refined inverse thermodynamic uncertainty relations, bounding the variance of generalized currents from above. We construct nonasymptotic confidence intervals for controlling uncertainty in thermodynamic inference from small data, i.e., from short trajectories and small samples, and provide the first quantitative answer to when a trajectory is sufficiently long and a sample is sufficiently large. As an illustration, we apply our results to currents observed on a two-dimensional Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process in and out of equilibrium and show how they can be used to rigorously detect broken detailed balance.

AI.tldr: The paper derives nonasymptotic concentration bounds for generalized currents of geometrically ergodic diffusions, showing that fluctuation behavior is governed by relaxation time, local dissipation rate, and intrinsic local fluctuations. It reveals qualitative and quantitative differences between equilibrium and non-equilibrium fluctuations, establishes refined inverse thermodynamic uncertainty relations, constructs nonasymptotic confidence intervals for thermodynamic inference from small data, and demonstrates applications on an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process including detecting broken detailed balance.
AI.motivation: To provide quantitative guarantees for thermodynamic inference from small datasets (short trajectories and small samples), addressing the gap of when data is "sufficiently long" or "sufficiently large" for reliable inference in stochastic thermodynamics.
AI.method: The authors derive nonasymptotic concentration inequalities for generalized currents of geometrically ergodic diffusions. They obtain upper bounds on deviation probabilities involving the relaxation time of the dynamics, the locally observed dissipation rate, and intrinsic local fluctuations of the observable. They also derive refined inverse thermodynamic uncertainty relations bounding current variances and construct explicit nonasymptotic confidence intervals.
AI.result: Universal concentration bounds for generalized currents parametrized by relaxation time, dissipation rate, and local fluctuation scales; stark differences identified between equilibrium and non-equilibrium fluctuation behaviors; refined inverse thermodynamic uncertainty relations; and first quantitative criteria for determining sufficient trajectory length and sample size. Applications demonstrate rigorous detection of broken detailed balance on a 2D Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides rigorous, finite-time guarantees for thermodynamic inference, establishing quantitative answers to data sufficiency questions and enabling accurate uncertainty control from small experimental or simulation datasets, with potential for detecting nonequilibrium signatures.

title: Evolution of electron spin resonance through a metallic quantum critical phase diagram
comment: accepted for Physical Review Letters, Editors Suggestion, 7 pages, 9 pages Supplementary Material, 4+7 figures
summary: In the heavy-fermion metal YbRh2Si2, quantum criticality at a suppressed antiferromagnetic order is governed by the interplay of local magnetic moments and itinerant conduction electrons. We demonstrate how this can be investigated by a new experimental approach that enables the observation of electron spin resonance (ESR) across a broad range of frequencies and fields at very low temperatures. This allowed us to cover a large part of the phase diagram from the paramagnetic Fermi-liquid phase to the phase with antiferromagnetic order and including the quantum-critical regime. Both the ESR g-factor and the linewidth present distinct behaviors in these three regimes, providing further insight into the physics across a quantum critical point. Notably, when cooling down at a field directly towards the quantum critical point, both g-factor and linewidth continuously decrease. Furthermore, we observe a very good matching of the g-factor behavior upon field-tuning and temperature-tuning towards the quantum-critical point. We analyze and discuss the results in the context of present theories on ESR in strongly correlated electron systems.

AI.tldr: This paper reports a new low-temperature, broad-frequency/field electron spin resonance (ESR) experimental approach applied to the heavy-fermion metal YbRh2Si2, enabling investigation of the quantum-critical regime at suppressed antiferromagnetic order. Distinct g-factor and linewidth behaviors are observed across the paramagnetic Fermi-liquid, antiferromagnetic, and quantum-critical phases, revealing universal scaling toward the quantum critical point via both field- and temperature-tuning.
AI.motivation: To understand the physics of quantum criticality in YbRh2Si2—specifically the interplay between local magnetic moments and itinerant conduction electrons—by overcoming prior experimental limitations in observing ESR across a broad range of frequencies and fields at very low temperatures.
AI.method: A novel experimental setup enables ESR measurements over a broad frequency and field range at very low temperatures, allowing coverage of a large portion of the phase diagram including the paramagnetic Fermi-liquid regime, antiferromagnetic-ordered phase, and quantum-critical regime. The g-factor and linewidth are tracked as functions of field and temperature tuning toward the quantum critical point.
AI.result: Both the ESR g-factor and linewidth exhibit distinct behaviors in the three regimes (paramagnetic Fermi liquid, antiferromagnetic order, and quantum critical). Cooling toward the quantum critical point causes both g-factor and linewidth to continuously decrease, and field-tuning strongly matches temperature-tuning behavior of the g-factor toward the quantum critical point.
AI.conclusion: The findings provide new insight into physics across a quantum critical point in a heavy-fermion system and are analyzed within the framework of current theories on ESR in strongly correlated electron systems.

title: High-Throughput Computational Discovery of Inverted Resistive Switching in Two-Dimensional Materials
summary: Atomristors, non-volatile resistive switching devices based on two-dimensional (2D) monolayers, are promising building blocks for energy-efficient memory and neuromorphic computing. However, their design remains restricted to a few materials such as MoS2 and h-BN, limiting functional diversity and design flexibility. Here, a high-throughput computational framework combining density functional theory, machine-learning molecular dynamics, and quantum transport simulations screens about 2,900 exfoliable monolayers for vacancy-mediated resistive switching, identifying 17 thermally stable candidates in two mechanistically distinct classes. In Class 1 monolayers, such as GaS, Au adsorption at the native vacancy introduces conducting states, switching the insulating monolayer from a high- to a low-resistance state (HRS-to-LRS). Class 2 monolayers, comprising ionically bonded metal oxyhalides and nitrohalides such as BiOCl, exhibit previously unreported inverted switching. Vacancy-released electrons delocalize and push the Fermi level into the conduction band, placing the device natively in the LRS; Au adsorption re-localizes these carriers and returns the Fermi level to the gap, driving LRS-to-HRS switching. Quantum transport simulations confirm both mechanisms, while migration-barrier calculations identify the electrode-2D separation as a key parameter governing Au migration and the resistance window. These findings expand the atomristor landscape and establish complementary switching as a design paradigm for multifunctional memory and neuromorphic hardware.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a high-throughput computational framework combining DFT, machine-learning molecular dynamics, and quantum transport simulations to screen ~2,900 exfoliable 2D monolayers for vacancy-mediated resistive switching, identifying 17 thermally stable atomristor candidates in two mechanistic classes. Class 1 (e.g., GaS) switches HRS-to-LRS via Au adsorption-induced conducting states, while Class 2 (e.g., BiOCl) exhibits novel inverted LRS-to-HRS switching due to vacancy-released delocalized electrons that are re-localized by Au adsorption.
AI.motivation: Current atomristor design is limited to a few materials like MoS2 and h-BN, restricting functional diversity and design flexibility. A broader search for new resistive switching materials is needed to realize the potential of 2D monolayers for energy-efficient memory and neuromorphic computing.
AI.method: The authors developed a high-throughput computational screening pipeline combining density functional theory (DFT), machine-learning molecular dynamics, and quantum transport simulations to evaluate ~2,900 exfoliable monolayers. They identified vacancy-mediated resistive switching candidates, characterized two mechanism classes via electronic structure analysis, and computed migration barriers to assess Au dynamics and resistance windows.
AI.result: The screening identified 17 thermally stable candidates in two mechanistically distinct classes. Class 1 includes GaS, where Au adsorption introduces conducting states (HRS-to-LRS). Class 2 includes ionically bonded metal oxyhalides/nitrohalides like BiOCl, exhibiting previously unreported inverted switching (LRS-to-HRS) driven by vacancy-released electron delocalization and Au-mediated re-localization. Electrode-2D separation was identified as the key parameter controlling Au migration and resistance window.
AI.conclusion: These findings dramatically expand the atomristor material landscape beyond MoS2 and h-BN and establish complementary switching (forward and inverted) as a new design paradigm for multifunctional memory and neuromorphic hardware.

title: Hydrodynamics of two-dimensional electrons due to scattering by disorder
summary: The hydrodynamic regime of electron transport, induced by fast inter-electron collisions, was discovered in high-quality nanostructures in recent ten years. However, signs of hydrodynamic transport, primarily, the giant negative magnetoresistance, were observed even at very low temperatures, when electron-electron scattering is too weak to affect the transport. To address this puzzle, here we develop a theory of mixed, hydrodynamic and non-Markovian, magnetotransport of two-dimensional electrons at zero temperature in samples with weak but still important disorder. Namely, we account for both the memory effects at electron scattering by localized defects in magnetic field and an unconventional viscosity effect due to electron scattering by defects in bulk and by rough sample edges. Solution of the model yields a strong negative magnetoresistance, which exhibits at zero magnetic field a sharp maximum in narrower samples or a blunt maximum in wider samples. This and other our results explain various properties of the giant negative magnetoresistance observed on ultra-high-quality GaAs quantum wells, thereby we apparently reveal the nature of low-temperature magnetotransport in these systems.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a theory of mixed hydrodynamic and non-Markovian magnetotransport for two-dimensional electrons at zero temperature, explaining the giant negative magnetoresistance observed in ultra-high-quality GaAs quantum wells at very low temperatures where electron-electron scattering is too weak to drive conventional hydrodynamics.
AI.motivation: The puzzle is that giant negative magnetoresistance—a hallmark of hydrodynamic transport—is observed at very low temperatures where electron-electron scattering is too weak to establish hydrodynamics. This discrepancy needs theoretical explanation.
AI.method: The theory accounts for both memory (non-Markovian) effects in electron scattering by localized defects in a magnetic field and unconventional viscosity effects arising from electron scattering by bulk defects and rough sample edges, within a model of two-dimensional electrons at zero temperature in samples with weak but non-negligible disorder.
AI.result: The model yields a strong negative magnetoresistance showing a sharp maximum at zero magnetic field in narrower samples or a blunt maximum in wider samples. These results explain various properties of the giant negative magnetoresistance observed in ultra-high-quality GaAs quantum wells.
AI.conclusion: The nature of low-temperature magnetotransport in these ultra-high-quality systems is apparently revealed: the giant negative magnetoresistance originates from a combination of memory effects and unconventional viscosity, rather than solely from conventional hydrodynamic electron-electron scattering.

title: HyperDet Wavefunction: A Phase-Agnostic Ansatz for Strongly Correlated Systems
summary: Describing competing phases of strongly correlated systems often requires trial wave functions built from phase-specific assumptions. We propose the \emph{hyperdeterminant (HyperDet) wavefunction} as a phase-agnostic ansatz for both bosonic and fermionic quantum many-body systems exhibiting spontaneous symmetry-breaking order, fractionalization, and/or topological order with anyonic excitations. The HyperDet structure emerges naturally by fusing auxiliary fermionic parton Slater determinants into physical orbitals through a fully learnable \emph{fusion tensor} $\mathcal F$. Optimized using variational Monte Carlo, a single HyperDet architecture can achieve exceptionally high overlaps $\geq 99.9\%$ with exact-diagonalization ground states throughout the entire fractional Chern insulator phase in both bosonic and fermionic models, and across their nearby competing phases. We introduce the singular-value spectrum of the \emph{bipartite fusion matrix} as a structural diagnostic of fusion tensor, and find that its redistribution tracks many-body phase transitions without computing phase-specific observables. The optimized fusion tensor also encodes the parton-level topological data: it reproduces the parton Chern numbers expected for the bosonic and fermionic FCI states, completing their field-theory descriptions and the resulting topological order. Its intrinsic gauge structure further determines whether physical symmetries admit virtual lifts and, when faithful lifts exist, extracts their projective class; for the bosonic FCI, this recovers the expected parton translation fractionalization. We thus anticipate the HyperDet wavefunction to be a promising variational platform for both accurate ground-state searches and phase-diagram explorations across strongly correlated phases, and for providing interpretable theoretical insights from parton-level microscopics to field-theory descriptions.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the hyperdeterminant (HyperDet) wavefunction, a phase-agnostic variational ansatz for strongly correlated quantum many-body systems. Built by fusing auxiliary fermionic parton Slater determinants into physical orbitals via a learnable fusion tensor, it achieves ≥99.9% overlaps with exact ground states across fractional Chern insulator phases in both bosonic and fermionic models, and its internal structure (singular-value spectrum and fusion tensor) provides interpretable diagnostics of phase transitions, topological data (parton Chern numbers), and projective symmetry classes.
AI.motivation: Conventional trial wave functions for strongly correlated systems rely on phase-specific assumptions, limiting their utility when exploring unknown or competing phases. A phase-agnostic ansatz is needed that can uniformly describe symmetry-breaking, fractionalized, and topological phases while remaining computationally tractable and interpretable.
AI.method: The authors construct the HyperDet wavefunction by fusing multiple auxiliary fermionic parton Slater determinants into physical orbitals through a fully learnable fusion tensor F. The ansatz is optimized with variational Monte Carlo. They introduce the singular-value spectrum of the bipartite fusion matrix as a structural diagnostic of the tensor, and analyze the gauge structure and the fusion tensor to extract parton Chern numbers, virtual lifts of physical symmetries, and projective classes.
AI.result: A single HyperDet architecture achieves exceptionally high overlaps (≥99.9%) with exact-diagonalization ground states across the entire fractional Chern insulator phase in both bosonic and fermionic models, and across nearby competing phases. The redistribution of the bipartite fusion matrix singular-value spectrum tracks many-body phase transitions without phase-specific observables. The optimized fusion tensor reproduces the expected parton Chern numbers and the parton translation fractionalization for the bosonic FCI, completing the field-theory description and topological order.
AI.conclusion: The HyperDet wavefunction offers a promising unified variational platform for accurate ground-state searches and phase-diagram exploration across strongly correlated phases, while providing interpretable theoretical insights linking parton-level microscopics to field-theory descriptions.

title: Gd-4f Exchange Splitting and Mo-4d Crystal-Field Redistribution in Gd/W Co-doped La2Mo2O9: A DFT+U Study
comment: Conference: International Conference on Advanced Functional Materials and Devices (AFMD-2026)
summary: La2Mo2O9 (LAMOX) is a promising oxide-ion conductor for intermediate-temperature solid oxide fuel cells, but its practical application is limited by a first-order monoclinic-to-cubic (alpha to beta) phase transition. Here, we investigate the electronic structure of pristine La2Mo2O9 and the Gd/W co-doped composition La1.6Gd0.4Mo1.7W0.3O9 using spin-polarized density functional theory with an on-site Hubbard correction for the localized Gd-4f states. The projected density of states reveals that pristine La2Mo2O9 is an O-2p/Mo-4d charge-transfer oxide in which La contributes negligibly near the band edges. Gd/W co-doping introduces a strongly exchange-split Gd-4f manifold with a majority-minority separation of approximately 1011 eV, substantially redistributes the Mo-4d electronic states through a threefold increase in crystal-field splitting, and reduces the O-2p contribution near the valence-band maximum from 78% to 66%. These electronic signatures are consistent with the experimentally observed lattice contraction, MoO Raman-mode softening, and the non-monotonic evolution of oxide-ion conductivity across the co-doped series. In particular, the pronounced crystal-field splitting and localized Gd magnetism at the highest doping level provide a microscopic electronic explanation for the observed suppression of ionic conductivity. The present results establish an atomistic electronic-structure framework for understanding dopant-induced phase stabilization and oxide- ion transport in Gd/W co-doped LAMOX electrolytes, providing design principles for improved solid oxide fuel cell materials.

AI.tldr: DFT+U study reveals that Gd/W co-doping in La2Mo2O9 introduces exchange-split Gd-4f states, triples Mo-4d crystal-field splitting, and reduces O-2p character at the valence-band maximum, providing an electronic explanation for lattice contraction, Raman mode softening, and suppressed oxide-ion conductivity at high doping levels.
AI.motivation: La2Mo2O9 is a promising oxide-ion conductor but its practical use in intermediate-temperature SOFCs is hindered by an alpha-to-beta phase transition. Understanding the electronic-structure origins of dopant-induced phase stabilization and ionic transport is needed to engineer improved materials.
AI.method: Spin-polarized density functional theory with an on-site Hubbard correction (DFT+U) was applied to pristine La2Mo2O9 and Gd/W co-doped La1.6Gd0.4Mo1.7W0.3O9, analyzing projected densities of states, crystal-field splitting, exchange splitting, and orbital contributions near band edges.
AI.result: Pristine La2Mo2O9 is an O-2p/Mo-4d charge-transfer oxide with negligible La contribution at band edges. Gd/W co-doping creates a strongly exchange-split Gd-4f manifold (~10-11 eV separation), triples the Mo-4d crystal-field splitting, and reduces O-2p contribution at the VBM from 78% to 66%. These signatures align with measured lattice contraction, MoO Raman softening, and non-monotonic conductivity behavior.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes an atomistic electronic-structure framework linking dopant-induced electronic redistribution to phase stabilization and oxide-ion transport in Gd/W co-doped LAMOX, offering design principles for improved SOFC electrolyte materials.

title: Non-uniform quantum geometry stabilizes generalized Wigner crystals
summary: Moiré materials host fractional Chern insulators and electron crystals in close proximity, but the mechanism selecting between them remains an open question. We address this competition in Chern bands with ideal but momentum-dependent quantum geometry -- Aharonov-Casher bands. We present an ansatz wave function for generalized Wigner crystals and, by comparing its energy to that of the competing Laughlin-like state, map out the phase diagram at filling fraction $ν=1/m$ as a function of the degree of geometric non-uniformity. Our work identifies quantum geometry-controlled zero point fluctuations of the charge density of the generalized Wigner crystal as the mechanism controlling its relative stability, implying a kind of quantum Lindemann criterion for the crystal-liquid phase boundary.

AI.tldr: The paper studies the competition between fractional Chern insulators (Laughlin-like states) and generalized Wigner crystals in Chern bands with ideal but momentum-dependent quantum geometry (Aharonov-Casher bands). Using an ansatz wave function for generalized Wigner crystals and comparing energies with competing Laughlin-like states, they map a phase diagram at filling ν=1/m as a function of geometric non-uniformity, identifying quantum geometry-controlled zero-point fluctuations of charge density as the mechanism governing crystal stability, implying a quantum Lindemann criterion.
AI.motivation: Moiré materials host both fractional Chern insulators and electron crystals in close proximity, but the mechanism that selects between these competing phases remains an open question. Understanding this competition is crucial for predicting and engineering quantum phases in moiré systems.
AI.method: The authors introduce an ansatz wave function for generalized Wigner crystals in Aharonov-Casher bands—Chern bands with ideal but momentum-dependent quantum geometry. They compare the energy of this crystal state to that of the competing Laughlin-like fractional Chern insulator state to map out the phase diagram at filling fraction ν=1/m as a function of the degree of geometric non-uniformity.
AI.result: The phase diagram at ν=1/m as a function of geometric non-uniformity reveals that quantum geometry-controlled zero-point fluctuations of the charge density of the generalized Wigner crystal control its relative stability versus the Laughlin-like state.
AI.conclusion: The work identifies a kind of quantum Lindemann criterion for the crystal-liquid phase boundary in these systems, where the stability of the generalized Wigner crystal is governed by quantum geometry-driven zero-point charge density fluctuations rather than purely energetic considerations.

title: Multimodal and Multiscale Interrogation of a Mechanically Tough Glass Forming Copper-Based Metal-Organic Framework
summary: A copper-based metal-organic framework, Cu(Im)2, was synthesized using a sol-gel process and subsequently melt-quenched into glass upon heating above 240 °C. In this paper, we present a multimodal, multiscale interrogation of the MOF nanocrystals and the resulting glasses. Structural characterization using X-ray diffraction, atomic force microscopy, and electron microscopy was performed to understand the morphology and size of the synthesized nanocrystals and glasses. Thermogravimetric analysis and differential scanning calorimetry were employed to understand the melting process of the crystals to form the glass. Synchrotron pair distribution function analysis was performed to verify that the framework structure is maintained upon melting, and nearfield infrared nanospectroscopy provided insight into the local chemical structure of the materials. The mechanical characterization via nanoindentation revealed that the resulting glasses exhibit an appreciably high elastic modulus (~10 GPa) and the highest fracture toughness (K_1c ~ 0.5 MPa m^1/2) yet reported for MOF glasses. This development is central to the emerging field of MOF-based materials processing and shaping, while upholding mechanical robustness and resistance to cracking.

AI.tldr: A copper-based metal-organic framework (Cu(Im)2) was synthesized via sol-gel processing and converted into glass by melt-quenching above 240 °C. A multimodal, multiscale characterization approach confirmed framework retention upon melting and revealed that the resulting MOF glasses exhibit ~10 GPa elastic modulus and record fracture toughness (~0.5 MPa·m^1/2) for MOF glasses, highlighting their mechanical robustness for MOF-based materials processing.
AI.motivation: To expand the emerging field of MOF glasses by developing melt-quenchable MOF systems that maintain their framework structure while achieving strong mechanical robustness and crack resistance, enabling new materials processing and shaping capabilities for MOF-based applications.
AI.method: Cu(Im)2 MOF nanocrystals were synthesized via sol-gel processing and melt-quenched into glass above 240 °C. A multimodal, multiscale characterization suite was employed: X-ray diffraction, atomic force microscopy, and electron microscopy for morphology/size; thermogravimetric analysis and differential scanning calorimetry for melting behavior; synchrotron pair distribution function analysis to verify framework retention; nearfield infrared nanospectroscopy for local chemical structure; and nanoindentation for mechanical property assessment.
AI.result: The framework structure is maintained upon melting to form glass. Nanoindentation revealed that the resulting MOF glasses possess an appreciably high elastic modulus (~10 GPa) and the highest fracture toughness (K_1c ~ 0.5 MPa·m^1/2) yet reported for MOF glasses.
AI.conclusion: Cu(Im)2-derived MOF glasses combine preserved framework architecture with outstanding mechanical properties, representing a significant milestone for MOF-based materials processing and shaping while retaining mechanical robustness and resistance to cracking.

title: Ion-Engineered Insulator-to-Semiconductor Transition in Natural 2D Biotite
summary: Naturally occurring layered silicates offer an abundant yet unexplored class of 2D materials, but their insulating nature limits their functional utility. Here, we demonstrate a chemical strategy that transforms liquid-phase-exfoliated biotite nanosheets into a tunable 2D semiconductor through controlled NaOH treatment. The resulting insulator-to-semiconductor transition originates from Na incorporation, defect generation, and local structural reconstruction while largely preserving the layered framework. Structural and chemical analyses reveal lattice distortion, interlayer reorganization, hydroxylation, and partial Na+-K+ exchange, establishing the origin of the electronic restructuring. This transformation broadens the optical response, shifting the approximately 221 nm absorption toward approximately 280 and 975 nm, reducing the optical bandgap from approximately 5.2 to 3.2-3.5 eV, and introducing low-energy transitions at approximately 1.12-1.17 eV. Electrical measurements reveal nonlinear transport with currents reaching close to 10 microA, demonstrating activated carrier conduction. Ultrafast transient absorption reveals pronounced excited-state absorption, with carrier cooling (0.16-0.38 ps) followed by fast (35-60 ps) and long-lived (336-491 ps) relaxation associated with trap-mediated recombination. Fluence-dependent dynamics reveal a hot-phonon bottleneck at elevated carrier densities. Together with density functional theory calculations, these results establish chemical defect and ion engineering as a powerful route for converting naturally abundant layered minerals into electronically tunable 2D materials for emerging optoelectronic and ultrafast photonic technologies.

The authors aim to develop a chemical strategy to convert these abundant insulating minerals into electronically tunable semiconductors.

They employ structural and chemical analyses (to characterize lattice distortion, interlayer reorganization, hydroxylation, and partial Na+-K+ exchange), optical spectroscopy (absorption and bandgap measurements), electrical transport measurements, ultrafast transient absorption spectroscopy (including fluence-dependent studies), and density functional theory (DFT) calculations to understand the insulator-to-semiconductor transition.
