title: Heesch Nodal Lines in Inadmissible Achiral Antiferromagnets
comment: 19 pages, 6 figures, and 4 tables, including Supplementary Information
summary: Recently, a new class of Weyl semimetals in antiferromagnets named Heesch Weyl semimetals was discovered, which have inadmissible chiral magnetic point group symmetries (inadmissible magnetic point groups are incompatible with ferromagnetic order) and distinctive surface Fermi arcs. In Heesch Weyl semimetals, the Weyl points are pinned at high symmetry momenta with two-dimensional irreducible corepresentations in the Brillouin zone. As the Weyl points are pinned, the Weyl points with opposite topological charges cannot emerge or be brought together for creation and annihilation as in conventional Weyl semimetals. In this work, we show that when mirror or rotoinversion symmetries are restored so that the point group becomes achiral, long doubly degenerate lines connecting Weyl points with opposite topological charges emerge. We call these lines the Heesch nodal lines (HNLs) and their host materials the Heesch nodal line antiferromagnets. HNLs result in a large number of two-dimensional massless Dirac cones for planes intercepting the HNLs in the Brillouin zone. Moreover, a large subset of the HNL antiferromagnets has the special property that the lowest nonvanishing order of the nonlinear anomalous Hall effect starts with the third order. First-principles calculations on representative collinear and noncollinear antiferromagnets, such as MnTe, CrSb, and Mn$_3$GaN, confirm our predictions on the presence of HNLs. When the inadmissible symmetry is broken by strain, the double degeneracy of the HNLs is lifted and the associated massless Dirac cones are gapped out, providing a route to realizing sizable anomalous Hall effects in antiferromagnetic crystals. We conclude that all inadmissible antiferromagnets without parity-time symmetry are topological. They are either Heesch Weyl antiferromagnets or Heesch nodal line antiferromagnets.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces "Heesch nodal line antiferromagnets" (HNLs), a new class of topological antiferromagnets arising from Heesch Weyl semimetals when mirror or rotoinversion symmetries restore achirality. HNLs are long doubly degenerate lines connecting Weyl points with opposite topological charges, producing numerous 2D massless Dirac cones. A large subset exhibits third-order nonlinear anomalous Hall effects as the lowest order. First-principles calculations on MnTe, CrSb, and Mn3GaN confirm the predictions, and strain lifting of HNL degeneracy gaps Dirac cones, enabling sizable anomalous Hall effects. The authors conclude that all inadmissible (Heesch) antiferromagnets without parity-time symmetry are topological—either Heesch Weyl or Heesch nodal line antiferromagnets.
AI.motivation: Building on the recent discovery of Heesch Weyl semimetals in antiferromagnets with inadmissible magnetic point groups, the authors seek to explore the topological consequences when additional achiral symmetries (mirror or rotoinversion) are restored, and to unify the classification of topological antiferromagnets.
AI.method: The authors perform symmetry analysis of inadmissible magnetic point groups, identifying conditions under which restoring mirror or rotoinversion symmetries leads to doubly degenerate nodal lines connecting pinned Weyl points of opposite charge (Heesch nodal lines). They analyze the resulting Dirac cone structure and nonlinear anomalous Hall response order, and validate predictions with first-principles calculations on representative collinear and noncollinear antiferromagnets (MnTe, CrSb, Mn3GaN), including strain effects.
AI.result: They establish the existence of Heesch nodal lines connecting Weyl points of opposite topological charges, yielding numerous 2D massless Dirac cones. A large subset of these materials exhibits third-order (rather than lower-order) nonlinear anomalous Hall effects as the lowest nonvanishing order. First-principles results on MnTe, CrSb, and Mn3GaN confirm HNL presence. Breaking the inadmissible symmetry via strain lifts double degeneracy, gaps the Dirac cones, and enables sizable anomalous Hall effects.
AI.conclusion: All inadmissible (Heesch-type) antiferromagnets lacking parity-time symmetry are topological, being either Heesch Weyl antiferromagnets or Heesch nodal line antiferromagnets. This provides a unified picture and offers a strain-tunable route to anomalous Hall effects in antiferromagnetic crystals.

title: Exciton multipolarity controls coherent and squeezed phonons in van der Waals heterostructures
summary: Photoexcitation-driven changes in the electronic distribution displace atoms, generating coherent phonons on ultrafast timescales. Two-dimensional (2D) materials and their heterostructures offer a powerful platform for engineering these phonons. Yet, despite the widespread observation of photoexcited coherent phonons, a design principle for controlling their character remains elusive. Here, using detailed atomistic simulations of multilayers of alternating MoSe$_2$ and WSe$_2$, we reveal exciton multipolarity as a design principle for tuning photoinduced phonons from coherent to squeezed. These phonons are interlayer breathing modes, with dipolar excitons coupling linearly to generate coherent states and quadrupolar excitons coupling quadratically to produce squeezed states. Moreover, an out-of-plane electric field enables switch-like control, converting quadrupolar excitons into dipolar excitons and switching the phonon state from squeezed to coherent. For example, in trilayer WSe$_2$/MoSe$_2$/WSe$_2$, the photoexcited 1.04-THz breathing mode switches from a squeezed state at zero field to a coherent state under an applied vertical field. Experimentally, these phonon states can be directly probed by ultrafast X-ray or electron diffraction and indirectly through transient reflectivity. Our results open new avenues for ultrafast control of lattice and electronic dynamics on picosecond timescales, with implications for THz quantum phononics, nanophotonic technologies, and quantum-noise-limited sensing.

AI.tldr: This paper reveals exciton multipolarity (dipolar vs. quadrupolar) as a design principle for controlling photoinduced coherent phonons in layered 2D materials. Dipolar excitons generate coherent phonon states (linear coupling), while quadrupolar excitons produce squeezed states (quadratic coupling). An applied out-of-plane electric field provides switch-like control, converting quadrupolar excitons to dipolar and switching phonon states from squeezed to coherent, as demonstrated in trilayer WSe2/MoSe2/WSe2.
AI.motivation: Despite widespread observation of photoexcited coherent phonons in 2D materials and heterostructures, no design principle exists for controlling their character (coherent vs. squeezed quantum states). This work aims to establish such a principle.
AI.method: Detailed atomistic simulations of alternating MoSe2/WSe2 multilayer heterostructures, analyzing interlayer breathing modes via exciton-phonon coupling. The approach relates exciton multipole symmetry (dipole vs. quadrupole) to the linear or quadratic coupling that generates coherent or squeezed phonon states, and tests field-induced switching via an out-of-plane electric field.
AI.result: Excitonic multipolarity controls phonon character: dipolar excitons linearly couple to generate coherent phonon states, whereas quadrupolar excitons couple quadratically to yield squeezed states. In trilayer WSe2/MoSe2/WSe2, the 1.04-THz interlayer breathing mode switches from squeezed (zero field) to coherent under a vertical electric field. Phonon states are predicted to be observable via ultrafast X-ray/electron diffraction or transient reflectivity.
AI.conclusion: Exciton multipolarity provides a design principle for ultrafast engineering of phonon quantum states in 2D heterostructures, enabling switchable coherent-to-squeezed conversion with implications for THz quantum phononics, nanophotonics, and quantum-noise-limited sensing.

title: Experimentally constrained modeling of the Pockels response of KNbO3 and KTaNbO3
summary: The soft-mode of electro-optic (EO) metal-oxide perovskites plays a critical role in determining their Pockels responses. This is the case of potassium tantalate niobate (KTN), which exhibits an intrinsic Pockels response 2.5 times larger than that of state-of-the-art barium titanate (BTO), highlighting its potential for high-performance EO applications. By combining ab initio calculations at the density-functional theory level and far-IR measurements, we reveal that the harmonic approximation combined with semi-local exchange-correlation functionals fails to accurately capture the soft transverse optical (TO) Slater mode of both potassium niobate and KTN, which dominates the technologically relevant r51 Pockels coefficient. Replacing the calculated mode frequency with its measured value provides an experimentally constrained approach that substantially improves the predicted Pockels response. For that purpose, the previously unreported TO Slater-mode frequency of KTN is extracted from far-IR reflectivity measurements. The results emphasize the potential of KTN-based EO modulators as an alternative to standard lithium niobate and BTO technologies, with a potentially lower energy consumption and device footprint.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates the soft transverse optical (TO) Slater mode in potassium tantalate niobate (KTN) and potassium niobate, showing that standard DFT harmonic approximations with semi-local functionals fail to accurately capture this mode, which dominates the r51 Pockels coefficient. By constraining theory with experimentally measured TO Slater-mode frequencies (newly extracted from far-IR reflectivity for KTN), the predicted Pockels response improves substantially, highlighting KTN's intrinsic Pockels response as 2.5× larger than BTO.
AI.motivation: To accurately predict and understand the Pockels electro-optic response of KTN, whose soft TO Slater mode dominates the r51 coefficient, given that standard DFT calculations fail to capture this critical mode. This is motivated by KTN's potential as a superior alternative to BTO and lithium niobate for EO modulators with lower energy consumption and footprint.
AI.method: The authors combine (1) ab initio DFT calculations with semi-local exchange-correlation functionals under the harmonic approximation to compute TO Slater-mode frequencies and Pockels coefficients of potassium niobate and KTN, and (2) far-IR reflectivity measurements to experimentally extract the previously unreported TO Slater-mode frequency of KTN. The measured frequency is then substituted into the theoretical framework to provide an experimentally constrained prediction of the Pockels response.
AI.result: The harmonic approximation with semi-local functionals fails to accurately capture the soft TO Slater mode of both potassium niobate and KTN. Replacing the calculated mode frequency with measured far-IR values substantially improves the predicted Pockels response. The intrinsic Pockels response of KTN is found to be 2.5× larger than that of BTO, the current state of the art.
AI.conclusion: KTN-based EO modulators represent a promising alternative to standard lithium niobate and BTO technologies, offering potentially lower energy consumption and smaller device footprint. The experimentally constrained theoretical approach provides a reliable route for predicting Pockels responses in materials where the soft-mode frequency is poorly captured by standard DFT.

title: Hierarchical automation of scanning probe microscopy through agentic orchestration and algorithmic control
summary: Rapid advances in agentic artificial intelligence enable scientific systems to interpret open-ended objectives, combine heterogeneous information, invoke specialized tools, and revise experimental strategies as evidence accumulates. However, physical experimentation also contains many tasks for which agentic reasoning provides little advantage and can reduce reliability. Quantitative analysis, optimization, spatial targeting, validation, and instrument execution are often better posed as deterministic or algorithmic operations with explicit objectives and verifiable outputs. Here, we introduce a hierarchical architecture for autonomous experimentation that separates these roles. Agentic components interpret scientific intent, construct task-dependent experimental representations, evaluate accumulated evidence, and select high-level actions, whereas deterministic algorithms perform numerical analysis, coordinate selection, validation, and physical execution. We implement this architecture in piezoresponse force microscopy. Starting from a broad scientific question concerning the relation between local domain structure and polarization switching, the system constructs spatial descriptors from multichannel imaging, selects and analyzes local hysteresis measurements, adapts the spectroscopy waveform, and terminates the experiment when additional measurements cease to provide new evidence. The autonomous trajectory also identifies a confounding relationship between polarization state and domain-wall proximity and recognizes that the requested contrast is not independently represented within the available field of view. These results demonstrate a route toward scientific autonomy in which agents determine what evidence is required while algorithms determine how that evidence is acquired reproducibly and within validated physical constraints.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a hierarchical architecture for autonomous scientific experimentation that separates agentic reasoning (interpreting intent, evaluating evidence, selecting high-level actions) from deterministic algorithms (analysis, optimization, validation, execution). This is implemented in piezoresponse force microscopy, where the system autonomously investigates the relationship between local domain structure and polarization switching, adapts its spectroscopy waveform, terminates when measurements yield no new evidence, and even identifies confounding relationships and unrecognized requested contrasts within the field of view.
AI.motivation: Physical experimentation contains tasks where agentic reasoning provides little advantage and can reduce reliability. Quantitative analysis, optimization, spatial targeting, validation, and instrument execution are better posed as deterministic/algorithmic operations with explicit objectives and verifiable outputs, motivating a distinction between agentic and algorithmic roles in autonomous laboratories.
AI.method: A hierarchical architecture is proposed that separates agentic components (scientific intent interpretation, task-dependent experimental representation construction, evidence evaluation, high-level action selection) from deterministic algorithms (numerical analysis, coordinate selection, validation, physical execution). The architecture is implemented in piezoresponse force microscopy to automate an investigation linking local domain structure and polarization switching.
AI.result: The autonomous system constructed spatial descriptors from multichannel imaging, selected and analyzed local hysteresis measurements, adapted the spectroscopy waveform, and terminated when additional measurements ceased to provide new evidence. It also discovered a confounding relationship between polarization state and domain-wall proximity, and recognized that the requested contrast was not independently represented in the available field of view.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate a route toward scientific autonomy where agents determine what evidence is required while algorithms determine how that evidence is acquired reproducibly and within validated physical constraints, offering a generalizable design principle for autonomous experimentation systems.

title: Synthesis and Characterization of Compositionally Complex (Gd/Ho/Er/Dy)2Zr2O7 Thin Film Combinatorial Library
summary: High-throughput synthesis and characterization of novel ceramic materials with improved thermomechanical properties and phase stability are needed to accelerate the discovery of next-generation thermal barrier materials. A combinatorial thin film material library of (GdDyHoEr)2Zr2O7 were created via combinatorial magnetron reactive sputtering with rare-earth/zirconium alloy targets. Structural, chemical, and thermal property characterization mapping across the four component composition space was performed and correlated with thermal transport measurements. Steady state thermoreflectance mapping identifies a pronounced minimum in thermal conductivity within the Dy/Gd-rich quadrant. This minimum does not coincide with either the equiatomic composition or the region predicted to exhibit maximum cation size disorder. Instead, it corresponds to the largest experimentally observed lattice parameter, despite deviating from Vegard-like chemical averaging, and is independent of grain size and whole-pattern microstrain. These observations suggest that the way the fluorite lattice accommodates compositional complexity, rather than cation size disorder alone, provides a more informative descriptor of thermal transport. Overall, this work establishes a high-throughput workflow for combinatorial thin-film synthesis and multimodal characterization, enabling the rapid identification of previously inaccessible structure-property relationships in compositionally complex ceramics.

AI.tldr: A combinatorial thin-film library of (GdDyHoEr)2Zr2O7 high-entropy rare-earth zirconates was synthesized and characterized to map thermal conductivity across the four-component composition space. A minimum in thermal conductivity was found in the Dy/Gd-rich quadrant, correlating with the largest lattice parameter rather than maximum cation size disorder or equiatomic composition, suggesting that lattice accommodation of compositional complexity is a better descriptor of thermal transport than cation size disorder alone.
AI.motivation: To accelerate the discovery of next-generation thermal barrier materials by establishing high-throughput workflows that enable rapid identification of structure-property relationships in compositionally complex ceramic systems.
AI.method: Combinatorial magnetron reactive sputtering was used to create a (GdDyHoEr)2Zr2O7 thin-film material library using rare-earth/zirconium alloy targets. Structural, chemical, and thermal property mapping was performed via multimodal characterization, with steady-state thermoreflectance used to map thermal transport across the four-component composition space.
AI.result: A pronounced minimum in thermal conductivity was identified in the Dy/Gd-rich quadrant, which does not coincide with the equiatomic composition or the region of predicted maximum cation size disorder. Instead, it corresponds to the largest experimentally observed lattice parameter, independent of grain size and microstrain.
AI.conclusion: The way the fluorite lattice accommodates compositional complexity—rather than cation size disorder alone—is a more informative descriptor of thermal transport in these ceramics. The established high-throughput combinatorial workflow enables rapid screening and discovery of structure-property relationships in compositionally complex ceramics.

title: Strengthened Silicate Glasses by Residual Stress: Depth of Compression and Surface Flaws Stability Conditions
comment: 35 pages, 15 figures, 6 tables, 27 equations, 1 appndix with 10 equations, 27 references
summary: The application of silicate glasses in severe service environments requires a precise evaluation of structural strength under mechanical loads and surface tribological conditions. Because glass strength is governed by surface flaws and microcracks rather than being an intrinsic material property, residual surface compression fields, balanced by interior tensile zones, are widely implemented to inhibit flaw opening. Rather than relying on conventional allowable stress criteria to establish product acceptance, this study adopts a fracture mechanics framework based on the stress intensity factor KI and fundamental material limits: the critical stress intensity factor KIC for rapid fracture and the threshold stress intensity factor KIth for time-delayed static fatigue failure. Using the Weight Function Method (WFM), KI is evaluated across generic surface flaw depths for two-dimensional continuous (2D-Continuous) surface cracks subjected to non-uniform internal residual stress fields and external loads. Flaw stability criteria are established for both zero-risk and moderate-risk design methodologies. Finally, the interaction and superposition of externally applied mechanical and thermal stresses with internal residual stress fields are evaluated.

AI.tldr: This paper applies a fracture mechanics framework using stress intensity factors (KI, KIC, KIth) and the Weight Function Method to evaluate structural strength of silicate glasses with residual surface compression fields, covering flaw stability, design criteria, and superposition of mechanical/thermal and residual stresses.
AI.motivation: Silicate glasses in severe service environments require precise structural strength evaluation, but glass strength is governed by surface flaws and microcracks rather than intrinsic material properties. Conventional allowable stress criteria are insufficient, so a fracture mechanics-based approach is needed to properly assess flaw behavior under residual stresses and external loads.
AI.method: The study adopts a fracture mechanics framework based on the stress intensity factor KI and material limits (KIC for rapid fracture, KIth for static fatigue). The Weight Function Method (WFM) is used to compute KI across generic surface flaw depths for 2D-continuous surface cracks subjected to non-uniform internal residual stress fields and external loads. Flaw stability criteria are established for both zero-risk and moderate-risk design methodologies, and superposition of mechanical/thermal and residual stresses is evaluated.
AI.result: The paper establishes flaw stability criteria under residual surface compression fields for both zero-risk and moderate-risk design approaches, and clarifies how externally applied mechanical and thermal stresses interact and superpose with internal residual stress fields.
AI.conclusion: A fracture mechanics-based evaluation framework (using KIC and KIth thresholds via WFM) provides a more rigorous alternative to conventional allowable stress criteria for assessing silicate glass strength and product acceptance under residual stresses and combined external loads.
